fullMarks: For bond-formation answers, first name the bond and state what happens to the electrons: transfer, sharing, or donation of a shared pair.
For ionic bonding, show the electron transfer, write each ion with its correct charge, and state that oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically.
For covalent structures, show every shared pair, any lone pairs, and the correct single, double or triple bond. In dot-and-cross diagrams, use different symbols for electrons from different atoms.
For coordinate bonds, show that both bonding electrons come from the donor and draw the arrow towards the acceptor.

For questions about metal properties, link each property to the metallic structure: mobile electrons conduct heat and electricity; strongly held, closely arranged atoms explain hardness; sliding rows explain shaping into wires and sheets.
For comparisons, organise the answer by property—structure, melting and boiling points, solubility, and electrical conductivity—and explain each property using the type and movement of particles.
For a question asking for examples or formulas, write each formula clearly with correct subscripts and ion charges; finish with the requested conclusion, such as the white precipitate formed.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying ionic bonding is just electron transfer. Fix: Explain that transfer forms oppositely charged ions, which are held together by electrostatic attraction.
Mistake: Drawing an ionic compound as a separate pair of atoms. Fix: Show ions with charges; where a lattice is asked for, show a repeating arrangement of oppositely charged ions.
Mistake: Showing only one electron in a double or triple covalent bond. Fix: Show two shared pairs for a double bond and three for a triple bond.
Mistake: Drawing a coordinate-bond arrow in the wrong direction. Fix: Draw it from the electron-pair donor towards the acceptor.

Mistake: Claiming that solid ionic compounds conduct electricity because they contain ions. Fix: State that the ions are fixed in the solid; conduction occurs when ions are free to move in the molten state or solution.
Mistake: Saying metals conduct because their positive ions move through the solid. Fix: Explain that the mobile electrons carry heat and electric charge.
Mistake: Writing HF and HCl have equally strong intermolecular forces. Fix: Explain that hydrogen bonding makes attraction between HF molecules stronger than attraction between HCl molecules.

shortTheory.question: What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?
shortTheory.answer: Metals lose their outer electrons easily, while non-metals gain electrons easily.

shortTheory.question: Give one example of an element which exists as a crystalline solid and has covalent bonds between its atoms.
shortTheory.answer: Diamond is a crystalline solid in which carbon atoms are joined by covalent bonds.

shortTheory.question: Is a coordinate covalent bond a strong bond?
shortTheory.answer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond. After it is formed, it behaves like an ordinary covalent bond.

shortTheory.question: How do metals conduct heat?
shortTheory.answer: Metals conduct heat because they contain freely moving electrons.

shortTheory.question: Why is HF a liquid while HCl is a gas?
shortTheory.answer: Strong intermolecular forces, including hydrogen bonding, act between HF molecules. The intermolecular forces between HCl molecules are weaker, so HF is a liquid while HCl is a gas at room temperature.

shortTheory.question: Why are covalent compounds generally not soluble in water?
shortTheory.answer: Covalent compounds are generally non-polar, whereas water is polar. Therefore, covalent compounds usually do not dissolve in water.

writtenQuestions.text: How would you differentiate between the chemical formula of an element and that of a compound? Give examples.
modelAnswer: An element’s formula represents one kind of atom; for example, Na or O₂.
A compound’s formula represents two or more kinds of atoms or ions in a fixed ratio; for example, H₂O or NaCl.

explain.title: Elements can have different formula forms
explain.body: Some elements are represented by their symbols alone, such as Na, Ca, C and Fe. Other elements exist as molecules, such as O₂, N₂ and H₂. O₃ is ozone: each molecule contains three oxygen atoms.

explain.title: Ionic compounds use formula units
explain.body: In an ionic solid such as sodium chloride, oppositely charged ions form a crystal. Its formula unit shows the minimum ratio of the ions. NaCl has a 1:1 ratio; CaCl₂ has a 1:2 ratio of calcium to chlorine.

explain.title: Covalent compounds have molecular formulae
explain.body: Covalent compounds generally exist as molecules. The textbook defines a molecular formula this way: “A chemical compound is thus, represented by a chemical formula which is called the molecular formula of that compound and which shows all the types of atoms bonded together in one molecule of that compound.” For example, H₂O shows two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in one molecule.

explain.title: Read subscripts carefully
explain.body: A small number after a symbol tells you how many of that atom are present. No subscript means one. In NH₃ there is one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.

explain.title: Formula and structure are not always the same thing
explain.body: A formula can show the simplest ratio in an ionic or extended solid without meaning that separate molecules exist. For example, SiO₂ represents the 1:2 ratio of silicon to oxygen in sand’s structure.

mistakes: Treating an ionic formula unit as if it described a separate molecule.
Forgetting that an element can exist as a molecule, such as O₂, rather than as single atoms.
Reading a missing subscript as zero; no subscript means one atom.
Changing a polyatomic ion’s subscripts instead of putting brackets around the ion, for example writing NH₄₂CO₃ instead of (NH₄)₂CO₃.
Writing a formula with charges that do not balance, or not reducing the ion ratio to the simplest whole numbers.
Assuming that every different compound must have a different molecular formula; structural isomers can share one.

examTips: A short question may ask for the definition of empirical formula or for examples where the empirical and molecular formulas are the same.
For a formula-conversion question, divide every subscript by the same greatest common factor; show the division so the method earns marks.
For an explanation question, state what each formula tells you and include a suitable example such as benzene and acetylene.
Remember that an ionic compound is represented by its empirical formula, which shows the simplest ratio between its ions.

steps.why: The section gives C₆H₆ as the molecular formula of benzene.
steps.text: Molecular formula of benzene = C₆H₆.

steps.why: The common factor lets us reduce the subscripts to the simplest ratio.
steps.text: The greatest common factor of 6 and 6 is 6.

steps.why: Dividing each subscript by 6 gives the simplest whole-number ratio.
steps.text: C₆H₆ ÷ 6 = CH.

steps.why: CH is the simplest formula that represents the ratio of carbon to hydrogen atoms.
steps.text: Empirical formula of benzene = CH.

example.question: Find the empirical formula of benzene, whose molecular formula is C₆H₆.
example.answer: CH

explain.title: Definition
explain.body: Empirical Formula of a compound shows the simplest whole number ratio of atoms present in that compound.

explain.title: Ionic compounds
explain.body: All the ionic compounds are represented by their empirical formulas. These formulas show the simplest ratio present between their ions. Calcium fluoride, CaF₂, shows the ratio present between calcium and fluoride ions in its crystal.

explain.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
explain.body: For covalent chemical compounds, which exist as molecules, the empirical formulas may be different from their molecular formulas. Hydrogen peroxide is H₂O₂ and its empirical formula is HO; benzene is C₆H₆ and its empirical formula is CH.

explain.title: Same empirical formula
explain.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest ratio, not the actual number of atoms. Benzene (C₆H₆) and acetylene (C₂H₂) both have the empirical formula CH. Water's molecular and empirical formulas are both H₂O.

mistakes: Copying the molecular formula as the empirical formula without checking whether all the subscripts can be divided by the same number.
Reducing only one subscript instead of dividing every subscript by the same greatest common factor.
Thinking that the empirical formula always tells the actual number of atoms in a molecule.
For ionic compounds, treating the formula as a discrete molecule instead of a simplest ratio between ions.

explain.title: Start with the two ions
explain.body: In order to write down the formula of an ionic compound, first identify the cations and anions and the number of charges present on them. Finally combine the two ions together to form an electrically neutral compound.

explain.title: Use the ion charges
explain.body: Write the symbol of the cation with its charge, then the symbol of the anion with its charge. The charges tell you how many of each ion are needed for a neutral compound.

explain.title: Apply the crisscross method
explain.body: In this method, the numerical value of each of the ion charges is crossed over to become the subscript of the other ion. Signs of the charges are then dropped.

explain.title: Check the result
explain.body: The compound must be electrically neutral. For Mg₃N₂, three Mg²⁺ ions give +6 and two N³⁻ ions give −6, so the charges balance.

mistakes: Leaving the charge signs in the final formula instead of dropping them.
Putting each charge number on the same ion instead of crisscrossing it to the other ion.
Writing a formula that does not have equal total positive and negative charges.
Forgetting that a subscript of 1 is not written.

explain.title: Empirical formula
explain.body: Your textbook explains: “To calculate the empirical formula of a compound, you need to determine the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in the compound.” It is the simplest ratio, not necessarily the actual number of atoms in a molecule.

explain.title: Molecular formula
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Molecular formula of a compound can be found out if we know its empirical formula.” The molecular formula gives the actual number of each type of atom in a molecule.

explain.title: Calculate the multiplier
explain.body: Your textbook gives the relationship: “Molecular formula = n (Empirical Formula)” and “Where n = Molar Mass / Empirical Formula mass”. Calculate n, then multiply every subscript by it. If n is one, the molecular and empirical formulas are the same.

mistakes: Using the molar mass as n without dividing by the empirical formula mass.
Forgetting to calculate the empirical formula mass using the correct atomic masses.
Multiplying only one subscript instead of every subscript in the empirical formula.
Leaving the final result in bracket form instead of writing the molecular formula in its simplest notation.
Treating an empirical formula as if it always gives the actual atom counts in a molecule.

explain.title: The value of Avogadro's number
explain.body: 6.022 × 10²³ is the number selected in the section. It is called Avogadro's number and is represented by Nₐ.

explain.title: A mole counts units
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “Avogadro's number is the number of units in one mole of a substance.” The units may be atoms or molecules, depending on the substance.

explain.title: Using the number in calculations

explain.title: A mole counts particles
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “the quantity of a substance containing Avogadro's number of particles (Nₐ) is called a Mole.” One mole means 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Always say whether the particles are atoms, molecules or ions.

explain.title: The particles depend on the substance
explain.body: A mole of carbon means 6.022 × 10²³ carbon atoms. A mole of O₂ means 6.022 × 10²³ oxygen molecules. A mole of NaCl means 6.022 × 10²³ formula units.

explain.title: Molar mass is mass per mole
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “The mass of one mole of a substance is called Molar mass.” For a compound, multiply each element’s atomic mass by the subscript in its formula, then add the contributions.

explain.title: Use the formula to count every atom
explain.body: In H₂SO₄ there are 2 H atoms, 1 S atom and 4 O atoms. Its molar mass is 2(1) + 1(32) + 4(16) = 98 g mol⁻¹. Include the correct unit and particle name in your answer.

mistakes: Do not treat Avogadro’s number and a mole as exactly the same idea: the number is 6.022 × 10²³; a mole is an amount containing that number of specified particles.
Do not forget to multiply an atomic mass by its subscript, such as using 4(16) for the four oxygen atoms in H₂SO₄.
Do not confuse atoms with molecules: one O₂ molecule has two atoms, while one mole of O₂ contains one mole of O₂ molecules.
Do not leave off g mol⁻¹ when giving a molar mass, or atoms/molecules when giving a particle count.

explain.title: What a chemical equation represents
explain.body: Representing a chemical change in this way is called a chemical equation. It uses element symbols and compound formulas to show the substances reacting and the substances produced.

explain.title: Reactants and products
explain.body: The reacting substances are called as reactants while those being produced are called products. Reactants are written on the left-hand side and products on the right-hand side, with an arrow between them.

explain.title: Why equations are balanced
explain.body: A chemical equation must obey the law of conservation of mass. This means that no atom should be destroyed or produced during a chemical change. The total number and the type of atoms must remain the same during a chemical change.

explain.title: States and direction
explain.body: Physical states are shown as subscripts: solid is (s), liquid is (l), gas is (g), and aqueous is (aq). A single arrow shows the direction of change; ⇌ indicates a reversible reaction.

explain.title: Reversible reactions and precipitates
explain.body: Such reactions are called as reversible reactions and are indicated by (⇌) sign. An insoluble product such as AgCl comes out of an aqueous solution in the form of a precipitate.

mistakes: Writing the names of substances instead of their correct chemical formulas.
Changing subscripts in formulas to balance an equation; use coefficients instead.
Forgetting that the number and type of atoms must match on both sides.
Putting reactants on the right or products on the left.
Confusing (aq), which means aqueous, with (l), which means liquid.
Using a one-way arrow for a reaction described as reversible.

explain.title: A balanced equation is a recipe
explain.body: A balanced chemical equation tells you the relative numbers of moles that react and form. The coefficients are the mole ratio.

explain.title: Use the ratio for masses
explain.body: Find the molar mass of each substance. Combine these masses with the mole ratio to get the mass ratio, then scale it to the amount given in the question.

explain.title: Convert to the quantity asked for
explain.body: Some questions ask for moles or particles rather than grams. Use the equation ratio first, then use molar mass or Avogadro's number for any further conversion.

explain.title: Keep the equation correct
explain.body: A chemical equation tells the reacting and producing elements or compounds in a chemical reaction. It also tells the mole ratio between reactants or products and between reactants and products. A chemical equation must be balanced and should show the correct formulas of all the participating elements and compounds.

explain.title: Mass ratios come from mole ratios
explain.body: The mole ratio between reactants and products as shown by a chemical equation enables us to find out the mass ratio of these substances. A chemical equation is used to calculate the masses of the reactants as well as the products, which take part in a chemical reaction.

mistakes: Using an unbalanced equation or incorrect chemical formula gives the wrong mole ratio.
Using the coefficients as a mass ratio without taking molar masses into account.
Reversing the ratio—for example, using reactant mass divided by product mass when the opposite is needed.
Leaving out a conversion step when changing grams to moles or moles to particles.
Giving a number without naming the substance or including its unit.

recap.answer: Reactants are on the left; products are on the right. The equation must have the same number and type of atoms on both sides.

According to this equation

solutions.question: How many molecules of water will be produced if we react 5 g of hydrogen gas with excess of oxygen gas?
steps: Mass of H₂ used = 5g    Molecules of water produced = ?
The balanced chemical equation for the reaction:
2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
2 moles  1 mole  2 moles
According to this equation
4 g of hydrogen produce H₂O = 36 g of H₂O
5 g of hydrogen will produce H₂O = 36/4 × 5 = 45g of H₂O
18g (1 mole) of H₂O contain molecules = 6.022 × 10²³
36g of H₂O contain molecules = 6.022 × 10²³ × 2
45g of H₂O contain = 45/36 × 12.04 × 10²³
= 1.505 × 10²⁴ molecules
KEY POINTS
1. Molecular formula of an element or a compound shows the actual number of atoms present in the molecule of the element or a compound.

2. The formula of a compound which gives the minimum ratio present between its atoms is called its Empirical formula. All the ionic compounds and some of the covalent compounds are represented by their empirical formulas.
3. Chemical formula of a binary ionic compounds can be written if you know their names and the charges present on the ions.
4. Chemical formula of a compound is n times its empirical formula where n is the ratio of molar mass to empirical formula mass.
5. Avogadro's number has been calculated to know the mass ratio of reactants and products in a chemical reaction. The value of this number is 6.022 × 10²³.
6. The quantity of an element or a compound, which contains Avogadro's number of particles, is called a Mole and the mass of a substance present in it is called the Molar Mass.

7. A chemical equation tells the reacting and producing elements or compounds in a chemical reaction. It also tells the mole ratio between reactants or products and between reactants and products. A chemical equation must be balanced and should show the correct formulas of all the participating elements and compounds.

8. The mole ratio between reactants and products as shown by a chemical equation enables us to find out the mass ratio of these substances. A chemical equation is used to calculate the masses of the reactants as well as the products, which take part in a chemical reaction.

steps.text: Given: mass of CH₄ = 10 g; oxygen is in excess. Equation: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g).

steps.why: A mass must be converted to moles before using the equation's coefficients.
steps.text: Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + 4(1) = 16 g mol⁻¹.

steps.why: Dividing the given mass by the molar mass finds the amount of methane.
steps.text: Moles of CH₄ = 10 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 0.625 mol.

steps.why: The equation has a 1:1 mole ratio of CH₄ to CO₂.
steps.text: Moles of CO₂ = 0.625 mol CH₄ × (1 mol CO₂ ÷ 1 mol CH₄) = 0.625 mol.

steps.why: Multiplying product moles by its molar mass gives the requested mass.
steps.text: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g mol⁻¹; mass of CO₂ = 0.625 mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 27.5 g CO₂.

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
example.answer: 27.5 g CO₂

explain.title: Formula writing and balancing
explain.body: Write the correct formula for every reactant and product, then balance the equation with coefficients. Do not change the subscripts in a formula when balancing.

explain.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
explain.body: A mole is an amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Avogadro's number is the number of particles in one mole.

explain.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
explain.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule and is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

explain.title: Mass and percentage composition
explain.body: Use molar mass to convert between mass and moles. To calculate an element's percentage by mass, divide its mass by the total sample mass and multiply by 100.

explain.title: Stoichiometric calculations
explain.body: A balanced equation gives mole ratios. Convert the given quantity to moles, use the ratio, and then convert the answer to the requested mass or number of particles.

mistakes: Changing formula subscripts instead of adding coefficients when balancing an equation.
Using an unbalanced equation to obtain a mole ratio.
Forgetting to convert grams into moles before using the equation coefficients.
Counting molecules when the question asks for atoms; multiply by the atoms in each molecule.
Confusing the mole, which is an amount of substance, with Avogadro's number, which is a number of particles.
Leaving out units or failing to label which element or substance a final value belongs to.

recap.answer: 27.5 g of CO₂

recap.answer: 3 mol

solutions.question: Write down the chemical formula of barium nitride.
steps: Barium forms Ba²⁺ ions and nitride forms N³⁻ ions.
Balance the charges: 3(Ba²⁺) and 2(N³⁻) give a neutral compound.
Therefore, the chemical formula is Ba₃N₂.
solutions.answer: Ba₃N₂

solutions.question: Find out the molecular formula of a compound whose empirical formula is CH₂O and its molar mass is 180.
steps: Empirical formula = CH₂O.
Empirical formula mass = 12 + 2(1) + 16 = 30 g mol⁻¹.
n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass = 180 ÷ 30 = 6.
Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆.
solutions.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆

solutions.question: How many molecules are present in 1.5 g H₂O?
steps: Given: mass of H₂O = 1.5 g; molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹; Avogadro’s number = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Required: number of H₂O molecules.
Formula: n = m ÷ M; number of molecules = n × Avogadro’s number.
Substitution: n = 1.5 g ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0833 mol.
Working: number of molecules = 0.0833 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 5.02 × 10²² molecules.
solutions.answer: 5.02 × 10²² molecules

solutions.question: What is the difference between a mole and Avogadro's number?
steps: A mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions or other entities).
Avogadro’s number, 6.02 × 10²³, is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance.
solutions.answer: A mole is an amount of substance; Avogadro’s number is the number of particles in one mole.

solutions.question: Write down the chemical equation of the following reaction.
steps: The reactants or the description of the reaction are not provided.
A chemical equation cannot be written unless the substances taking part in the reaction are specified.
solutions.answer: The reaction is not specified, so its chemical equation cannot be determined.

solutions.question: Different compounds will never have the same molecule formula but they can have the same empirical formula. Explain
steps: The statement is incorrect: different compounds can have the same molecular formula.
Such compounds are called isomers; their atoms are arranged differently.
For example, glucose and fructose are different compounds, but both have the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
Their empirical formula is also the same, CH₂O, because it shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms.
solutions.answer: Different compounds can share a molecular formula if they are isomers; glucose and fructose both have molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and empirical formula CH₂O.

solutions.question: Write down the chemical formulas of the following compounds. Calcium phosphate, Aluminium nitride, Sodium acetate, Ammonium carbonate and Bismuth sulphate.
steps: Calcium phosphate: Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
Aluminium nitride: AlN.
Sodium acetate: CH₃COONa.
Ammonium carbonate: (NH₄)₂CO₃.
Bismuth sulphate: Bi₂(SO₄)₃.
solutions.answer: Calcium phosphate: Ca₃(PO₄)₂; aluminium nitride: AlN; sodium acetate: CH₃COONa; ammonium carbonate: (NH₄)₂CO₃; bismuth sulphate: Bi₂(SO₄)₃.

solutions.question: Why does Avogadro's number have an immense importance in chemistry?
steps: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance.
It is 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole.
Atoms and molecules are extremely small, so their number cannot be counted individually; Avogadro’s number makes it possible to relate the number of particles to a measurable amount of substance.
It is therefore used to convert between the number of particles and the number of moles.
solutions.answer: Avogadro’s number links the measurable mole to the number of atoms, molecules or other particles.

solutions.question: When 8.657g of a compound were converted into elements, it gave 5.217g of carbon, 0.962g of hydrogen and 2.478g of oxygen. Calculate the percentage of each element present in this compound.
steps: Given: Mass of compound = 8.657 g; mass of carbon = 5.217 g; mass of hydrogen = 0.962 g; mass of oxygen = 2.478 g.
Required: Percentage of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the compound.
Formula: Percentage of an element = (Mass of element ÷ Mass of compound) × 100
For carbon: Percentage of carbon = (5.217 g ÷ 8.657 g) × 100 = 60.26%.
For hydrogen: Percentage of hydrogen = (0.962 g ÷ 8.657 g) × 100 = 11.11%.
For oxygen: Percentage of oxygen = (2.478 g ÷ 8.657 g) × 100 = 28.62%.
solutions.answer: Carbon = 60.26%; hydrogen = 11.11%; oxygen = 28.62%.

solutions.question: How can you calculate the masses of the products formed in a reversible reaction?
steps: Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
Convert the given mass of the reactant into moles.
Use the mole ratio in the balanced equation to find the moles of the product.
Convert the moles of the product into mass using its molar mass.
solutions.answer: Use the balanced equation’s mole ratio to calculate product moles, then convert them into masses.

solutions.question: Which conditions must be fulfilled before writing a chemical equation for a reaction?
steps: The reactants and products of the reaction must be known.
The correct chemical formulae of the reactants and products must be known.
The chemical equation must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
solutions.answer: Know the reactants, products and their correct formulae, and write a balanced equation.

solutions.question: Explain the concepts of Avogadro's number and mole.
steps: Avogadro’s number is 6.02 × 10²³, the number of particles present in one mole of a substance.
The particles may be atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.
A mole is the amount of a substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
For example, one mole of carbon atoms contains 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms.
solutions.answer: One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles, the number known as Avogadro’s number.

solutions.question: How many grams of CO₂ will be produced when we react 10 g of CH₄ with excess of O₂ according to the following equation? CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
steps: Given: Mass of CH₄ = 10 g; molar mass of CH₄ = 16 g mol⁻¹; molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹.
Required: Mass of CO₂ produced.
From the balanced equation: 1 mol CH₄ produces 1 mol CO₂.
Moles of CH₄ = Mass ÷ Molar mass = 10 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 0.625 mol.
Moles of CO₂ produced = 0.625 mol.
Mass of CO₂ = Moles × Molar mass = 0.625 mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 27.5 g.
solutions.answer: 27.5 g CO₂

solutions.question: How many moles of coal are needed to produce 10 moles of CO according to the following equation? 3C(s) + O₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂(g) + 3CO(g)
steps: Given: Amount of CO required = 10 mol.
Required: Amount of coal (carbon) needed.
From the balanced equation: 3 mol C produce 3 mol CO.
Mole ratio C : CO = 3 : 3 = 1 : 1.
Moles of C required = 10 mol CO × (3 mol C ÷ 3 mol CO) = 10 mol.
solutions.answer: 10 mol of coal (carbon)

solutions.question: How much SO₂ is needed in grams to produce 10 moles of sulphur? 2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 3S(s)
steps: Given: Amount of sulphur produced = 10 mol; molar mass of SO₂ = 64 g mol⁻¹.
Required: Mass of SO₂ needed.
From the balanced equation: 1 mol SO₂ produces 3 mol S.
Moles of SO₂ required = 10 mol S × (1 mol SO₂ ÷ 3 mol S) = 3.333 mol.
Mass of SO₂ = Moles × Molar mass = 3.333 mol × 64 g mol⁻¹ = 213.3 g.
solutions.answer: 213.3 g SO₂

solutions.question: How much ammonia is needed in grams to produce 1 kg of urea fertilizer? 2NH₃(aq) + CO₂(aq) → CO(NH₂)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
steps: Given: Mass of urea = 1 kg = 1000 g; molar mass of urea, CO(NH₂)₂ = 12 + 16 + 2(14) + 4(1) = 60 g mol⁻¹; molar mass of NH₃ = 14 + 3(1) = 17 g mol⁻¹.
Required: Mass of NH₃ needed to produce 1000 g of urea.
From the balanced equation: 2 mol NH₃ produce 1 mol urea.
Therefore, 2 × 17 = 34 g NH₃ produce 60 g urea.
Formula: Mass of NH₃ required = (Mass of urea × mass of 2 mol NH₃) ÷ molar mass of urea.
Substitution: Mass of NH₃ required = (1000 g × 34 g) ÷ 60 g.
Working: Mass of NH₃ required = 566.7 g.
Result: 566.7 g of ammonia is needed.

solutions.question: Calculate the number of atoms in the following. (a) 3g of H₂
steps: Given: Mass of H₂ = 3 g; molar mass of H₂ = 2 g mol⁻¹; Avogadro’s number = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹.
Required: Number of atoms in 3 g of H₂.
Formula: Number of atoms = (mass ÷ molar mass) × Avogadro’s number × 2.
Substitution: Number of atoms = (3 g ÷ 2 g mol⁻¹) × 6.02 × 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹ × 2 atoms molecule⁻¹.
Working: Number of atoms = 1.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ × 2 = 1.806 × 10²⁴ atoms.
Result: 3 g of H₂ contains 1.806 × 10²⁴ atoms.
solutions.answer: 1.806 × 10²⁴ atoms

solutions.question: Calculate the number of atoms in the following. (b) 3.4 moles of N₂
steps: Given: Amount of N₂ = 3.4 mol; Avogadro’s number = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹; each N₂ molecule contains 2 atoms.
Required: Number of atoms in 3.4 mol of N₂.
Formula: Number of atoms = moles of N₂ × Avogadro’s number × 2.
Substitution: Number of atoms = 3.4 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹ × 2 atoms molecule⁻¹.
Working: Number of atoms = 4.0936 × 10²⁴ atoms ≈ 4.09 × 10²⁴ atoms.
Result: 3.4 mol of N₂ contains 4.09 × 10²⁴ atoms.
solutions.answer: 4.09 × 10²⁴ atoms

solutions.question: Calculate the number of atoms in the following. (c) 10g of C₆H₁₂O₆.
steps: Given: Mass of C₆H₁₂O₆ = 10 g; molar mass of C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180 g mol⁻¹; Avogadro’s number = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹.
Required: Total number of atoms in 10 g of C₆H₁₂O₆.
Each molecule of C₆H₁₂O₆ contains 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 atoms.
Formula: Number of atoms = (mass ÷ molar mass) × Avogadro’s number × 24.
Substitution: Number of atoms = (10 g ÷ 180 g mol⁻¹) × 6.02 × 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹ × 24 atoms molecule⁻¹.
Working: Number of atoms = 8.03 × 10²³ atoms.
Result: 10 g of C₆H₁₂O₆ contains 8.03 × 10²³ atoms.
solutions.answer: 8.03 × 10²³ atoms

solutions.question: It is generally believed that drinking eight glasses of water every day is required to keep oneself hydrated especially in the summer. If a glass occupies 400 cm³ of water on the average, how many moles of water are needed for a single adult?
steps: Given: Number of glasses = 8; volume of each glass = 400 cm³ = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³; density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³; molar mass of water = 18 g mol⁻¹.
Required: Number of moles of water needed for one adult.
Formula: Total volume = number of glasses × volume of each glass.
Substitution: Total volume = 8 × 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 3.20 × 10⁻³ m³.
Formula: Mass = density × volume.
Substitution: Mass of water = 1000 kg m⁻³ × 3.20 × 10⁻³ m³ = 3.20 kg = 3200 g.
Formula: Number of moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
Substitution: Number of moles = 3200 g ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹.
Working: Number of moles = 177.8 mol.
Result: About 178 mol of water are needed.

solutions.question: The chemical formula for sand is SiO₂ but the sand does not exist in the form of discrete molecules like H₂O. How has its formula been determined keeping in view its structure?
steps: Sand has a giant network structure and does not exist as separate SiO₂ molecules.
Its formula is determined from the simplest whole-number ratio of silicon atoms to oxygen atoms in the structure.
The ratio of silicon atoms to oxygen atoms is 1:2; therefore, the formula is SiO₂.
solutions.answer: The formula SiO₂ represents the 1:2 ratio of silicon to oxygen atoms in the giant structure.

definitions.text: It is based on the law of conservation of mass which states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed.
The stoichiometric coefficient used to balance a chemical equation provides the mole ratio between reactants and products.

A chemical compound is thus, represented by a chemical formula which is called the molecular formula of that compound and which shows all the types of atoms bonded together in one molecule of that compound.
Empirical Formula of a compound shows the simplest whole number ratio of atoms present in that compound.

The number 6.022 × 10²³ is called Avogadro's number after the name of an Italian chemist Amaedo Avogadro. Avogadro's number is the number of units in one mole of a substance. This number is represented as Nₐ.
The quantity of a substance containing Avogadro's number of particles (Nₐ) is called a Mole.
The mass of one mole of a substance is called Molar mass.

Representing a chemical change in this way is called a chemical equation. A chemical equation tells us the elements or compounds which are reacting and those which are being produced as a result of a chemical change.
The reacting substances are called as reactants while those being produced are called products.
Such reactions are called as reversible reactions and are indicated by (⇌) sign, e.g.:

definitions.term: Rule for writing a chemical equation: conservation of atoms
definitions.text: A chemical equation must obey the law of conservation of mass. This means that no atom should be destroyed or produced during a chemical change. The total number and the type of atoms must remain the same during a chemical change. Thus the total number and kind of atoms on both sides of the equation must be equal or the chemical equation must be balanced.

definitions.term: Rule for writing a chemical equation: correct formulas
definitions.text: The formulas of elements and compounds must be written correctly.

definitions.term: Rule for writing a chemical equation: mole ratio
definitions.text: A chemical equation must determine the correct mole ratio among the reactants, the products and between the reactants and the products.

definitions.term: Rule for writing a chemical equation: direction
definitions.text: A chemical equation must also point out the direction in which the change is proceeding.

definitions.term: Rule for writing a chemical equation: physical states
definitions.text: It is a usual practice to show the normal physical states of reactants and products as a subscript. Solid, liquid and gas are symbolized as s, l and g respectively. Aqueous (aq) represents the solvated ion.
In this method, the numerical value of each of the ion charges is crossed over to become the subscript of the other ion. Signs of the charges are then dropped.

definitions.term: Steps to deduce a molecular formula from a structural formula
definitions.text:
1. Write down the structural formula of the compound.
2. Count the number of atoms of each type in the structural formula.
3. Write the symbols of all the elements.
4. Write the total number of atoms of each kind as a subscript.
5. Remove the subscript 1.

fullMarks: For an ionic formula, write the ions and their charges first, crisscross the charge numbers, remove the charge signs, and reduce subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio. Check that the total charge is zero.
For an equation, write the correct formulas of reactants and products first. Balance by changing coefficients only; do not change subscripts in formulas.
Show state symbols where relevant: (s), (l), (g) and (aq). Keep reactants on the left, products on the right, and use ⇌ only for a reversible reaction.
In a mole calculation, write the given data, convert to consistent units, write the formula, substitute with units, and give the final answer with its unit and sensible significant figures.
In a stoichiometry numerical, use the balanced equation's coefficients as the mole ratio. If the question asks for mass, convert the calculated moles using molar mass and show that step.
For particle questions, clearly show the mass-to-moles or moles-to-particles steps, use Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, and state whether the final count is atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.

For theory answers, state the definition or law first, then explain it or give the requested example. In formula questions, include every requested compound and write element symbols with correct capitalisation.
mistakes: Mistake: Treating Avogadro's number as a mole. Fix: A mole is an amount of substance; Avogadro's number is the number of particles in one mole.
Mistake: Giving the number of molecules when the question asks for atoms. Fix: Multiply the molecule count by the number of atoms per molecule; for N₂, multiply by 2.
Mistake: Changing a formula's subscripts to balance an equation. Fix: Keep formulas unchanged and adjust only the coefficients in front of them.
Mistake: Using an unbalanced equation for a mole ratio. Fix: Balance the equation first, then use its coefficients.
Mistake: Forgetting to reduce ionic-formula subscripts or to check charge neutrality. Fix: Reduce to the simplest whole-number ratio and confirm total positive and negative charges cancel.
Mistake: Mixing up empirical and molecular formulas. Fix: The empirical formula gives the simplest ratio; the molecular formula gives the actual atom count in one molecule.
Mistake: Leaving off units or the kind of particle in a numerical answer. Fix: Include units for mass and molar mass, and label the final count as atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.

writtenQuestions.text: What is the difference between enthalpy and enthalpy change?
modelAnswer: Enthalpy (H) is the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound.
Enthalpy change is the change in the system's enthalpy when energy is transferred during a change or reaction.
It is positive when energy enters the system and negative when energy leaves it.

solution: The water molecules are the system; the beaker, burner and other things around it are the surrounding.

example.answer: The water is the system; the beaker and burner are part of the surrounding. Heat energy moves from the surrounding into the system, so the change is endothermic and positive.

explain.title: The system and its surrounding
explain.body: In Chemistry, any physical or chemical change under study may also be called a system. The chemical reaction includes reactants, products, catalyst, solvent and anything else which is important to study this reaction. Everything else which does not fall in this system is called the surrounding. In the beaker example, the water is the system and the beaker and burner are in the surrounding.

explain.title: Energy entering or leaving
explain.body: When energy is transferred from surrounding to the system, the change is called endothermic and it has a positive sign. When energy is transferred from system to surrounding, the change is called exothermic and it carries a negative sign. The surroundings get cooler when they supply energy and warmer when they receive energy.

explain.title: Enthalpy and heat
explain.body: Enthalpy (H) or heat content, is defined as the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound. The unit of its measurement is kJ mol⁻¹. Energy absorbed during a reaction increases the total enthalpy of the system; energy evolved during a reaction decreases it.

mistakes: Do not call everything in the experiment the system; the system is the part or change being studied.
Do not reverse the direction: endothermic energy goes from the surrounding into the system.
Do not give a negative sign to an endothermic change; it is positive. Exothermic change is negative.
Do not treat heat and enthalpy as identical: heat is transferred energy, while enthalpy is thermal energy stored in a compound.
When describing a beaker example, do not name the beaker or burner as the water system; they are part of the surrounding.

Heat is the transfer of thermal energy, while enthalpy is a property of the system.
At constant pressure, the enthalpy change is equal to the heat evolved or absorbed.

explain.title: Enthalpy and its symbols
explain.body: “The total amount of heat energy present in a molecule under standard conditions (0°C temperature and 760 mm pressure) is also called its heat content. Enthalpy is the measurement of energy in a thermodynamic system. The quantity of enthalpy is equal to the total heat content of a system. Enthalpy of a system is represented by (H) while the change in enthalpy which a system undergoes is represented by ΔH.” In questions, keep H and ΔH distinct.

explain.title: What can be measured?
explain.body: “The total enthalpy (H) of a system cannot be measured directly. However, the change in enthalpy ΔH brought about in a system can be measured comparatively easily.” So chemistry questions usually compare the energy before and after a change.

explain.title: Standard enthalpy of reaction
explain.body: “In Chemistry, the standard enthalpy of reaction (ΔH°) is the enthalpy change when reactants in their standard states undergo reaction to produce products in their standard states.” It is also called the standard enthalpy change or heat of reaction at constant pressure.

explain.title: Heat compared with enthalpy
explain.body: “Heat is a form of energy that flows from hot body to a cold body because of a difference in temperature.” Enthalpy is part of a system and depends on its molecules, composition and structure. At constant pressure, enthalpy change equals the heat evolved or absorbed.

mistakes: Do not use H and ΔH as if they mean the same thing: H is enthalpy, while ΔH is its change.
Do not describe heat as energy stored in the system; heat is energy being transferred.
Do not say a negative ΔH means heat is absorbed. Negative ΔH means heat is released to the surroundings.
When defining standard enthalpy of reaction, do not leave out that reactants and products are in their standard states.
Do not forget to state the constant-pressure condition when giving the equality between enthalpy change and heat.

explain.title: Heat of a reaction
explain.body: Heat, which is evolved or absorbed during a chemical reaction, is called the heat of that reaction.

explain.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
explain.body: Chemical reactions in which heat energy is evolved are called exothermic reactions while those in which heat energy is absorbed are called endothermic reactions. Heat from an exothermic reaction goes to the surroundings and container, making them warmer. An endothermic reaction takes heat from the surroundings, so the container becomes cooler.

explain.title: The sign of ΔH
explain.body: When energy evolved is shown separately, an exothermic reaction has a negative ΔH. An endothermic reaction has a positive ΔH. Reversing a reaction reverses the direction of the heat change.

explain.title: Bond energy and the overall reaction
explain.body: Breaking bonds absorbs energy, while forming bonds evolves energy. The overall reaction is exothermic if more energy is released by bond formation than is absorbed in bond breaking. It is endothermic if more energy is absorbed than released.

explain.title: Exothermic reactions in everyday life
explain.body: Combustion of fuels releases heat used for cooking, heating and generating electricity. During metabolism, chemical energy in food is converted to heat. Fireworks are combustion reactions that produce heat, light and sound.

mistakes: Do not give a positive ΔH for a reaction that evolves heat; its ΔH is negative.
Do not say that bond breaking releases energy. Breaking a bond absorbs energy.
Do not forget to multiply a bond energy by the number of bonds formed or broken.
When bond-formation energy is given as a negative value, keep its negative sign in the calculation.
Do not assume that the reverse reaction has the same sign of ΔH; it has the opposite sign.
In a bond-energy calculation, show both the bond-breaking and bond-forming contributions before giving the final answer.

recap.question: Can the total enthalpy of a system be measured directly?
recap.answer: The total enthalpy H cannot be measured directly; the enthalpy change ΔH can be measured.

recap.question: Which statement best describes the enthalpy of a system?
recap.answer: The total heat content of a system

solutions.question: Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas react to give liquid water in an exothermic reaction.
steps: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 571.6 kJ
Hydrogen  Oxygen  Water

571.6 kJ heat energy is evolved during this reaction. If the energy evolved is shown separately it is expressed as ΔH = -571.6 kJ. The same amount of energy will be absorbed when the reaction will move in the backward direction i.e. water will decompose to give hydrogen and oxygen back.
Example: Carbon dioxide gas is produced when solid carbon burns in oxygen gas.
(Figure: C (s) + O₂ (g) → CO₂ (g) + 393.5 kJ; labels: Carbon, Oxygen, Carbon dioxide.)

It is also an exothermic reaction and 393.5 kJ heat energy is evolved during this reaction. When this reaction is carried out in the reverse direction, the same amount of energy i.e. 393.5 kJ will be absorbed. The enthalpy change (ΔH) for this reaction is -393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Both the reactions mentioned above are the examples of exothermic changes.
The following reactions represent endothermic changes.
(Figure: H₂ (g) + I₂ (s) → 2HI (g) − 53.08 kJ; labels: Hydrogen, Iodine, Hydrogen Iodide.)
The enthalpy change for the reaction is ΔH = 53.08 kJ
Hydrogen gas reacts with solid iodine only at high temperature and 53.08 kJ of heat energy is absorbed.
Formation of NO in air due to lightning in the clouds.
(Figure: N₂ (g) + O₂ (g) → 2NO (g) − 180.6 kJ; labels: Nitrogen, oxygen, Nitric Oxide.)
The enthalpy change for the reaction is ΔH = 180.6 kJ.
INTERESTING INFORMATION:

Heat evolved or absorbed during a reaction is used in self-heating or self-cooling packs. These packs contain reactants that undergo an exothermic or an endothermic reaction providing high or low temperature.

Our present-day living conditions depend heavily on the availability of energy in its various forms. Exothermic chemical reactions are extensively used to fulfill this requirement. In such reactions, chemical energy is converted into heat energy. We burn fuels like gas, oil and coal to cook food and for other heating purposes in our homes and industry. During this burning process called
combustion, substances present in fuels react with oxygen of the air to produce a certain amount of heat.
Foods such as fats and carbohydrates are important biological fuels. During metabolism, the chemical energy present in this food is converted to heat to keep us warm.

A large portion of electricity is produced at power stations by burning fuels such as natural gas, oil and coal. The heat which comes out from their combustion is used to produce steam at high pressure. This high pressure steam is then used to rotate turbines, which in turn generate electricity.

While driving a vehicle, it is the combustion of petrol or diesel that gives off energy and drives it forward. The one example of exothermic reactions people seem to enjoy the most is that of fireworks. Fireworks are the result of combustion reactions that yield heat, light and sound. Different metal salts alongwith oxidising agents produce a variety of colours when burnt, Fig. (5.2).
(Figure: Fireworks bursting in the sky above a lit area with strings of lights.)

writtenQuestions.text: Explain why the reaction between atmospheric gases oxygen and nitrogen does not take place under normal conditions? But in the presence of lightning these gases react to give NO. The reaction stops as soon as the lightning stops.

solution: Under normal conditions, the oxygen and nitrogen molecules do not have enough energy to overcome the activation energy.

yourTurn.question: A reaction between natural gas (CH₄) and atmospheric oxygen does not take place when you mix them. As soon as you show a burning match stick, the reaction starts immediately and then it continues until one or both of the reactants is/are used up. Explain.

The reaction releases heat, which supplies energy for further reaction.

steps.why: The reactants must first collide for the reaction to proceed.
steps.text: A₂ and B₂ molecules move randomly and collide.

steps.why: Collisions with average or less than average kinetic energy may not produce a result.
steps.text: Only a collision involving molecules with enough energy may produce the transition state.

steps.text: The transition state may then return to the reactants or change into products.

explain.title: Molecules move and collide
explain.body: Reactant molecules are in random motion and have different kinetic energies. They collide with one another, but collisions involving molecules with average or less than average kinetic energy may not produce a reaction.

explain.title: The transition state
explain.body: The textbook says: “The transition state is shown at the peak of curve in Fig (5.4).” A transition state exists for a very short time and may return to reactants or proceed to products.

explain.title: Activation energy
explain.body: The textbook defines it this way: “The energy absorbed by the reactant or product molecules in order to be converted into the transition state is called the activation energy (Eₐ) of the reaction.”

explain.title: Catalysts speed up reactions
explain.body: The textbook defines a catalyst as: “a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.” A catalyst changes the path of the reaction and substantially decreases activation energy, so more reactants can form products.

mistakes: Do not say that every collision causes a reaction; many collisions do not have enough energy.
Do not confuse activation energy with the difference in energy between reactants and products.
Do not say a catalyst is permanently used up; it does not undergo permanent chemical change.
Do not say a catalyst speeds a reaction by increasing activation energy. It decreases activation energy.
On an energy profile, do not label the product level as the transition state; the transition state is at the peak.

explain.title: Aerobic respiration
explain.body: The process that occurs in the presence of oxygen is called aerobic respiration. In the textbook's reaction, glucose is first split into pyruvate in the cytoplasm. The next stage uses oxygen and occurs in the mitochondria, producing carbon dioxide, water, and energy.

explain.title: Glycolysis and ATP
explain.body: During glycolysis one molecule of glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvate. This series of enzyme-catalysed reactions has a net production of 2 ATP. Cells use ATP and break it down when they need energy for metabolic activities.

explain.title: Anaerobic respiration
explain.body: In certain organisms like bacteria and algae respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen and it is called anaerobic respiration. The section describes glucose being converted into carbon dioxide and ethanol with the evolution of energy.

explain.title: Lipids and glycogen
explain.body: Lipids serve as an energy reserve within our body; excess food can be stored as lipids in adipose cells. Glycogen is the primary storage form of glucose and is stored in the liver and muscles.

mistakes: Do not confuse aerobic respiration, which occurs in the presence of oxygen, with anaerobic respiration, which occurs in its absence.
Do not say glycolysis produces 2 molecules of ATP; the textbook states that its net production is 2 ATP.
Do not give only the storage location when asked for glycogen's role; state that it is the primary storage form of glucose.
Do not describe lipids only as stored excess food; explain that they provide an energy reserve used between meals and during exercise.

yourTurn.question:
Q5.1. Find out the enthalpy change of the following reaction using the given data.

N₂ + O₂ → 2NO

Bond dissociation energy of N₂ = 958.38 kJ/mol
Bond dissociation energy of O₂ = 498 kJ/mol
Bond formation energy of NO = −626 kJ/mol
solution: Energy of bonds broken = 958.38 + 498 = 1456.38 kJ mol⁻¹.
Energy of bonds formed = 2 × 626 = 1252 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH = energy of bonds broken − energy of bonds formed.
yourTurn.answer: +204.38 kJ mol⁻¹

explain.title: Enthalpy and enthalpy change
explain.body: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. Enthalpy change compares the enthalpy of the products with that of the reactants.

explain.title: Breaking and forming bonds
explain.body: Breaking a bond absorbs energy because energy is needed to separate the bonded atoms. Forming a bond releases energy as atoms move into a more stable arrangement.

explain.title: Exothermic and endothermic changes
explain.body: An exothermic change releases energy to its surroundings and has a negative enthalpy change. An endothermic change absorbs energy and has a positive enthalpy change.

explain.title: Activation energy and transition state
explain.body: Activation energy is the energy needed to start a reaction. At the top of the reaction pathway, the atoms pass through a short-lived, unstable transition state.

explain.title: Respiration and energy in the body
explain.body: Aerobic respiration releases energy when glucose reacts with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water. Glycogen stores energy in the body, while lipids store energy and also help form membranes, insulate the body and protect organs.

mistakes: Do not say that breaking bonds releases energy; bond breaking absorbs energy.

Remember to count how many bonds form, and include the reaction coefficients.
Do not omit the sign or unit from an enthalpy answer.
Do not assume that every exothermic reaction starts immediately; a high activation energy can prevent it from happening readily.
Do not confuse heat, which is transferred, with enthalpy, which is a property describing the system's heat content.

solutions.question: What is the difference between enthalpy and enthalpy change?
steps: Enthalpy (H) is the total heat content of a system at constant pressure.
Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the difference between the enthalpy of the products and the enthalpy of the reactants.
ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
At constant pressure, enthalpy change is the heat absorbed or released during a process.
solutions.answer: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system; enthalpy change is the difference between the enthalpies of products and reactants.

solutions.question: Why is breaking of a bond an endothermic process?
steps: Energy is required to overcome the attractive forces between the atoms joined by a bond.
Therefore, bond breaking absorbs energy from the surroundings and is an endothermic process.
solutions.answer: Breaking a bond is endothermic because energy must be absorbed to overcome the attraction between the bonded atoms.

solutions.question: Depict the transition state for the following reaction. H₂ + Cl₂ ⟶ 2HCl
steps: Draw the H—H and Cl—Cl bonds as dotted, partially broken bonds in a four-atom activated complex.
Show dotted H—Cl bonds forming in the complex and enclose it in brackets with the symbol ‡.
Write the products as 2HCl.
solutions.answer: The transition state is the activated complex [H₂Cl₂]‡, with the H—H and Cl—Cl bonds breaking as H—Cl bonds form.
solutions.figure:
H₂ + Cl₂  →  [
                         H ⋯⋯⋯ H
                         ⋮       ⋮
                         Cl ⋯⋯⋯ Cl
                       ]‡  →  2HCl

The dotted lines show partially broken and partially formed bonds; ‡ marks the transition state.

solutions.question: Draw the reaction profiles for two exothermic reactions one of which moves faster than the other.
steps: Draw a vertical axis labelled Potential energy and a horizontal axis labelled Reaction progress for each reaction profile.
Place the products at a lower energy level than the reactants in both profiles to show that both reactions are exothermic.
Draw a higher energy peak for the slower reaction and a lower energy peak for the faster reaction; label the reactants R and the products P.
solutions.answer: Both profiles are exothermic; the faster reaction has the lower activation energy.
solutions.figure:
(a) SLOWER EXOTHERMIC REACTION                 (b) FASTER EXOTHERMIC REACTION
Potential energy                                  Potential energy
      ↑                                                  ↑
      │                 /\                               │          /\
      │                /  \                              │         /  \
      │ R ___________/    \________                     │ R _____/    \________
      │                              \___ P             │                         \___ P
      └────────────────────────→                       └────────────────────────→
            Reaction progress                               Reaction progress

The reactants and products are at the same relative energy levels in both profiles; the slower reaction has the higher activation-energy peak.

solutions.question: Explain why the reaction between atmospheric gases oxygen and nitrogen does not take place under normal conditions? But in the presence of lightning these gases react to give NO. The reaction stops as soon as the lightning stops.
steps: Nitrogen and oxygen do not react under normal conditions because the reaction requires a large activation energy.
Lightning supplies the energy needed to overcome this activation energy, so nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitric oxide (NO).
The reaction stops when the lightning stops because the continuous supply of activation energy is removed.
solutions.answer: Lightning provides the activation energy needed for nitrogen and oxygen to form NO; without it, the reaction does not continue.

solutions.question: A reaction between natural gas (CH₄) and atmospheric oxygen does not take place when you mix them. As soon as you show a burning match stick, the reaction starts immediately and then it continues until one or both of the reactants is/are used up. Explain.
steps: Natural gas (methane) and oxygen do not react at room temperature because the reaction requires activation energy.
A burning match stick supplies the activation energy needed to start the reaction.
The reaction is exothermic and releases heat, which supplies activation energy for further reaction.
Therefore, the reaction continues until one or both of the reactants are used up.
solutions.answer: The match supplies the activation energy to start methane combustion, and the heat released sustains it until a reactant is used up.

solutions.question:
Find out the enthalpy change of the following reaction using the given data. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO Bond dissociation energy of N₂ = 958.38 kJ/mol
Bond dissociation energy of O₂ = 498 kJ/mol
Bond formation energy of NO = −626 kJ/mol
steps: Given: Bond dissociation energy of N₂ = 958.38 kJ/mol; bond dissociation energy of O₂ = 498 kJ/mol; bond formation energy of NO = −626 kJ/mol.
Required: Enthalpy change (ΔH) for N₂ + O₂ → 2NO.
Formula: ΔH = sum of bond dissociation energies + sum of bond formation energies.
Substitution: ΔH = 958.38 kJ/mol + 498 kJ/mol + 2(−626 kJ/mol).
Working: ΔH = 1456.38 kJ/mol − 1252 kJ/mol = 204.38 kJ/mol.
The positive sign shows that the reaction is endothermic.

solutions.question: Explain the difference between the terms heat and enthalpy.
steps: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference.
Enthalpy is the total heat content of a system at constant pressure; it is represented by H and is given by H = U + PV.
Heat is energy in transit, whereas enthalpy is a property of a system.
solutions.answer: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference, while enthalpy is the total heat content of a system at constant pressure.

solutions.question: Explain why formation of a bond is always an exothermic process.
steps: When a bond forms, atoms attain a more stable state with lower potential energy.
The excess energy is released to the surroundings.
Therefore, bond formation is an exothermic process.
solutions.answer: Bond formation releases energy as atoms attain a more stable, lower-energy state, so it is exothermic.

solutions.question: Explain the role of lipids in our body.
steps: Lipids are an important source and storage form of energy in the body.
They form part of cell membranes.
They insulate the body and help protect internal organs.
solutions.answer: Lipids store energy, form part of cell membranes, and insulate and protect the body.

solutions.question: Explain the following term: Activation energy.
steps: Activation energy is the minimum energy that reacting particles must possess for a chemical reaction to occur.
solutions.answer: Activation energy is the minimum energy required for a chemical reaction to occur.

solutions.question: Explain the following term: Transition state.
steps: A transition state is the unstable, high-energy state formed temporarily as reactants are converted into products.
In this state, old bonds are partly broken and new bonds are partly formed.
solutions.answer: A transition state is the temporary, unstable high-energy state in which bonds are partly broken and formed.

solutions.question: Explain the following term: Aerobic respiration.
steps: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy
solutions.answer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water, and energy.

solutions.question: Why is it essential to cook some of the food items while others we can eat without cooking?
steps: Cooking softens many foods and makes them easier to chew and digest.
Cooking also destroys many harmful microorganisms present in food.
Some foods are already soft and digestible, so they can be eaten without cooking.
solutions.answer: Some foods need cooking to make them safer and easier to digest, while soft, digestible foods can be eaten raw.

solutions.question: Why does fireworks look spectacular? What type of chemical compounds undergo chemical reactions during this activity?
steps: Fireworks look spectacular because chemical reactions release heat, light, sound, and coloured flames.
The reactions involve fuel and oxidising compounds; metal salts produce the different colours.
solutions.answer: Fireworks are spectacular because reactions release heat, light, and sound; metal salts in the fireworks produce their colours.

definitions.text: This energy is stored in a molecule in which atoms are bonded to each other.
This form of energy is released when a bond is formed and absorbed when it is broken.
Enthalpy (H) or heat content, is defined as the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound. The unit of its measurement is kJ mol⁻¹.
Heat is a form of energy that flows from hot body to a cold body because of a difference in temperature.

In Chemistry, the standard enthalpy of reaction (ΔH°) is the enthalpy change when reactants in their standard states undergo reaction to produce products in their standard states. This quantity is called the standard enthalpy change or heat of reaction at constant pressure.
In Chemistry, any physical or chemical change under study may also be called a system.
Everything else which does not fall in this system is called the surrounding.
When energy is transferred from surrounding to the system, the change is called endothermic and it has a positive sign.
When energy is transferred from system to surrounding, the change is called exothermic and it carries a negative sign, Fig. (5.1).
Heat, which is evolved or absorbed during a chemical reaction, is called the heat of that reaction.
Chemical reactions in which heat energy is evolved are called exothermic reactions
those in which heat energy is absorbed are called endothermic reactions.
The energy absorbed by the reactant or product molecules in order to be converted into the transition state is called the activation energy (Eₐ) of the reaction.
A catalyst is thus, defined as a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.
This process that occurs in the presence of oxygen is called aerobic respiration.
In certain organisms like bacteria and algae respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen and it is called anaerobic respiration.
During glycolysis one molecule of glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvate.
Lipids are a group of organic compounds which include fats, waxes, sterols, etc.

definitions.term: Bond strength and reaction energy rule
definitions.text: When weaker bonds are broken while stronger bonds are formed, the reaction is overall exothermic and vice versa.
A catalyst increases the rate of reaction by decreasing its activation energy.
The reaction is exothermic if the energy of the products is less than that of reactants and endothermic if the energy of the products is more them that of reactants.

mistakes: Writing that exothermic reactions have a positive ΔH. Fix: energy leaves the system, so ΔH is negative.
Confusing heat with enthalpy. Fix: heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; enthalpy is a property of the system.
Saying bond breaking releases energy. Fix: bond breaking absorbs energy; bond formation releases energy.
Forgetting that the bond-formation term is negative when using the signed bond-formation energies given in a question. Fix: check how the data are stated before choosing the formula.
Drawing products at the wrong energy level on a profile. Fix: exothermic products are lower than reactants; endothermic products are higher.
Showing a catalyst changing the reactant or product energy levels. Fix: keep both levels the same and show the catalyst lowering the activation-energy peak.
Mixing up glycogen and lipids. Fix: glycogen is the main stored form of glucose in liver and muscles; lipids act as energy reserves.

shortTheory.question: What is the difference between enthalpy and enthalpy change?
shortTheory.answer: Enthalpy of a system is represented by (H) while the change in enthalpy which a system undergoes is represented by ΔH. The total enthalpy (H) of a system cannot be measured directly. However, the change in enthalpy ΔH brought about in a system can be measured comparatively easily.

shortTheory.question: Why is breaking of a bond an endothermic process?
shortTheory.answer: Breaking of bonds of H₂ and O₂ absorb energy (endothermic process) while making of bonds between H and O evolve energy (exothermic process).

shortTheory.question: Depict the transition state for H₂ + Cl₂ ⟶ 2HCl.
shortTheory.answer: H—H + Cl—Cl ⟶ [H···H···Cl···Cl]‡ ⟶ 2H—Cl. Show the transition state in brackets, with bonds breaking and forming represented by dotted lines.

shortTheory.question: What is the role of glycogen in our body?
shortTheory.answer: Glycogen is the primary storage form of glucose. It is stored in the liver and muscles.

shortTheory.question: Why does the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and nitrogen not take place under normal conditions, but occur in the presence of lightning?
shortTheory.answer: Nitrogen of the atmosphere reacts with oxygen to produce nitric oxide in the presence of lightning. This is because reaction is highly endothermic, so only lightning can provide enough energy for this reaction to take place.

shortTheory.question: Explain the difference between the terms heat and enthalpy.
shortTheory.answer: Heat is a form of energy that flows from hot body to a cold body because of a difference in temperature. We measure heat in joules. Heat is what we call the transfer of thermal energy. Contrary to this, enthalpy is an essential part of a system since it depends on the number of molecules present in that system, its chemical composition and its structure. Heat is not essential part of a system, it just comes and goes. When heat leaves or enters a system, it results in a change of enthalpy. At a constant pressure the enthalpy change is equal to heat evolved or absorbed.

shortTheory.question: Explain why formation of a bond is always an exothermic process.
shortTheory.answer: Since energy is needed to break a bond while energy is evolved when a bond is formed, such reactions take place always with the evolution of heat.

shortTheory.question: Explain activation energy, transition state and aerobic respiration.
shortTheory.answer: The energy absorbed by the reactant or product molecules in order to be converted into the transition state is called the activation energy (Eₐ) of the reaction. The transition state is shown at the peak of curve in Fig. (5.4). This process that occurs in the presence of oxygen is called aerobic respiration.

writtenQuestions.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward changes continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, there is no change or movement.

rubric.why: This distinguishes static equilibrium from continuing dynamic changes.

writtenQuestions.text: Why are some reactions irreversible while others are reversible?
modelAnswer: An irreversible reaction moves in the forward direction only and may go to completion.
In a reversible reaction, the products react among themselves to give back the reactants under the same conditions.
Therefore, a reversible reaction proceeds in both forward and backward directions.
writtenQuestions.followUp: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?

rubric.description: Explains that an irreversible reaction proceeds only forwards.
rubric.why: This gives the defining direction of an irreversible reaction.
rubric.how: State that it moves in the forward direction only.

rubric.description: Notes that an irreversible reaction can go to completion.
rubric.why: Going to completion explains the usual outcome of an irreversible reaction.
rubric.how: Explain that the reactants are converted into products.

rubric.description: Explains that reversible reactions proceed forwards and backwards.
rubric.why: A reversible reaction is characterised by reaction in both directions.

rubric.description: Explains that products can react to give the reactants again under the same conditions.

writtenQuestions.text: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
modelAnswer: Combustion releases a large amount of heat.
Its products do not readily react to give back the original reactants under the same conditions.
Therefore, combustion reactions generally proceed in the forward direction and are irreversible.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask you to define or distinguish reversible and irreversible reactions. State the direction or directions of reaction clearly.
For a symbol question, use ⇌ for a reversible reaction and → for an irreversible reaction.
For a longer explanation, earn marks by giving the observation, the change in substances, and the reason a product can or cannot react back.
For calcium carbonate in an open container, mention that carbon dioxide escapes; in a closed container it can react with calcium oxide to give back the reactants.
For hydrated salts, include both the colours and the effect of heating or moisture: hydrated copper sulphate is blue and anhydrous copper sulphate is white.

hints: Think about what the blue copper sulphate contains.
On heating it loses water; name the white product and say what happens when it absorbs moisture again.
yourTurn.question: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?
solution: Copper sulphate pentahydrate is blue and contains water.
When it is heated, it loses water and forms white anhydrous copper sulphate.
CuSO₄ · 5 H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(g)
White anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture from the atmosphere and turns blue again.
yourTurn.answer: Hydrated copper sulphate is blue. Heating removes water and forms white anhydrous copper sulphate; absorbing moisture changes it back to blue.

steps.why: This equation is the textbook's example of a reaction that proceeds forwards only.

steps.text: The reaction goes to completion.

steps.why: This conclusion follows because the reaction moves in the forward direction only.

example.question: Use the reaction NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) to identify whether the reaction is reversible or irreversible.
example.answer: It is an irreversible reaction; it goes to completion and moves in the forward direction only.

explain.title: Irreversible reactions
explain.body: An irreversible reaction moves in the forward direction only. The textbook's example is the reaction between aqueous sodium chloride and silver nitrate, which goes to completion.

explain.title: Reversible reactions
explain.body: A reversible reaction proceeds forwards and backwards under the same conditions. Its products can react among themselves to give back the reactants. The symbol ⇌ has two half arrowheads pointing in opposite directions.

explain.title: Open and closed containers
explain.body: If a product is removed, or a gas escapes into the atmosphere, a reversible reaction may be forced to go to completion. In a closed container, the gas can remain and react back.

explain.title: Reversible changes in hydrated salts
explain.body: Heating blue hydrated copper sulphate forms white anhydrous copper sulphate and water. Anhydrous copper sulphate absorbs moisture and turns blue again. Heating pink cobalt chloride hexahydrate forms blue anhydrous cobalt chloride; with limited moisture it can form a purple dihydrate, and with more moisture it can form the pink hexahydrate.

mistakes: Do not use → for a reversible reaction; use ⇌.
Do not describe a reversible reaction as one that must go to completion. It can proceed in both directions under the same conditions.
Do not say that a product escaping promotes the backward reaction. An escaping gas cannot react back in the container.
Do not confuse the hydrated and anhydrous colours: hydrated copper sulphate is blue and anhydrous copper sulphate is white.
Do not confuse cobalt chloride colours: anhydrous is blue, the dihydrate is purple, and the hexahydrate is pink.

modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.

writtenQuestions.text: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
modelAnswer: Use a catalyst and suitable conditions to make the reaction rates faster.
For example, the formation and decomposition of ammonia are reasonably fast at around 400°C in the presence of a catalyst, so equilibrium is reached within minutes.

writtenQuestions.text: Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?
modelAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible.
Ice melts to liquid water and liquid water freezes to ice.
Liquid water evaporates to vapour and vapour condenses to liquid water.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask for the meaning of dynamic equilibrium or how it differs from static equilibrium.
For a definition, include both key points: the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, and concentrations remain constant.
A descriptive question may ask how the rates change as equilibrium is approached: the backward reaction begins as products build up, and the rates become equal at equilibrium.
If asked how quickly equilibrium is reached, explain that the time depends on the reaction and its conditions; use the textbook ammonia example if useful.

hints: N₂O₄ is colourless and NO₂ is brown.
As brown NO₂ forms, the reverse reaction begins; at equilibrium, concentrations stop changing.
yourTurn.question: Dinitrogen tetraoxide (N₂O₄) is a colourless gas. It slowly changes to brown coloured nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) at 100° C. Predict how the colour of the mixture will change if N₂O₄ is kept in a sealed flask at 100°C.
solution: At first, colourless N₂O₄ changes into brown NO₂, so the mixture becomes brown.
As NO₂ builds up, the reverse reaction also begins.
When the forward and backward reaction rates become equal, the concentrations stop changing.
The brown colour then remains at a constant shade.
yourTurn.answer: The mixture becomes brown as NO₂ forms. At equilibrium, its brown colour stops changing.

steps.why: The reaction starts in the forward direction when the reactants are mixed.
steps.text: At first, colourless N₂O₄ changes into brown NO₂.

steps.why: The increasing amount of product makes the reverse reaction possible.
steps.text: As NO₂ builds up, the backward reaction starts and forms N₂O₄.

steps.why: Equal rates mean neither direction causes an overall change in concentration.
steps.text: At equilibrium, the forward and backward reaction rates are equal.

steps.why: Constant concentrations mean the visible colour no longer changes.
steps.text: The mixture becomes brown, and its colour then remains at a constant shade.

example.question: Dinitrogen tetraoxide (N₂O₄) is a colourless gas. It slowly changes to brown coloured nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) at 100° C. Predict how the colour of the mixture will change if N₂O₄ is kept in a sealed flask at 100°C.

explain.title: A reversible reaction goes in two directions
explain.body: When a reversible reaction starts, it initially moves in the forward direction. As products build up, they can react to form the original reactants in the backward direction.

explain.title: The rates become equal
explain.body: At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction. The reaction has not stopped; both directions continue.

explain.title: Concentrations stay constant
explain.body: Because the two directions balance, the concentrations of reacting species do not change overall at equilibrium. They do not have to be equal to each other.

explain.title: The time depends on the reaction
explain.body: The time taken to reach equilibrium depends on the nature of the reaction and the conditions. Your textbook gives the ammonia reaction at around 400°C with a catalyst as an example that reaches equilibrium within minutes.

mistakes: Do not write that the reaction stops at equilibrium; both directions continue.
Do not say that reactant and product concentrations must be equal; they remain constant, but need not be equal.
Do not confuse equal reaction rates with equal amounts of reactants and products.
When explaining the changing rates, remember that the backward reaction begins after products have built up.

recap.question: What does the symbol ⇌ show?
recap.answer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions under the same conditions; an irreversible reaction proceeds only in the forward direction.

recap.question: Which description best identifies a reversible reaction?
recap.answer: Reactants form products, and products can form reactants under the same conditions.
