yourTurn.question: What will happen if the gas mixture is compressed?
solution: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), there is 1 mole of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right.
Compression increases the pressure.
The equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas.
Therefore, the equilibrium shifts backward and more PCl₅ is formed.
yourTurn.answer: The equilibrium shifts backward, towards PCl₅, because that side has fewer moles of gas.

hints: Cl₂ is a product in this equation.

Adding Cl₂ disturbs the equilibrium by increasing the product concentration.
The reaction shifts backward to use some of the added Cl₂.
More PCl₅ is formed as the system reaches a new equilibrium.

explain.title: A reversible system can be disturbed

explain.title: Reversible reactions
explain.body: A reversible reaction can proceed in the forward and backward directions. The symbol ⇌ shows that both directions are possible.

explain.title: Dynamic equilibrium
explain.body: In a closed system, equilibrium is reached when the forward and backward reaction rates are equal. Both reactions continue, but the concentrations stay constant.

explain.title: Changing equilibrium
explain.body: Changing concentration, pressure, or temperature can favour one direction. The system responds by shifting in the direction that reduces the effect of the change.

explain.title: Pressure and temperature
explain.body: Increased pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. Increased temperature favours the endothermic direction; cooling favours the exothermic direction.

explain.title: Catalysts

recap.question: What does a catalyst do to a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
recap.answer: The forward and backward reaction rates increase equally; the catalyst makes equilibrium take less time to reach.

recap.question: At equilibrium, more N₂ is added to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). What happens as the system restores equilibrium?

solutions.question: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
steps: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
In static equilibrium, no reaction or movement takes place; the system is at rest.
solutions.answer: Dynamic equilibrium has continuing reactions at equal rates, whereas static equilibrium has no reaction or movement.

solutions.question: How the following reversible reaction will be affected if its temperature is increased? Electricity 2H₂O(l) ⇌ 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
steps: The decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen is an endothermic reaction.
According to Le Chatelier’s principle, increasing the temperature favours the endothermic direction.
Therefore, the equilibrium shifts to the right and the yield of hydrogen and oxygen increases.
solutions.answer: Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of hydrogen and oxygen.

solutions.question: How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?
steps: The yield of products can be increased by changing the conditions to favour the forward reaction.
Choose a suitable temperature and pressure according to the heat change and the number of gaseous molecules in the reaction.
Remove the products as they form, where possible, to shift the equilibrium towards the products.
solutions.answer: Use conditions that favour the forward reaction and remove products as they form.

solutions.question: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
steps: Add a suitable catalyst to the reaction mixture.
A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner.
A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
solutions.answer: A suitable catalyst decreases the time required to attain equilibrium.

solutions.question: What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium? N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
steps: There are two moles of gaseous reactants and two moles of gaseous products.
An increase in pressure does not favour either side when the number of gaseous molecules is equal on both sides.
Therefore, the equilibrium position does not change.
solutions.answer: Increasing the pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

solutions.question: Why are some reactions irreversible while others are reversible?
steps: A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and reverse directions because its products can react to form the original reactants under the same conditions.
An irreversible reaction proceeds mainly in one direction because its products do not readily react to form the original reactants under the same conditions.
solutions.answer: Reactions differ in reversibility because their products differ in their ability to form the original reactants under the same conditions.

solutions.question: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
steps: Combustion reactions are generally highly exothermic.
Their products are stable and do not readily react to form the original substances under ordinary conditions.
Therefore, combustion reactions proceed mainly in the forward direction and are generally irreversible.
solutions.answer: Combustion reactions are generally irreversible because they release much heat and their stable products do not readily reform the reactants.

solutions.question: Can you make an irreversible reaction reversible and vice versa?
steps: A reversible reaction can be made to proceed practically in one direction by continuously removing one of its products.
An apparently irreversible reaction may be reversed if suitable conditions are provided for its products to react back.
Thus, reversibility depends on the reaction conditions; not every irreversible reaction can be reversed.
solutions.answer: Changing conditions can make a reversible reaction proceed one way, and may reverse an apparently irreversible reaction when suitable conditions allow.

solutions.question: How do you know if a reaction is reversible or irreversible?
steps: A reaction is reversible if the products can react with one another to form the original reactants.
A reversible reaction proceeds in both forward and backward directions and is represented by ⇌.
A reaction is irreversible if it proceeds only in one direction and the products do not reform the reactants under the same conditions.
solutions.answer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions; an irreversible reaction proceeds only in one direction.

solutions.question: Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?
steps: The phase changes of water from solid to liquid and from liquid to vapour are reversible.
On cooling, liquid water freezes to ice and water vapour condenses to liquid water.
solutions.answer: Yes. These phase changes are reversible because cooling reverses them.

solutions.question: How can you drive the reversible reaction at equilibrium in the forward direction?
steps: Increase the concentration of the reactants or remove the products as they are formed.
The equilibrium shifts in the forward direction to oppose this change.
solutions.answer: Increase the reactant concentration or remove products to drive the reaction forward.

solutions.question: How can you drive the reversible reaction at equilibrium in the backward direction?
steps: Increase the concentration of the products or remove the reactants.
The equilibrium shifts in the backward direction to oppose this change.
solutions.answer: Increase the product concentration or remove reactants to drive the reaction backward.

solutions.question: Explain how the rates of forward and backward reactions change when the system approaches equilibrium.
steps: At the start, the rate of the forward reaction is high and the rate of the backward reaction is very low.
As the reaction proceeds, the concentration of reactants decreases, so the forward reaction rate decreases.
The concentration of products increases, so the backward reaction rate increases.
At equilibrium, the rates of the forward and backward reactions become equal.
solutions.answer: As equilibrium is approached, the forward rate decreases and the backward rate increases until they are equal.

solutions.question: Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.
steps: A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and backward reactions equally.
It helps the system reach equilibrium more quickly but does not change the position of equilibrium.
solutions.answer: A catalyst speeds up both reactions equally and makes equilibrium occur sooner without changing its position.

solutions.question: How can a reversible reaction be forced to go to completion?
steps: A reversible reaction can be forced to go to completion by continuously removing one of the products as it is formed.
solutions.answer: Continuously remove one of the products as it forms.

solutions.question: How does change in temperature affect the reaction at equilibrium?
steps: An increase in temperature favours the endothermic direction of a reversible reaction.
A decrease in temperature favours the exothermic direction.
Thus, changing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the direction that opposes the temperature change.
solutions.answer: Heating favours the endothermic direction, while cooling favours the exothermic direction.

solutions.question: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?
steps: Hydrated copper sulphate crystals are blue because they contain water of crystallization.
On heating, blue copper sulphate pentahydrate loses its water of crystallization and becomes white anhydrous copper sulphate.
CuSO₄·5H₂O  —heat→  CuSO₄ + 5H₂O
The water vapours condense as droplets on the cooler part of the test tube.
Adding water to the white anhydrous copper sulphate makes it blue again.
solutions.answer: Hydrated copper sulphate is blue because of its water of crystallization; heating removes this water, changing it into white anhydrous copper sulphate.

solutions.question: Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.
steps: Ammonia is prepared by the Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat.
The reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature favours the formation of ammonia; in practice, about 450°C is used to obtain a suitable rate.
The product side has fewer gas molecules, so high pressure favours the formation of ammonia; about 200 atmospheres is used.
Finely divided iron is used as a catalyst to increase the rate of reaction.
Nitrogen and hydrogen are used in the ratio 1:3, and unreacted gases are recycled.
solutions.answer: Use nitrogen and hydrogen in a 1:3 ratio at about 450°C and 200 atmospheres with a finely divided iron catalyst; recycle unreacted gases.

definitions.text: Such a reaction is called an irreversible reaction. It moves in the forward direction only.
The reaction is called a reversible reaction and it is denoted by a symbol ⇌ which has two half arrowheads one pointing in each direction.
At this stage, the reaction is said to be in a state of chemical equilibrium.

Since the reaction did not cease at this state of equilibrium, rather it keeps on going in both the directions, this state is called dynamic equilibrium. The concentrations of reacting species (reactants and products) remain constant at equilibrium.

definitions.term: Rule for forcing a reversible reaction to completion
definitions.text: A reversible reaction never goes to completion. However, it may be forced to go to completion if one or all the products are withdrawn from the reaction mixture as soon as it is or they are formed.

definitions.term: Effect of a catalyst on a reversible reaction
definitions.text: A catalyst increases both the rates of forward and back reactions of a reversible reaction. So if a reversible reaction is carried out in the presence of a catalyst it will decrease the time taken by the reaction to attain the state of equilibrium.

formulas.formula: rate of forward reaction = rate of backward reaction
formulas.use: Condition for dynamic equilibrium; each rate has units of concentration per time, e.g. mol m⁻³ s⁻¹.
Haber equilibrium. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules: 2 moles of gas rather than 4. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate; in an open container, escaping CO₂ drives the reaction forward. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Heating blue hydrated copper sulphate forms white anhydrous copper sulphate; adding moisture reverses the change. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Heating pink hydrated cobalt chloride forms blue anhydrous cobalt chloride; moisture reverses the change. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Use to predict the effect of pressure, adding Cl₂, or changing temperature; the forward side has 1 mole of gas and the backward side 2. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Example of a sealed gas mixture changing from colourless N₂O₄ to brown NO₂. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Formation of ethyl acetate; removing water as it forms favours the forward reaction. The coefficients are dimensionless ratios.
Enthalpy change for forward ammonia formation; ΔH is in J mol⁻¹ in SI units (−92 400 J mol⁻¹).

Tests the central distinction between reactions that do and do not proceed in both directions.
A short explanation applying the idea of products reacting back to form reactants.

A standard structured response about disturbances that favour the forward direction.
Pairs with the forward-direction question and tests the effects of changing conditions.
A core explanation of how dynamic equilibrium is reached.
A standard structured response based on withdrawing products as they form.

fullMarks: For a definition, write the full statement, including the key idea that both reactions continue at dynamic equilibrium and concentrations remain constant.

When explaining a change at equilibrium, first name the disturbance (adding or removing a species, changing temperature or pressure, or adding a catalyst), then state which direction is favoured and why.
For pressure questions, compare the total gaseous moles on each side. Pressure changes equilibrium only when those totals differ; higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
For temperature questions, identify which direction is exothermic or endothermic before stating the direction favoured by heating or cooling.
For catalyst questions, state that it increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions and reduces the time to reach equilibrium; it does not shift the equilibrium position.
For questions about forcing completion, explain that removing a product as it forms drives the reaction forward. Give the relevant example if the question asks for one.
Write chemical equations with correct formulae, subscripts, state symbols and the reversible arrow ⇌. In an explanation, finish with a clear statement of the resulting direction or change.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying the reactions stop at equilibrium. Fix: State that both reactions continue, but at equal rates.
Mistake: Saying the concentrations of reactants and products become equal. Fix: They remain constant; they do not have to be equal to each other.
Mistake: Using → for a reversible reaction. Fix: Use ⇌ to show both forward and backward directions.
Mistake: Claiming a catalyst pushes equilibrium towards the products. Fix: It increases both reaction rates and helps the system reach equilibrium sooner; it does not favour either side.
Mistake: Saying increased pressure always shifts a gaseous equilibrium. Fix: Compare gas moles on both sides first; if the totals are equal, pressure does not shift it.
Mistake: Saying that heating always drives a reaction forward. Fix: Check which direction is endothermic; heating favours that direction.
Mistake: Saying that a reversible reaction cannot be made to go to completion. Fix: Explain that removing a product as it forms can force it to go to completion.

shortTheory.question: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
shortTheory.answer: At dynamic equilibrium, the reaction keeps on going in both the directions, and the concentrations of reacting species remain constant. In static equilibrium, no change is taking place.

shortTheory.question: How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?
shortTheory.answer: Withdraw one or all the products from the reaction mixture as soon as they are formed. The reaction is then driven in the forward direction.

shortTheory.question: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
shortTheory.answer: A catalyst increases both the rates of forward and backward reactions of a reversible reaction. So if a reversible reaction is carried out in the presence of a catalyst it will decrease the time taken by the reaction to attain the state of equilibrium.

shortTheory.question: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
shortTheory.answer: Combustion reactions are generally irreversible because the products formed do not react among themselves to give back the reactants under the same conditions.

shortTheory.question: Explain how the rates of forward and backward reactions change when the system approaches equilibrium.
shortTheory.answer: The forward reaction starts first. As products build up, they react to give back the reactants in the reverse reaction. Both reactions continue until the rate of forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of backward reaction.

shortTheory.question: How can a reversible reaction be forced to go to completion?
shortTheory.answer: A reversible reaction may be forced to go to completion if one or all the products are withdrawn from the reaction mixture as soon as they are formed.

explain.title: Acids
explain.body: Acids are known for their sour taste and their ability to change blue litmus paper to red. Lemon and curd are examples of everyday substances associated with acids.

explain.title: Natural and mineral acids
explain.body: Acids obtained from natural sources are called natural or organic acids. Mineral or man-made acids are prepared from minerals; hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid and nitric acid are examples.

explain.title: Bases and alkalis
explain.body: Bases are known for their bitter taste and slippery touch, and they change red litmus paper to blue. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are examples.

explain.title: Basic oxides and neutralization
explain.body: Metal oxides can be basic because they react with acids to form salt and water. Sodium oxide also reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide. When acids and bases cancel each other's properties, the reaction is called neutralization; salt and water form.

writtenQuestions.text: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
modelAnswer: A strong acid ionizes to a large extent in water.
A concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid in a given volume of solution.
Therefore, strength depends on ionization, whereas concentration depends on the amount of acid present.
A strong acid is not necessarily concentrated, and a concentrated acid is not necessarily strong.

explain.title: Arrhenius acids
explain.body: An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺). For example, HCl ionizes in water to form H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻.

explain.title: Arrhenius bases
explain.body: A base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻). For example, NaOH gives Na⁺ and OH⁻ in water.

explain.title: Water and neutralization
explain.body: Water surrounds the ions formed in solution. In a strong acid–strong base neutralization, H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ react to form water and release heat: H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + Heat.

explain.title: Strong and weak ionization
explain.body: The strength of an acid depends upon the extent to which it is ionized in water. Mineral acids such as HCl ionize extensively, while organic acids such as acetic acid ionize to a very limited extent. NaOH and KOH are strong bases; NH₄OH is a weak base that only partially ionizes.

explain.title: Acids in the stomach
explain.body: The stomach produces hydrochloric acid to digest food. Too much acid can cause stomach acidity. Weak bases such as calcium hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide are used in antacids to neutralize stomach acid.

mistakes: Writing OH⁻ as the ion produced by an Arrhenius acid; acids produce H⁺ or H₃O⁺.
Writing H₃O⁺ as the ion produced by an Arrhenius base; bases produce OH⁻.
Confusing acid strength with concentration: strength concerns ionization, while concentration concerns the amount of acid in solution.
Forgetting the charges on ions when writing ionization equations.
Saying that NaCl forms as solid crystals during neutralization in water; the textbook describes hydrated Na⁺ and Cl⁻ spectator ions in solution.

modelAnswer: Water can act as an acid by donating a proton (H⁺).
Water can act as a base by accepting a proton (H⁺).
Therefore, water can behave as both an acid and a base.
Water is called an amphoteric compound.

steps.why: The reaction shows HCl and H₂O as the reactants and the products formed after proton transfer.
steps.text: HCl(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻

steps.why: HCl gives H⁺ to water, so it is the proton donor and therefore the acid.
steps.text: HCl is the acid.

steps.why: H₂O receives H⁺ from HCl, so it is the proton acceptor and therefore the base.
steps.text: H₂O is the base.

steps.why: After HCl donates H⁺, Cl⁻ remains as its conjugate base; after H₂O accepts H⁺, H₃O⁺ is its conjugate acid.
steps.text: H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

example.question: For HCl(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid and conjugate base.

explain.title: The Brønsted–Lowry idea
explain.body: The section gives these definitions: “An acid is a substance that donates a proton.” and “A base is a substance that accepts a proton.” A proton is H⁺. Look for which substance gives H⁺ and which one receives it.

explain.title: How this differs from Arrhenius
explain.body: The Arrhenius definitions require water as the solvent. Brønsted–Lowry uses proton transfer, so the reaction may take place in the gas phase or in the presence of any solvent. A substance does not need to contain OH⁻ to behave as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

explain.title: Conjugate acid and conjugate base
explain.body: When an acid gives away H⁺, the species left is its conjugate base. When a base receives H⁺, the product is its conjugate acid. In HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid and Cl⁻ is the conjugate base.

explain.title: Water can do either job
explain.body: Water accepts H⁺ from HCl, so it acts as a base in that reaction. Water donates H⁺ to NH₃, so it acts as an acid there. A compound that can behave as both an acid and a base is called amphoteric.

mistakes: Do not label an acid or base just by looking for OH⁻; follow the proton transfer.
Do not call the proton acceptor an acid: accepting H⁺ makes it a base.
Do not assume water must be involved in every Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction.
Do not confuse a conjugate acid with a conjugate base: accepting H⁺ forms the conjugate acid, while donating H⁺ forms the conjugate base.
When describing water, include both behaviours and the term amphoteric.

yourTurn.question: State the effects of acid rain on soil, plants, aquatic life, and human-made structures.

Acid rain and dry deposition of acidic particles damage buildings, statues, automobiles, and other structures made of stone and metal.

yourTurn.question: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water for a long duration?
solution: The initial CaCO₃ precipitate reacts with excess CO₂ and water.
CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂
The soluble product makes the milkiness disappear.
yourTurn.answer: The milkiness disappears because soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate forms.

steps.why: Calcium is a metal and sulfuric acid supplies the sulfate ion; metals reacting with acids form a salt and hydrogen.
steps.text: Question: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?

steps.why: This is the reaction pattern for a metal with an acid: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
steps.text: Given: calcium metal, Ca; dilute sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄.

steps.why: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so their salt formula is CaSO₄.
steps.text: Products: calcium sulfate, CaSO₄, and hydrogen gas, H₂.

steps.why: One atom of each element is balanced on both sides, including two hydrogen atoms as H₂.
steps.text: Equation: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂.

steps.why: The equation gives the products and the balanced chemical result.
steps.text: Answer: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂.

example.question: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?
example.answer: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂

explain.title: Two ways to define acids and bases
explain.body: In the Arrhenius concept, an acid produces H⁺ in water and a base produces OH⁻ in water. In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺.

explain.title: Acids react in familiar patterns
explain.body: A metal reacting with an acid commonly forms a salt and hydrogen. An acid reacting with a carbonate forms a salt, carbon dioxide and water. An acid reacting with a base or basic oxide forms a salt and water.

explain.title: Acid strength is not concentration
explain.body: Strength describes the extent to which an acid ionizes in water. Concentration describes how much acid is present in a given volume of solution.

explain.title: Conjugate acid–base pairs differ by H⁺
explain.body: When an acid donates H⁺, the species left is its conjugate base. For example, CH₃COOH donates H⁺ to form CH₃COO⁻.

explain.title: Some oxides and ions can act both ways
explain.body: Non-metallic oxides generally show acidic character by reacting with bases. Water and HCO₃⁻ can take part in proton transfer as either an acid or a base.

mistakes: Do not confuse acid strength with acid concentration; one describes ionization and the other amount per volume.
Do not forget that acid–carbonate reactions produce carbon dioxide as well as salt and water.
Balance equations and write correct ion charges in formulas, such as CaSO₄ and BaCl₂.
A conjugate base is formed after an acid loses H⁺; it is not the species formed after gaining H⁺.
For the lime-water test, distinguish the short-duration milky precipitate from the clearing caused by excess CO₂.
Do not claim that every acidic substance must contain an ionised hydrogen already; explain proton transfer or ion formation in water as appropriate.

recap.question: Name two effects of acid rain.
recap.answer: Acid rain can harm soil and plants, make water too acidic for aquatic animals, and damage buildings and other structures.

recap.question: According to this section, which rain water is called acid rain?
recap.answer: Rain water with a pH between 4.2 and 4.4

solutions.question: Choose Arrhenius Acids among the following compounds. HF, NH₄⁺, H₂SO₃, SO₃, H₂S, H₂O
steps: An Arrhenius acid is a substance that ionizes in water to produce hydrogen ions (H⁺).
HF, H₂SO₃ and H₂S ionize in water to produce H⁺ ions.
NH₄⁺ can donate a proton to water, producing hydronium ions: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺.
SO₃ is an acidic oxide, not an Arrhenius acid; H₂O is not an Arrhenius acid.
Therefore, the Arrhenius acids are HF, NH₄⁺, H₂SO₃ and H₂S.
solutions.answer: HF, NH₄⁺, H₂SO₃ and H₂S are Arrhenius acids.

solutions.question: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?
steps: Calcium reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form calcium sulphate and hydrogen gas.
Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂↑
Calcium sulphate is sparingly soluble and forms a coating on the calcium metal, so the reaction soon slows down or stops.
solutions.answer: Calcium forms calcium sulphate and hydrogen gas; the CaSO₄ coating soon slows or stops the reaction.

solutions.question: Which salt is formed when HCl reacts with BaCO₃?
steps: Hydrochloric acid reacts with barium carbonate to form barium chloride, water and carbon dioxide.
BaCO₃ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑
solutions.answer: Barium chloride (BaCl₂) is formed.

solutions.question: How will you justify that HSO₄⁻ is a Brønsted – Lowry acid?
steps: According to the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid is a proton donor.
The hydrogen sulphate ion donates a proton to water, forming a sulphate ion and a hydronium ion.
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + H₃O⁺
solutions.answer: HSO₄⁻ is a Brønsted–Lowry acid because it donates a proton.

solutions.question: Why is HCl not edible although it is present in the stomach and responsible for digestion of food?
steps: Hydrochloric acid is corrosive and harmful if taken as food.
The stomach contains HCl in a dilute form, where it helps in digestion.
The stomach lining protects the stomach from the acid.
solutions.answer: HCl is corrosive and is not edible, although dilute HCl in the stomach helps digestion and is protected from damaging the stomach by its lining.

solutions.question: What chemical name will you give to soap as a compound?
steps: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a higher fatty acid.
For example, sodium stearate is a soap.
solutions.answer: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a higher fatty acid.

solutions.question: In the presence of a drop of an acid, water is known to ionize as follows: H₂O (l) ⇌ H⁺ (aq) + OH⁻ (aq). In your opinion, which name will be suitable for water: an acid, a base or both?
steps: Water can act as both an acid and a base; such a substance is called amphoteric.
Water can donate a proton to form OH⁻, as shown by H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻.
Water can also accept a proton to form H₃O⁺.
solutions.answer: Water is amphoteric because it can act as both an acid and a base.

solutions.question: Why does Na₂CO₃ behave like a base in water?
steps: Sodium carbonate is a salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H₂CO₃).
In water, the carbonate ion reacts with water to produce hydroxide ions.
CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻
The OH⁻ ions make the solution basic.
solutions.answer: Na₂CO₃ behaves as a base in water because it produces OH⁻ ions.

solutions.question: Is NaHCO₃ a base or an acid? Justify your answer.
steps: HCO₃⁻ can act as both an acid and a base; it is an amphiprotic ion.
It acts as a base by accepting a proton: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃.
It acts as an acid by donating a proton: HCO₃⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H⁺.
Therefore, NaHCO₃ is not classified only as an acid or only as a base; its HCO₃⁻ ion can behave as either.
solutions.answer: The HCO₃⁻ ion in NaHCO₃ can act as both an acid and a base.

solutions.question: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
steps: A strong acid ionizes completely in water, whereas a weak acid ionizes only partially.
A concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of solution, whereas a dilute acid contains a small amount.
Strength describes the extent of ionization; concentration describes the amount of acid in a given volume.
Thus, strength and concentration are different properties.
solutions.answer: Strength is the extent of ionization, while concentration is the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume.

solutions.question: Explain Arrhenius concept of acids and bases.
steps: According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water.
A base is a substance that produces hydroxide ions (OH⁻) when dissolved in water.
For example: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
solutions.answer: An Arrhenius acid produces H⁺ ions in water, and an Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ ions in water.

solutions.question: Compare Arrhenius and Brønsted – Lowry concepts of acids and bases.
steps: According to Arrhenius, an acid produces H⁺ ions and a base produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.
The Arrhenius concept is limited to reactions in water and explains acids and bases by the ions they produce.
According to Brønsted–Lowry, an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor.
The Brønsted–Lowry concept applies to proton-transfer reactions and is not restricted to aqueous solutions.
Thus, the Arrhenius concept is based on ion production in water, while the Brønsted–Lowry concept is based on proton transfer.
solutions.answer: Arrhenius defines acids and bases by the ions they produce in water; Brønsted–Lowry defines them as proton donors and acceptors.

solutions.question: How does sulphuric acid react with the following compounds? NH₄Cl, NH₄NO₃, MgO, MgCO₃
steps: Sulphuric acid reacts with ammonium chloride to form ammonium sulphate and hydrogen chloride: 2NH₄Cl + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2HCl.
Sulphuric acid reacts with ammonium nitrate to form ammonium sulphate and nitric acid: 2NH₄NO₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2HNO₃.
Sulphuric acid reacts with magnesium oxide to form magnesium sulphate and water: MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O.
Sulphuric acid reacts with magnesium carbonate to form magnesium sulphate, carbon dioxide and water: MgCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O.
solutions.answer: Sulphuric acid forms ammonium sulphate and an acid with the ammonium salts, magnesium sulphate and water with MgO, and magnesium sulphate, carbon dioxide and water with MgCO₃.

solutions.question: What happens when a base reacts with a non-metallic oxide. What do you infer about the nature of non-metallic oxide?
steps: A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form salt and water.
For example: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.
This reaction shows that non-metallic oxides have acidic nature.
solutions.answer: Non-metallic oxides react with bases to form salt and water; therefore, they are acidic in nature.

solutions.question: State the reason of showing acidic character by both dry HCl gas and HCl solution in water.
steps: Dry HCl gas consists of covalent HCl molecules and does not produce hydrogen ions in the absence of water.
Therefore, dry HCl gas does not show acidic character.
In water, HCl ionizes and forms hydronium ions: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
The hydronium ions are responsible for the acidic character of aqueous HCl.
solutions.answer: HCl shows acidic character in water because it forms H₃O⁺ ions; dry HCl gas does not show acidic character.

solutions.question: Differentiate between an acid and its conjugate base.
steps: An acid is a species that donates a proton (H⁺).
When an acid donates a proton, the species left behind is called its conjugate base.
A conjugate base can accept a proton to reform its acid.
For example: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻; HCl is the acid and Cl⁻ is its conjugate base.
solutions.answer: An acid donates a proton, and the species formed after it donates that proton is its conjugate base.

solutions.question: Acids play significant roles within human body. Comment on this statement.
steps: Hydrochloric acid is present in the stomach and helps in the digestion of food.
Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, which are essential for the growth and repair of the body.
Thus, acids are important for several functions in the human body.
solutions.answer: Acids help in digestion and are essential for the growth and repair of the body.

solutions.question: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water for a short duration?
steps: Lime water turns milky when carbon dioxide is passed through it for a short duration.
The milkiness is due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.
Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
solutions.answer: Lime water turns milky due to the formation of calcium carbonate.

solutions.question: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water for a long duration?
steps: On passing carbon dioxide through lime water for a long duration, the milkiness disappears.
The insoluble calcium carbonate reacts with excess carbon dioxide and water to form soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate.
CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂
solutions.answer: The milkiness disappears because soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate is formed.

definitions.text: Acids which are obtained from natural sources are called natural or organic acids.
Mineral or man-made acids are prepared from minerals like sodium chloride or sodium nitrate.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺).
Similarly, a base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻).
Define a strong acid and base as an acid or base that completely dissociates in aqueous solution
weak acid and base that partially dissociates in aqueous solution.
An acid is a substance that donates a proton.
A base is a substance that accepts a proton.
According to Bronsted-Lowry, an acid base reaction is that reaction in which a proton is transferred from a proton donor to its acceptor.
Water is therefore called an amphoteric compound which means a compound that can behave both as an acid and a base.

Both acids and bases are known to cancel the properties of each other when mixed together in equal amounts. The reaction is called neutralization reaction. A salt and water are formed as a result of this reaction.
When rain water has pH between 4.2 – 4.4, it is called acid rain.
Acids are those compounds which have a sour taste and which turn blue litmus red. They also give hydroxonium ions when dissolved in water.
Bases or alkalis are those compounds which are bitter in taste, have a slippery touch and which change red litmus blue. They also form hydroxide ions when dissolved in water.

fullMarks: For a concept question, state the relevant definition first, then apply it to the named substance; for Brønsted–Lowry questions, identify who donates H⁺ and who accepts H⁺.
For comparisons, give both definitions and then state the key difference: Arrhenius requires dissociation in water, while Brønsted–Lowry describes proton transfer and does not require water.
For reaction questions, write a complete balanced equation with correct formulas, charges, state symbols where given, and the required observation or product.
For acid–metal reactions, name the salt and state that hydrogen gas is evolved; for acid–carbonate reactions, state that carbon dioxide is evolved.
When explaining strong versus weak acids or bases, compare complete dissociation with partial dissociation; do not confuse strength with how concentrated a solution is.
For conjugate acid–base questions, show the proton transfer and identify each conjugate partner; conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺.
In acid-rain answers, give the stated pH range, explain that SO₂ and NO₂ form acidic droplets with moisture, and name effects on soil, plants, aquatic life, or structures.
For an observation question, state what is seen directly and connect it to the reaction; do not give only an equation when the question asks what is observed.
mistakes: Mistake: Calling every base an alkali. Fix: An alkali is specifically a base that dissolves in water; some bases are sparingly soluble or insoluble.
Mistake: Saying an Arrhenius acid simply contains hydrogen. Fix: State that it dissociates in water to give H⁺ or H₃O⁺.
Mistake: Calling HSO₄⁻ only a base because it has a negative charge. Fix: It can donate H⁺, so it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
Mistake: Confusing a strong acid with a concentrated acid. Fix: Strength is about the extent of ionization; concentration is a different property.
Mistake: Forgetting to balance reaction equations or leaving out gas products. Fix: Check atom counts and include H₂, CO₂, or NH₃ when the reaction calls for it.
Mistake: Saying acid plus carbonate produces only a salt. Fix: Include water and carbon dioxide in the products.
Mistake: Treating NaHCO₃ as having only one possible acid–base role. Fix: The HCO₃⁻ ion can donate or accept a proton, depending on the reaction.

shortTheory.question: What is an Arrhenius acid?
shortTheory.answer: An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺).

shortTheory.question: What is an Arrhenius base?
shortTheory.answer: Similarly, a base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻).

shortTheory.question: Define a Brønsted–Lowry acid and base.
shortTheory.answer:
An acid is a substance that donates a proton.
A base is a substance that accepts a proton.

shortTheory.question: Why is water called an amphoteric compound?
shortTheory.answer: Water is therefore called an amphoteric compound which means a compound that can behave both as an acid and a base.

shortTheory.question: What is a neutralization reaction?
shortTheory.answer: Both acids and bases are known to cancel the properties of each other when mixed together in equal amounts. The reaction is called neutralization reaction. A salt and water are formed as a result of this reaction.

shortTheory.question: What happens when an acid reacts with a reactive metal?
shortTheory.answer:
With reactive metals (Mg, Zn) they form salts and evolve hydrogen gas.
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

shortTheory.question: What happens when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
shortTheory.answer:
They decompose metal carbonates and hydrogen carbonates evolving carbon dioxide gas.
CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)

shortTheory.question: What happens when an alkali reacts with an ammonium salt?
shortTheory.answer:
Apart from reacting with acids in neutralization reactions, alkalies also react with ammonium salts and liberate ammonia gas.
NaOH(aq) + NH₄NO₃(aq) → NaNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) + NH₃(g)

writtenQuestions.text: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?
modelAnswer: Elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number.
In this arrangement, the properties of elements repeat after regular intervals.

yourTurn.question: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?
solution: Elements in the modern periodic table are arranged in increasing order of atomic number.
When arranged this way, the properties of elements repeat after regular intervals.
Therefore, atomic number is the basis of the modern periodic table.
yourTurn.answer: The modern periodic table is based on increasing atomic number, and element properties repeat regularly in this arrangement.

example.question: No worked example is provided in this section.

explain.title: The modern table is arranged by atomic number
explain.body: The modern periodic table is based upon the arrangement of elements according to increasing atomic number. Elements are arranged from left to right in ascending order of their atomic numbers.

explain.title: Periods and groups
explain.body: The horizontal rows of elements in the periodic table are called periods while the vertical columns are called groups.

explain.title: Why properties repeat
explain.body: In a period, electronic configuration changes from left to right, so properties change gradually. Elements in a group have similar electronic configurations in their outermost shells and show similar chemical properties. Properties repeat after regular intervals; this trend is called periodicity in the properties.

mistakes: Do not confuse periods and groups: periods are horizontal rows, while groups are vertical columns.
Do not say the modern periodic table is arranged by atomic mass; it is arranged by increasing atomic number.
Do not claim that elements in a group have identical properties; say that they show similar chemical properties.
Do not forget to explain that periodicity means properties repeat after regular intervals.

explain.title: Periods
explain.body: The horizontal rows in the modern periodic table are called periods. There are seven periods in total. Each period represents the completion of a shell. Table (8.1) shows the number of elements and the shell being filled in each period.

explain.title: Groups and families
explain.body: The vertical columns present in the periodic table are called groups. There are eighteen groups. Elements present in a group resemble one another in their chemical properties since they contain the same number of electrons in their outermost shells. A group is also called a family.

explain.title: Group configurations
explain.body: Learn the outermost-shell configurations in Table (8.2). For example, group 1 is ns¹, group 2 is ns², group 17 is ns² np⁵, and group 18 is ns² np⁶.

explain.title: Blocks
explain.body: Elements are classified into s, p, d and f blocks depending upon the type of subshell which is being filled. Groups 1 and 2 are s-block; groups 13 to 18 are p-block; groups 3 to 12 are d-block; and the two rows at the bottom are f-block elements.

explain.title: Lanthanides and actinides
explain.body: The first series of fourteen elements starts after lanthanum and is called lanthanides. The second series starts after actinium and is called actinides. Together these two series are also called rare earths or f-block elements.

mistakes: Mixing up periods and groups: periods are horizontal rows, while groups are vertical columns.
Saying there are eighteen periods; the table has seven periods and eighteen groups.
Naming a block from the group number alone without checking which subshell is being filled.
Forgetting that the period depends on the number of the shell being filled; shorthand such as s²p³ does not itself show that shell number.
Calling the lanthanides and actinides groups instead of two series placed at the bottom of the table.

recap.question: What are the horizontal rows and vertical columns of the periodic table called?
recap.answer: The horizontal rows are periods, and the vertical columns are groups.

explain.title: Why members of a group behave alike
explain.body: The chemical properties of elements depend largely upon the number of electrons present in their outermost shells. Since in a group of the periodic table all the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell, they are expected to show similar chemical properties.

explain.title: Groups 1 and 2 lose electrons
explain.body: Group 1 elements lose one outermost electron and form positive ions. They are thus known as electropositive metals. Group 2 elements tend to lose both of their outermost electrons and form dipositive ions. The tendency to lose electrons down the group increases due to gradual increase in their atomic sizes.

explain.title: Groups 16 and 17 gain electrons
explain.body: Group 17 elements tend to gain one electron to become an anion. They are called electronegative elements. Group 16 elements tend to accept two electrons to form a dinegative ion.

explain.title: Reactivity trends
explain.body: The reactivity of alkali metals gradually increases down the group. Unlike alkali metals, the reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

explain.title: Relating group position to ion charge
explain.body: Groups 1, 2 and 3 form cations with charges 1+, 2+ and 3+ respectively. Groups 17 and 16 form anions with charges 1− and 2− respectively, as they need one or two electrons to complete their octets.

mistakes: Do not confuse the direction of the reactivity trends: alkali-metal reactivity increases down the group, but halogen reactivity decreases.
Do not give an ion charge without stating whether electrons were gained or lost.
Do not mix up group 16 and group 17: group 16 tends to gain two electrons, while group 17 tends to gain one.
Write the ion charge as a superscript-style charge, such as Mg²⁺ or Cl⁻, rather than changing the element’s subscript.

explain.title: Periodicity
explain.body: Periodicity in the properties of the elements occur due to recurrence of similar electronic configuration in the outermost shells. These properties include atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

explain.title: Atomic radius
explain.body: Atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of the two identical bonded atoms. It is expressed in pm(1pm = 10⁻¹²m). Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases because increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer. Down a group, it increases because a new shell is added and inner electrons shield outer electrons.

explain.title: Ionization energy
explain.body: Ionization energy is the amount of energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom. A smaller atomic radius means stronger attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons, so ionization energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.

explain.title: Electron affinity
explain.body: Electron affinity is the amount of energy change when an electron is added up in the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom. In a group, electron affinity values decrease from top to bottom because atomic size increases and the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly.

explain.title: Electronegativity
explain.body: Electronegativity of an atom is its electron-attracting ability. It is defined as the force with which an atom attracts the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a bond. It increases from left to right in a period and decreases from top to bottom in a group.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic radius with the full distance between two identical bonded nuclei; the radius is half that distance.
Do not reverse the general trends: atomic radius increases down a group, while ionization energy and electronegativity decrease down a group.
Do not say that ionization energy is energy released when an electron is added; it is energy required to remove an electron.
When giving a trend across a period, include the reason: increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer.

explain.title: Meaning of metallic character
explain.body: The metallic character is the tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions or cations. An element that loses electrons readily has strong metallic character.

explain.title: Trend down a group
explain.body: Since the ionization energy decreases down the group, the elements have increased ability to lose electrons. For this reason both the metallic character and reactivity increase down the group.

explain.title: Trend across a period
explain.body: As we move from left to right in a period, the nuclear charge increases due to a gradual increase in the number of protons in the nucleus. Owing to this the valence electrons are pulled strongly by the nucleus making it difficult for the atoms to lose electrons. Hence the metallic character decreases in a period from left to right.

explain.title: Reactivity across a period and density
explain.body: The chemical reactivity gradually decreases as we move from left to right in a period through the metals, because losing electrons becomes more difficult. Moving further right towards non-metals, chemical reactivity gradually increases again. Density is mass per unit volume, is expressed in g/cm³, and generally increases down a group.

mistakes: Do not say metallic character increases from left to right; it decreases across a period.
Do not forget the reason for the trend: ionization energy decreases down a group, so losing electrons becomes easier.
Do not treat the reactivity trend across a whole period as a simple continuous decrease; it increases again towards non-metals.
Do not claim density rises at every step in the displayed Group 1 data; describe the trend as general.
Do not confuse electropositive (tendency to lose electrons) with electronegative (tendency to attract electrons).

explain.title: The modern periodic table
explain.body: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. The electronic configuration helps determine an element's period, group and block.

explain.title: Periods, groups and blocks
explain.body: A period is a horizontal row and a group is a vertical column. Elements in a group have related outer-shell arrangements. The four blocks are s, p, d and f.

explain.title: Periodic trends
explain.body: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases and ionization energy generally increases. Down a group, atomic size and metallic character generally increase.

explain.title: Electrons and bonding
explain.body: Metals tend to lose electrons, while non-metals tend to gain or attract electrons. Ionic bonding generally involves electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal.

explain.title: Using the table
explain.body: The periodic table helps organise elements, compare their properties and predict behaviour from their positions and electron arrangements.

mistakes: Do not confuse atomic number with atomic mass; the modern table is arranged by atomic number.
Do not reverse the across-period trends: atomic radius generally decreases, while ionization energy generally increases.
When explaining a trend, include its reason, not only the direction of change.
Do not say oxygen accepts three electrons; it needs two electrons to complete its outer shell.
Write both the comparison and the reason when a question asks for a reason.

recap.question: How does metallic character change down a group?
recap.answer: Metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group.

recap.question: What happens to metallic character as you move down a group?
recap.answer: It generally increases because atoms lose electrons more easily down the group.

solutions.question: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?
steps: Atomic number was chosen to arrange the elements because the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
When elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number, elements with similar properties occur at regular intervals.
This arrangement also places isotopes of an element in the same position, because they have the same atomic number.
solutions.answer: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers, so atomic number gives the correct basis for arranging the periodic table.

solutions.question: What is the significance of the word periodic?
steps: The word “periodic” means that something repeats at regular intervals.
In the periodic table, the properties of elements repeat at regular intervals when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
solutions.answer: “Periodic” means that the properties of elements repeat at regular intervals.

solutions.question: Why does the size of a period increase as we move down the periodic table?
steps: The size of a period depends on the number of electrons accommodated in the shells being filled.
As we move down the periodic table, new shells have greater capacity to accommodate electrons.
Therefore, more elements are needed to fill these shells and the size of the periods increases.
solutions.answer: Periods become larger down the table because the shells being filled can accommodate more electrons.

solutions.question: In a group, the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell. Why is it so?
steps: The elements in a group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell because their atoms have similar outer electronic configurations.
As we move down a group, new electron shells are added, but the number of electrons in the outermost shell remains the same.
solutions.answer: Elements in the same group have the same number of outermost-shell electrons because their outer electronic configurations are similar.

solutions.question: Do you expect calcium to be more reactive than sodium? Give the reason of your answer.
steps: No. Calcium is less reactive than sodium.
Sodium has one electron in its outermost shell and can lose it more readily than calcium can lose its two outermost electrons.
Therefore, sodium is more reactive than calcium.
solutions.answer: No. Sodium is more reactive because it loses its outermost electron more readily than calcium loses its electrons.

solutions.question: Which element has the maximum atomic radius and which element has the minimum atomic radius in third period?
steps: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period because nuclear charge increases and pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus.
In the third period, sodium has the maximum atomic radius and argon has the minimum atomic radius.
solutions.answer: Sodium has the maximum atomic radius and argon has the minimum atomic radius in the third period.

solutions.question: Why are the most electronegative elements present in sixth and seventh groups?
steps: Elements in the sixth and seventh groups have six and seven electrons, respectively, in their outermost shells.
They need only two or one electrons, respectively, to complete their outermost shell.
Therefore, they attract electrons strongly and have high electronegativity.
solutions.answer: Elements in the sixth and seventh groups are highly electronegative because they need only two or one electrons to complete their outermost shells.

solutions.question: The first ionization energy value of magnesium is less than the second one. Give reason.
steps: The first ionization energy removes an electron from a neutral magnesium atom.
After losing one electron, magnesium becomes a positively charged ion, Mg⁺.
The remaining electrons are attracted more strongly by the positively charged ion, so more energy is required to remove the second electron.
solutions.answer: The second ionization energy of magnesium is greater because the second electron is removed from the positively charged Mg⁺ ion.

solutions.question: Is it possible for two metals or two non-metals to form an ionic bond?
steps: No. Two metals tend to lose electrons, so neither can accept electrons from the other to form an ionic bond.
Two non-metals tend to gain or share electrons; they generally form covalent bonds by sharing electrons.
solutions.answer: Two metals or two non-metals do not generally form an ionic bond; ionic bonds form between a metal and a non-metal.

solutions.question: Which element has the least value of ionization energy and which element has the highest value of electronegativity?
steps: Cesium has the least value of ionization energy.
Fluorine has the highest value of electronegativity.
solutions.answer: Cesium has the least ionization energy, and fluorine has the highest electronegativity.

solutions.question: Suppose a new element is discovered. Where would you like to accommodate this element in the periodic table?
steps: I would first find the electronic configuration of the new element.
The number of occupied shells would show its period, and the number of valence electrons would help determine its group.
I would place it in the position that agrees with its electronic configuration and properties.
solutions.answer: I would place the new element according to its electronic configuration and properties.

solutions.question: What is the first element of the periodic table? Will it lose an electron or gain it?
steps: Hydrogen is the first element of the periodic table.
It has one electron in its first shell and can lose this electron to form H⁺.
It can also gain one electron to complete its first shell and form H⁻.
solutions.answer: Hydrogen is the first element; it can lose one electron or gain one electron.

solutions.question: Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?
steps: Aluminium is expected to lose an electron more easily than boron.
The atomic radius of aluminium (125 pm) is greater than that of boron (88 pm).
The outer electron in aluminium is farther from the nucleus and is held less strongly.
solutions.answer: Aluminium is expected to lose an electron more easily.

solutions.question: How would you find the atomic radius of an atom?
steps: The atomic radius is found by measuring the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.
The atomic radius is half this distance: r = d/2.
solutions.answer: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.

solutions.question: Why is it not possible for oxygen atom to accept three electrons to form O³⁻ ion like nitrogen which can accept electrons to form N³⁻?
steps: An oxygen atom has six electrons in its outermost shell and needs two more electrons to complete its octet.
After accepting two electrons, oxygen has a stable outermost shell.
Accepting a third electron would not be needed to complete the octet and would make the ion unstable.
solutions.answer: Oxygen accepts two electrons to complete its octet; accepting a third would make O³⁻ unstable.

solutions.question: Which information is needed to locate the elements in the periodic table if you do not know its atomic number? Is atomic mass helpful for this purpose?
steps: The electronic configuration is needed to locate an element when its atomic number is not known.
The number of occupied shells gives the period, and the number of valence electrons helps determine the group.
Atomic mass is not helpful for locating an element because elements in the periodic table are arranged according to increasing atomic number.
solutions.answer: Electronic configuration is needed; atomic mass is not used to locate an element in the periodic table.

solutions.question: How many blocks of elements are present in the periodic table? Are these blocks helpful in studying the properties of elements?
steps: There are four blocks of elements in the periodic table: s-block, p-block, d-block and f-block.
These blocks are helpful because elements in the same block have their last electron entering the same type of subshell.
The blocks help us study and compare the properties of elements.
solutions.answer: There are four blocks—s, p, d and f—and they help us study the properties of elements.

solutions.question: Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (a) Atomic radius
steps: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right in a period.
As we move across a period, the nuclear charge increases while the added electrons enter the same principal shell.
The increased attraction between the nucleus and the electrons pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
solutions.answer: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period because increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus.

solutions.question: Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (b) Ionization energy
steps: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right in a period.
Across a period, nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases.
The outermost electrons are attracted more strongly by the nucleus, so more energy is required to remove an electron.
solutions.answer: Ionization energy generally increases across a period because the outermost electrons are held more strongly by the nucleus.

solutions.question: Which physical properties of elements may lead us to know what type of bond it will form?
steps: Electronegativity and ionization energy help us predict the type of bond an element will form.
A large difference in electronegativity between two atoms generally favours ionic bond formation; a small difference generally favours covalent bond formation.
solutions.answer: Electronegativity, especially the difference between the atoms, and ionization energy help predict the type of bond formed.

solutions.question: Write down the names of four non-metals which exist in solid state at normal temperature.
steps: Four non-metals that are solids at normal temperature are carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.
solutions.answer: Carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine are solid non-metals at normal temperature.

solutions.question: Why do second and third periods have equal number of elements while all other periods contain different number of elements?
steps: The number of elements in a period depends on the number of electrons accommodated in the subshells being filled.
The first period has 2 elements because only the 1s subshell is filled, and this subshell can hold 2 electrons.
The second period has 8 elements because the 2s and 2p subshells are filled; together they can hold 2 + 6 = 8 electrons.
The third period also has 8 elements because the 3s and 3p subshells are filled; the 3d subshell starts filling in the fourth period.
The fourth and fifth periods have 18 elements because the s, d and p subshells are filled: 2 + 10 + 6 = 18.
The sixth period can have 32 elements because the s, f, d and p subshells can hold 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32 electrons; the seventh period is incomplete.
Thus, the second and third periods have equal numbers of elements, whereas the other periods have different numbers because different numbers of subshells are filled.
solutions.answer: The second and third periods each contain 8 elements because only the s and p subshells are filled in each; the first period fills only the 1s subshell, while other periods involve additional subshells.

solutions.question: Arrangement of the elements in the form of a periodic table is a remarkable achievement of chemists. Comment on this statement citing the benefits of this table.
steps: The periodic table arranges elements systematically according to their atomic numbers and recurring properties.
Elements with similar properties are placed in the same groups, making their properties easier to compare.
The table helps us study the properties of elements and understand how these properties vary periodically.
It also helps us predict the properties of elements and their compounds.
solutions.answer: The periodic table organizes elements by recurring properties, making them easier to study, compare and predict.

solutions.question: Both lithium and beryllium show behaviour different from rest of the alkali and alkaline earth metals respectively. Can you think of the possible reasons for this difference?
steps: Lithium and beryllium have very small atomic sizes compared with the other elements in their respective groups.
Their small size gives them high charge density, high ionization energy and strong polarizing power.
These properties make lithium and beryllium behave differently from the other alkali and alkaline earth metals, respectively.
solutions.answer: Lithium and beryllium differ from the other metals in their groups mainly because of their very small atomic size and high charge density.

solutions.question: Modern periodic table is the amended form of the earlier table developed by Mandeleev. Elaborate how these two tables are different from each other.
steps: In Mendeleev’s periodic table, elements were arranged in increasing order of their atomic masses; in the modern periodic table, they are arranged in increasing order of their atomic numbers.

Mendeleev stated that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses; the modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
Mendeleev’s table had 8 groups, each divided into subgroups A and B; the modern periodic table has 18 groups.
The arrangement by atomic mass resulted in anomalous pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, in Mendeleev’s table; the modern table places them correctly according to their atomic numbers.

Mendeleev’s table could not give isotopes separate positions according to their different atomic masses; isotopes occupy the same position in the modern table because they have the same atomic number.
Mendeleev’s original table did not include noble gases, which were discovered later; they are placed in Group 18 of the modern periodic table.
solutions.answer: Mendeleev’s table arranged elements by atomic mass and had 8 groups, while the modern table arranges them by atomic number and has 18 groups; it also resolves anomalous pairs, gives isotopes the same position, and includes noble gases in Group 18.

definitions.text: The modern periodic table is based upon the arrangement of elements according to increasing atomic number.
The horizontal rows of elements in the periodic table are called periods while the vertical columns are called groups.
The vertical columns present in the periodic table are called groups.
As a whole the periodic table shows the repetition of the properties of elements after regular intervals. This trend is called periodicity in the properties.
Atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of the two identical bonded atoms. It is expressed in pm(1pm = 10⁻¹²m).
Ionization energy is the amount of energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
Electron affinity is the amount of energy change when an electron is added up in the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
Electronegativity of an atom is its electron-attracting ability. It is defined as the force with which an atom attracts the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a bond.
The metallic character is the tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions or cations.
It is mass of a substance in a unit volume.
Atomic sizes of elements decrease from left to right in a period and increase from top to bottom in a group.
Ionization energy values increase from left to right in a period and decrease from top to bottom in a group.
Electron affinity and electronegativity values increase from left to right in a period and decrease from top to bottom in a group.
Metallic character increases from top to bottom in a group and decreases from left to right in a period.

Find density from mass and volume (ρ in kg m⁻³, m in kg, V in m³).

formulas.use: Use outer-shell configuration to identify a main-group family or recognise the transition-element configuration; subshell notation has no SI units.

formulas.formula: Across a period: atomic radius decreases; ionization energy and electronegativity generally increase. Down a group: atomic radius increases; ionization energy and electronegativity decrease.
formulas.use: Use these periodic trends to compare elements; these are qualitative relationships and have no SI units.

fullMarks: For a periodic-table location question, state the period from the number of occupied shells and the group from the outermost-shell electron configuration; name the block from the subshell being filled.
For trend explanations, state the direction of the trend first, then give the reason: increasing nuclear charge across a period, or an added shell and shielding down a group.
For ion formation, write the number of outermost electrons, whether they are lost or gained, and the resulting ion charge.
For atomic-radius questions, show that the radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms, and include the unit.
For numerical answers, write the given data in SI units, the formula, substitution with units, and the final answer with its unit and appropriate significant figures.
When describing a reaction, balance the equation and include correct state symbols if they are given in the question.
In a long answer, use a clear heading for each property and finish each part with a direct statement of the trend or conclusion.
mistakes: Mixing up groups and periods. Fix: periods are horizontal rows; groups are vertical columns.
Saying atomic radius increases across a period. Fix: it generally decreases from left to right and increases down a group.
Explaining the decrease in radius across a period by adding shells. Fix: electrons are added to the same outer shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling them closer.
Reversing the ionization-energy trend. Fix: it generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.

Confusing electron affinity with electronegativity. Fix: electron affinity concerns an electron added to an isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity is an atom’s attraction for a shared pair in a bond.
Forgetting the sign of an ion. Fix: losing electrons forms positive ions; gaining electrons forms negative ions.
Giving a numerical radius without halving the internuclear distance or writing a unit. Fix: use r = d ÷ 2 and state the answer in pm or m.

shortTheory.question: Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?
shortTheory.answer: The modern periodic table is based upon the arrangement of elements according to increasing atomic number.

shortTheory.question: What is the significance of the word periodic?
shortTheory.answer: As a whole the periodic table shows the repetition of the properties of elements after regular intervals. This trend is called periodicity in the properties.

shortTheory.question: Why does the size of a period increase as we move down the periodic table?
shortTheory.answer: Each period also represents the completion of a shell. Since the number of electrons to be accommodated in a particular shell is fixed, the number of elements in a period is also fixed. The number of elements in successive periods is 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32.

shortTheory.question: In a group, the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell. Why is it so?
shortTheory.answer: Elements present in a group resemble one another in their chemical properties since they contain the same number of electrons in their outermost shells.

shortTheory.question: Do you expect calcium to be more reactive than sodium? Give the reason of your answer.
shortTheory.answer: No. Sodium is more reactive than calcium because sodium has one electron in its outermost shell and loses it more easily, while calcium has two outermost electrons. The chemical reactivity of metals depends on their tendency to lose electrons.

shortTheory.question: The first ionization energy value of magnesium is less than the second one. Give reason.
shortTheory.answer: It is easier to remove the first electron from magnesium than the second one.

explain.title: Group 1 elements have one outermost-shell electron
explain.body: All the elements present in group 1 have ns¹ configuration in their outermost shells. They are also called alkali metals. Because the single outer electron can be removed easily, these metals are very reactive. Hydrogen is the exception: it is a gas and a non-metal.

explain.title: Reactivity increases down Group 1
explain.body: Atomic size increases down the group. The outer electron is then easier to lose, so the lower members are more reactive. For example, lithium reacts steadily with water, sodium vigorously and potassium violently.

explain.title: The metals become softer and their melting points decrease
explain.body: Increasing atomic size weakens the interatomic attraction of the atoms in the metals. The metals become softer down the group, and their melting points decrease.

explain.title: Density generally increases down the group
explain.body: Both atomic size and mass increase down the group. The increase in mass is greater than the increase in volume, so density, defined as mass per unit volume, increases gradually down the group.

explain.title: The textbook's definition and trends
explain.body: “relatively soft metals with general trends down the group limited to decreasing melting point, increasing density and increasing reactivity.”

mistakes: Do not say that Group 1 reactivity decreases down the group; it increases.
Do not confuse the physical trends: melting point decreases, while density generally increases.
When explaining softness, include the reason: increasing atomic size weakens interatomic attraction.
Do not describe lithium, sodium and potassium as reacting with water at the same rate.
Remember that the Group 1 metals react with chlorine with increasing vigour down the group.

yourTurn.question:
Q9.3. In the following reaction, chlorine acts as an oxidising agent. Which is the reducing agent?

Cl₂(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br₂(g)
solution: Br⁻ ions lose electrons to form Br₂.
The substance that loses electrons is the reducing agent.
Therefore, NaBr (the bromide ions) is the reducing agent.
yourTurn.answer: Sodium bromide (NaBr), specifically the bromide ions, is the reducing agent.

steps.why: This is the balanced displacement reaction shown in your textbook.
steps.text: Cl₂(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)

steps.why: Chlorine is above bromine in oxidising power, so it accepts electrons from bromide ions.
steps.text: Cl₂ is a stronger oxidising agent than Br₂.

steps.why: The products show chlorine taking the place of bromine in the salt.
steps.text: Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide solution.

example.question: Cl₂(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)
example.answer: Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide solution because chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent.

explain.title: Outer electrons and reactivity
explain.body: Group 17 elements have seven electrons in their outermost shells (ns², np⁵). They tend to accept one electron and form negative ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group because atomic size increases and the tendency to accept an electron decreases.

explain.title: Physical properties down the group
explain.body: Atomic radii, melting points and boiling points increase down the group. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a fuming red-brown liquid, and iodine is a shiny grey solid that forms dark purple vapour when warmed.

explain.title: Oxidation, reduction and displacement
explain.body: Oxidation is a process in which an electron is lost. The substance which loses an electron is called a reducing agent. Reduction is a process in which an electron is gained and the substance which accepts the electron is called an oxidizing agent. Halogens are oxidising agents, and their oxidising power decreases in the order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A stronger halogen can displace a weaker halogen from its compound.

explain.title: Hydrogen halides
explain.body: Halogens react with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX. Bond length increases down the group, so the bond gets weaker and needs less heat energy to break. Therefore, thermal stability decreases in the order HF > HCl > HBr > HI.

mistakes: Do not reverse the trends: halogen reactivity and oxidising power decrease down Group 17.
Do not confuse oxidation with reduction: oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Do not say that the weaker halogen displaces the stronger one. The stronger oxidising halogen does the displacement.
When explaining hydrogen-halide stability, include the full chain: larger halogen atom, longer and weaker bond, less energy to break it, lower thermal stability.
Use the exact order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ for oxidising power and HF > HCl > HBr > HI for thermal stability.

recap.question: Why does reactivity increase down Group 1?
recap.answer: Potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium because it loses its outer electron more easily.

recap.question: Which statement about the outermost shells of Group 1 elements is correct?
recap.answer: They have one electron in their outermost shell.
