explain.title: Where transition elements are found
explain.body: Elements present at the centre of the modern periodic table from group 3 to group 12 are called d block elements or transition elements. They are metals.

explain.title: Properties of transition elements
explain.body: Transition elements are often hard and have higher densities. Their melting and boiling points are high. They show variable oxidation states, and the compounds they form are often coloured. They are malleable and ductile.

explain.title: Transition metals as catalysts
explain.body: Transition metals and their compounds function as catalysts in many important chemical reactions. Metals often absorb other substances on their surface and activate them in this process.

explain.title: Catalyst uses in the section
explain.body: Iron is used in the Haber process to make ammonia. Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) is now preferred over platinum for oxidising sulphur dioxide in the contact process. modules.title: 9.5 Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals

writtenQuestions.text: Why are almost all the metals solids while non-metals generally exist as gases and solids?
modelAnswer: Metals have strong metallic bonds.
Therefore, metals generally have high melting points and are solids at room temperature.
Non-metals have weaker bonds and a wider range of melting points.
Therefore, non-metals generally exist as gases or solids at room temperature.

example.question: Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.
example.answer: Metals are generally good conductors, malleable, ductile, lustrous, tough, strong, and have high melting and boiling points. Non-metals are generally poor conductors, brittle, dull, and neither tough nor strong, and have a wide range of melting and boiling points. Graphite conducts electricity, iodine is lustrous, and mercury is a liquid metal.

explain.title: Metals can be shaped
explain.body: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets. This property is called malleability. Metals can also be drawn into wires; this property is called ductility.

explain.title: Metals conduct and shine
explain.body: Metallic bonding allows metals to conduct heat and electricity well. Metals are usually lustrous, which means they have a shiny appearance.

explain.title: Non-metals are usually brittle
explain.body: Non-metals cannot generally be hammered into sheets or drawn into wires. They break because they are brittle and their bonds are weak.

explain.title: Remember the exceptions
explain.body: Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity. Iodine is an exception to the usual dull appearance of non-metals. Mercury is an exception to metals being solids, and graphite and diamond are exceptions to non-metals having low melting points.

mistakes: Do not swap the meanings of malleability and ductility: sheets are malleability; wires are ductility.
Do not write that all non-metals are gases; they can be solids, liquids, or gases at room temperature.
Do not say non-metals never conduct electricity: graphite is an exception.
Do not forget exceptions when a question asks for a comparison: mercury, iodine, graphite, and diamond matter in this section.
Do not explain the strength of metals by saying they are simply hard; connect the explanation to strong metallic bonds.

steps.text: The outer electron is held less strongly by the nucleus.

steps.why: An electron that is held less strongly is removed more easily in a reaction.

example.question: Q9.1. Why does it become easier to cut an alkali metal when we move from top to bottom in a group?
example.answer: Metallic bonding becomes weaker down the group, so the alkali metals become softer and easier to cut.

explain.title: Alkali metals
explain.body: Alkali metals have one outer electron and readily lose it to form positive ions. Their reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron becomes easier to remove. They are generally soft metals with low melting points.

explain.title: Halogens
explain.body: Halogens gain one electron to form negative ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group because the atoms become larger and attract an incoming electron less strongly. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its salt.

explain.title: Metallic and non-metallic properties
explain.body: Strong metallic bonding makes metals generally strong, malleable and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals do not have this metallic bonding and may be gases or brittle solids.

explain.title: Transition elements and catalysts
explain.body: Transition elements show distinctive properties such as variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic activity. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

explain.title: Noble gases and physical states
explain.body: Noble gases are monoatomic and unreactive. Weak attractions between their atoms give them low boiling points. Halogen molecules become larger down the group, so their attractions increase and their physical states change from gases to liquid to solid.

mistakes: Do not reverse the trends: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group, while halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
Do not say that chlorine is less reactive than bromine; chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent.
In a redox question, distinguish the oxidising agent from the reducing agent: the oxidising agent gains electrons, while the reducing agent loses electrons.
Do not give a trend without its reason when the question asks “why”; link it to electron loss, electron gain, atomic size or bond strength.
When describing a catalyst, explain how it helps the reaction rather than saying it is used up.

recap.question: Which non-metal is an exception because it conducts electricity?
recap.answer: Metals are usually good conductors; non-metals are usually poor conductors. Graphite is an exception.

recap.question: Which property allows a metal to be hammered into thin sheets?
recap.answer: They can be hammered into thin sheets.

solutions.question: Why does it become easier to cut an alkali metal when we move from top to bottom in a group?
steps: The atomic size of alkali metals increases from top to bottom in a group.
The outermost electron becomes farther from the nucleus, so the attraction between the nucleus and this electron decreases.
The metallic bonding becomes weaker, making the metals softer and easier to cut.
solutions.answer: Alkali metals become softer down the group because their metallic bonding becomes weaker.

solutions.question: Predict the reactivity of potassium towards halogens.
steps: Potassium loses its single outermost electron readily and reacts vigorously with halogens.
It forms ionic potassium halides; for example: 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl.
solutions.answer: Potassium reacts vigorously with halogens to form potassium halides.

solutions.question: In the following reaction, chlorine acts as an oxidising agent. Which is the reducing agent? Cl₂(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br₂(g)
steps: Sodium bromide is the reducing agent.
Bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised to bromine: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
solutions.answer: Sodium bromide (Br⁻ ions) is the reducing agent.

solutions.question: Why does iodine exist in the solid state at room temperature?
steps: Iodine molecules are larger and have more electrons than the molecules of the other halogens.
The intermolecular forces between iodine molecules are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate them.
Therefore, iodine is a solid at room temperature.
solutions.answer: Iodine is solid at room temperature because strong intermolecular forces hold its molecules together.

solutions.question: How does Ni catalyse the reaction involving hydrogenation of oil?
steps: Nickel provides a surface on which the oil and hydrogen are adsorbed.
This brings the reactants close together and helps hydrogen add to the double bonds in the oil.
The oil is converted into saturated fat; nickel speeds up the reaction and remains chemically unchanged.
solutions.answer: Nickel catalyses hydrogenation by providing a surface that brings oil and hydrogen together.

solutions.question: Which noble gas should have the lowest boiling point and why?
steps: Helium should have the lowest boiling point among the noble gases.
Its atoms are the smallest, so the intermolecular forces between them are the weakest.
The least energy is therefore needed to separate its atoms.
solutions.answer: Helium has the lowest boiling point because the forces between its atoms are the weakest.

solutions.question: Compare the reactions of alkali metals with chlorine.
steps: Alkali metals react with chlorine to form ionic chlorides: 2M + Cl₂ → 2MCl.
The reaction becomes more vigorous down the group as the metals lose their outermost electron more readily.
Thus, lithium reacts least vigorously and potassium more vigorously than sodium.
solutions.answer: Alkali metals form chlorides with chlorine, and the vigour of the reaction increases down the group.

solutions.question: Why are almost all the metals solids while non-metals generally exist as gases and solids?
steps: Metals generally have strong metallic bonds, which hold their atoms together and make most metals solids.
Non-metals have weaker forces between their molecules, so many are gases; those with stronger attractions are solids.
Mercury and bromine are exceptions, as they are liquids at room temperature.
solutions.answer: Most metals are solids because of strong metallic bonding, while non-metals are generally gases or solids because their intermolecular forces vary.

solutions.question: Name any three elements in the periodic table which exist as liquids.
steps: Mercury, bromine and gallium are elements that can exist as liquids near ordinary room temperature.
Mercury and bromine are liquid at ordinary room temperature; gallium melts just above it.
solutions.answer: Mercury, bromine and gallium.

solutions.question: Why are transition elements different from normal elements?
steps: Transition elements have partially filled d-orbitals in their atoms or in at least one of their ions.
They differ from normal elements because they commonly show variable oxidation states and form coloured compounds.
Many transition elements and their compounds also act as catalysts.
solutions.answer: Transition elements have partially filled d-orbitals and commonly show variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic properties.

solutions.question: Compare the reactivity of chlorine and bromine as an oxidising agent.
steps: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.
Chlorine gains electrons more readily and can displace bromine from a bromide salt.
For example: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.
solutions.answer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.

solutions.question: Which element is the most reactive and which is the least reactive among halogens? Give two reasons to explain your answer.
steps: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen; iodine is the least reactive among the commonly studied halogens.
Down the group, atomic size increases and the attraction of the nucleus for an incoming electron decreases.
Therefore, the tendency of halogen atoms to gain an electron and form halide ions decreases down the group.
solutions.answer: Fluorine is the most reactive and iodine is the least reactive among the commonly studied halogens.

solutions.question: Explain the role of catalytic converter in an automobile.
steps: A catalytic converter is fitted in the exhaust system of an automobile.
It contains catalysts, such as platinum, palladium and rhodium, which convert harmful exhaust gases into less harmful substances.
Carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons are converted into carbon dioxide and water; nitrogen oxides are converted into nitrogen.
solutions.answer: A catalytic converter uses catalysts to change harmful automobile exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

solutions.question: Why do the chemical reactivities of alkali metals increase down the group whereas they decrease down the group in case of halogens?
steps: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell and react by losing it.
Down the group, atomic size increases and the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily; hence reactivity increases.
Halogens react by gaining one electron to complete their outermost shell.
Down the group, atomic size increases and the attraction for an incoming electron decreases; hence the tendency to gain an electron, and their reactivity, decreases.
solutions.answer: Alkali-metal reactivity increases down the group because their outer electron is lost more easily, whereas halogen reactivity decreases because attraction for an incoming electron becomes weaker.

solutions.question: Why are metals generally tough and strong whereas non-metals are neither tough nor strong?
steps: Metals generally have strong metallic bonds: positive metal ions are held together by attraction to a sea of delocalised electrons.
These strong forces make metals generally tough and strong.
Non-metals generally lack metallic bonding; many consist of atoms or molecules held together by comparatively weaker forces.
Therefore, solid non-metals are generally brittle and are neither tough nor strong.
solutions.answer: Strong metallic bonding makes metals generally tough and strong, while non-metals generally lack this bonding and are brittle.

solutions.question: Both alkali metals and halogens are very reactive elements with roles opposite to each other. Explain.
steps: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell and readily lose it to form positive ions.
By donating electrons, alkali metals act as reducing agents.
Halogens need one electron to complete their outermost shell and readily gain it to form negative ions.
By accepting electrons, halogens act as oxidising agents.
Thus, alkali metals and halogens react in opposite ways and combine to form ionic compounds.
solutions.answer: Alkali metals donate electrons and act as reducing agents, whereas halogens accept electrons and act as oxidising agents.

solutions.question: Why hydrogen bromide is thermally unstable as compared to hydrogen chloride?
steps: The thermal stability of hydrogen halides decreases down the group.
The chlorine atom is smaller than the bromine atom, so the H—Cl bond is stronger than the H—Br bond.
The weaker H—Br bond breaks more readily on heating; therefore, hydrogen bromide is thermally less stable than hydrogen chloride.
solutions.answer: Hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable because its H—Br bond is weaker than the H—Cl bond in hydrogen chloride.

solutions.question: Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.
steps: Metals are generally solids at room temperature; non-metals may be solids, liquids or gases.
Metals are generally lustrous, whereas non-metals are generally dull.
Metals are malleable and ductile; solid non-metals are generally brittle.
Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity; non-metals are generally poor conductors.
Metals are generally sonorous; non-metals are non-sonorous.
Metals generally form positive ions by losing electrons; non-metals generally form negative ions by gaining electrons.
Metal oxides are generally basic, whereas non-metal oxides are generally acidic.
solutions.answer: Metals are generally lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors and form positive ions; non-metals generally show the opposite properties and form negative ions.

solutions.question: V₂O₅ catalyst is preferred over platinum in the oxidation of sulphur dioxide. Give reasons.
steps: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) is less expensive than platinum.
Platinum is easily poisoned by impurities present in the reacting gases, which reduces its catalytic activity.
V₂O₅ is not poisoned as readily and is an effective catalyst for the oxidation of sulphur dioxide.
solutions.answer: V₂O₅ is preferred because it is cheaper than platinum and is less readily poisoned by impurities.

solutions.question: Explain the role of sodium as heat transfer agent in the atomic nuclear power plant. Which property of sodium is utilized in this role?
steps: Liquid sodium is circulated through the reactor core, where it absorbs heat produced during nuclear reactions.
The hot sodium carries this heat to a heat exchanger, where it is transferred to water to produce steam.
The steam is used to drive a turbine and generate electricity.
Sodium is used because it is an excellent conductor of heat.
solutions.answer: Sodium transfers heat from the reactor core to water in a heat exchanger; its high thermal conductivity is utilized.

solutions.question: Why and how does lithium behave differently from the rest of the alkali metals?
steps: Lithium behaves differently from the other alkali metals because its atom and ion are very small.
Its small size gives the lithium ion a high charge density and strong polarising power.
Lithium is harder and has higher melting and boiling points than the other alkali metals; it is also the least reactive.
When heated in oxygen, lithium forms the normal oxide, Li₂O, whereas the heavier alkali metals form peroxides or superoxides.
Lithium reacts directly with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, Li₃N.
solutions.answer: Lithium’s small size and high charge density cause its anomalous behaviour: it is harder and less reactive, has higher melting and boiling points, and forms Li₂O and Li₃N.

solutions.question: Why aluminum metal is used in the manufacture of cooking utensils whereas magnesium is not considered useful for this purpose?
steps: Aluminium is a good conductor of heat, so it is suitable for cooking utensils.
It is light and malleable, so it can be made into utensils easily.
A thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide forms on its surface and prevents further corrosion.
Magnesium is more reactive and can burn in air; therefore, it is not considered suitable for cooking utensils.
solutions.answer: Aluminium is used for cooking utensils because it conducts heat well and resists corrosion, while the more reactive magnesium may burn in air.

definitions.text: Elements present in a group of the periodic table show similar chemical properties owning to the presence of same number of electrons in their outermost shells. However, a small variation in the chemical properties of elements is expected because the atomic size increases down the group.
All the elements present in group 1 have ns¹ configuration in their outermost shells. They are also called alkali metals.
These elements are thus named as Halogens which means salt-forming elements.
Oxidation is a process in which an electron is lost. The substance which loses an electron is called a reducing agent.
On the contrary, reduction is a process in which an electron is gained and the substance which accepts the electron is called an oxidizing agent.
Oxidation-reduction are simultaneous reactions. In other words an, electron is lost only when there is a substance to accept it.
Elements present at the centre of the modern periodic table from group 3 to group 12 are called d block elements or transition elements.
Elements present in group 18 of the modern periodic table are called noble elements.
Metals are defined as the elements which can generally form cations easily. They also tend to form metallic bond.
Metals can be hammered into thin sheets. This property is called malleability.
Metals can also be drawn into wires and this property is named as ductility.
Atomic size increases from top to bottom for elements of group-1. It becomes easier for these elements to lose their single electron.
Chemical reactivity of the elements in group-1 increases down the group.
Due to increase in their atomic sizes, the interatomic attraction decrease down the first group elements. This makes them softer and their melting points decrease down the group.
Due to increase in the size and volume of atoms, the densities of alkali metals increases down the group.
Group 17 elements or halogens exist as diatomic molecules. They are very reactive non-metals and react with alkali and alkaline earth metals.
Halogens are oxidising agents and their oxidising power decreases down the group.
In hydrogen halides the bond between hydrogen and halogen gets weaker as we go down the group. Hence, the thermal stability of hydrogen halides decreases down the group.
d – block elements or transition elements are all metals. They are often hard and have higher densities. These elements and their compounds are used as catalysts in important industrial reactions.
Noble gases are all unreactive gases because their outermost shells are complete.

fullMarks: For a trend question, state the direction first (up or down the group), then link it to atomic size and the resulting ease of losing or accepting electrons.
When comparing alkali metals reacting with chlorine, write the balanced equations and describe the reaction strength in order: lithium, steady; sodium, vigorous; potassium, violent.
For displacement and redox questions, identify which species is oxidized and which is reduced; chlorine displaces bromide or iodide because its oxidizing power is greater.
For hydrogen-halide stability, explain the chain clearly: halogen size increases down the group, the H–halogen bond gets weaker, less heat is needed to break it, and thermal stability decreases.

For a catalyst question, name the catalyst, the process and the change it helps bring about; for a catalytic converter, state that harmful exhaust gases are converted to less harmful gases and name platinum, palladium and rhodium.

For comparisons of metals and non-metals, cover conductivity, malleability and ductility, strength, and melting/boiling points; include graphite as an exception for electrical conduction and mercury as an exception for metals being solid.
For any calculation, write the given data in SI units, state the formula, substitute values with units, and give the final answer with its unit and appropriate significant figures.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying alkali metals become less reactive down the group. Fix: Their atomic size increases, so their outer electron is lost more easily and reactivity increases.
Mistake: Reversing the halogen trend and claiming reactivity increases down the group. Fix: Larger atoms attract an incoming electron less strongly, so halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
Mistake: Calling sodium the reducing agent in the chlorine–sodium bromide equation. Fix: Bromide ions lose electrons to form bromine, so bromide is oxidized and acts as the reducing agent.
Mistake: Saying iodine is solid only because it is a large atom. Fix: Explain that larger halogen molecules attract one another more strongly, raising melting and boiling points.
Mistake: Saying HBr is more thermally stable than HCl because bromine is below chlorine. Fix: The H–Br bond is weaker, so it takes less heat to break than the H–Cl bond.

Mistake: Naming only one metal in a catalytic converter or saying it removes all exhaust gases. Fix: Name platinum, palladium and rhodium, and state that the device converts more harmful gases into gases that do not pollute the atmosphere.
Mistake: Giving an unbalanced reaction or omitting physical state symbols when reproducing an equation. Fix: Check atom counts on both sides and copy the equation with its printed state symbols.

shortTheory.question: Why does it become easier to cut an alkali metal when we move from top to bottom in a group?
shortTheory.answer: Increase in the atomic size down the first group also weakens the interatomic attraction of the atomic metals. This fact makes them softer down the group and their melting points decrease.

shortTheory.question: Predict the reactivity of potassium towards halogens.
shortTheory.answer: Halogens are very reactive non-metals and react with alkali and alkaline earth metals. The chemical reactivity of the elements in group-1 increases down the group. Therefore, potassium reacts vigorously with halogens to form potassium halides.

shortTheory.question: Which noble gas should have the lowest boiling point and why?
shortTheory.answer: Helium should have the lowest boiling point because noble gases have very low boiling points and helium is the smallest noble gas.

shortTheory.question: Why does iodine exist in the solid state at room temperature?
shortTheory.answer: Atomic radii, melting and boiling points of halogens increase when you go down the group. This is because the atoms get larger as they have more electrons. As a result the molecules which are formed from these atoms will attract each other with a stronger force.

shortTheory.question: Why are transition elements different from normal elements?
shortTheory.answer: Transition elements are often hard with higher densities. Their melting and boiling points are also high. These metals show variable oxidation states and the compounds they form are often coloured. They are malleable and ductile.

shortTheory.question: Explain the role of catalytic converter in an automobile.
shortTheory.answer: A catalytic converter is a device used in the exhaust of an automobile which converts more harmful gases produced in the engine to such gases which do not pollute the atmosphere. Platinum, palladium and rhodium are the catalysts used in catalytic converters.

explain.title: Air pollutants
explain.body: Your textbook defines an air pollutant as: “Any substance (solid, liquid or gas) in the air which has adverse effect on human health and quality of life is called an air pollutant.” Remember that pollutants may be solids, liquids or gases.

explain.title: Concentration in ppm
explain.body: Your textbook says: “The concentration of a pollutant is expressed in parts per million (ppm). A concentration of one ppm means one part of pollutant per million part of solid, liquid or gas mixture in which the pollutant is formed.” In simple terms, ppm tells how much pollutant is present in a very large amount of mixture.

explain.title: Major sources and smog
explain.body: Burning fossil fuels is a major source of air pollution and releases gases and particles. The section describes winter smog as smoke in the atmosphere mixed with fog. Industrial pollution, vehicle emissions and crop burning contribute to it.

explain.title: Harmful effects
explain.body: Different pollutants have different effects. For example, carbon monoxide interferes with oxygen transport in blood, sulphur oxides can cause breathing difficulties and acid rain, and particulate matter can irritate the eyes and reduce visibility.

mistakes: Do not say that every air pollutant is a gas; the definition includes solids, liquids and gases.
Do not reverse the meaning of ppm: one ppm means one part of pollutant per million parts of the mixture.
Do not confuse smoke mixed with fog (smog) with the chemical process that forms ozone.
When asked how smog affects plants, include reduced carbon dioxide absorption during photosynthesis, not only “plants are harmed.”
Do not confuse the effects of carbon monoxide with those of carbon dioxide: CO is poisonous and interferes with oxygen transport; higher CO₂ levels increase global warming.

explain.title: What acid rain means
explain.body: When rain water has pH between 4.2 and 4.4, it is known as acid rain. Learn this range exactly for a definition or short-answer question.

explain.title: How acid rain forms
explain.body: Burning fossil fuels releases SO₂. In the atmosphere, SO₂ can be converted to SO₃, which reacts with water to form H₂SO₄. Nitrogen oxides also react with water: 2NO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HNO₃(g) + HNO₂(g). The acids form droplets that can be carried far by wind before falling as rain, hail, snow or fog.

explain.title: Effects of acid rain
explain.body: Acid rain makes soil more acidic and washes away nutrients. It can damage plants and forests, make water too acidic for aquatic animals, and contribute to harm from toxic substances leached from soil. It also damages crops and human-made structures such as buildings, statues, automobiles and bridges.

explain.title: Reducing agricultural damage
explain.body: Farmers can monitor soil conditions and, when necessary, add crushed lime (CaO) to neutralize acid.

mistakes: Do not give a pH range other than 4.2–4.4 when using the textbook definition.
Do not confuse the gases with the acids: SO₂ and NO₂ are oxides; H₂SO₄, HNO₃ and HNO₂ are acids.
Do not leave out HNO₂ when writing the products of the nitrogen-dioxide reaction with water.
Do not say that acid rain only harms plants; it can also affect soil, aquatic life, human health, agriculture and structures.

Other gases do not absorb this radiation sufficiently, so they do not cause the greenhouse effect in this way.

steps.why: This is the textbook definition, so begin by stating what the greenhouse effect means.
steps.text: The progressive warming up of the Earth's surface due to blanketing effect of man-made carbon dioxide, methane, water vapours and other gases in the atmosphere is called Greenhouse Effect.

steps.why: The explanation begins with the Sun’s short-wave radiation reaching Earth.
steps.text: The sun emits short wave radiation that passes through greenhouse gases to heat the surface of the Earth.

steps.why: Earth gives out long-wave radiation, and greenhouse gases absorb most of it.
steps.text: At night, the hot Earth's surface emits longwave radiation that is mostly absorbed by green house gases.

steps.why: Absorption slows the escape of heat, so Earth cools more slowly and warms overall.
steps.text: This process of absorption prevents the radiation to reach space, reducing the speed at which the Earth can cool off.

steps.why: Finish by stating the result of the process.
steps.text: This increases the temperature of the Earth and causes global warming.

explain.title: Air pollutants and their sources
explain.body: Air pollution includes harmful gases and particulate matter. Vehicles, industries, fuel burning and dust can add pollutants to the air. Carbon monoxide is poisonous, while fine particles can harm the respiratory system.

explain.title: Greenhouse effect and global warming
explain.body: Some gases, including carbon dioxide and methane, absorb outgoing heat. More of these gases can strengthen the greenhouse effect and cause global warming and climate change.

explain.title: Acid rain and smog
explain.body: Sulphur and nitrogen oxides can contribute to acid rain. Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen dioxide and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

recap.question: Name one strategy that can reduce harmful emissions from automobiles.
recap.answer: Planting trees, using catalytic converters, reducing sulphur dioxide from flue gas and using renewable energy can help reduce environmental issues.

recap.question: How do plants help clean the air through photosynthesis?
recap.answer: It absorbs carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.

solutions.question: What is the main objective of environmental education?
steps: The main objective of environmental education is to create awareness and understanding of the environment and its problems.
It helps people gain the knowledge, skills and attitudes needed to protect and improve the environment.
solutions.answer: Environmental education develops awareness and understanding of environmental problems and helps people protect and improve the environment.

solutions.question: How is particulate matter released in the atmosphere?
steps: Particulate matter consists of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air.
It is released into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels, industrial processes and vehicle exhaust.
Dust from roads, construction and other activities also adds particulate matter to the air.
solutions.answer: Particulate matter enters the atmosphere from fuel burning, industries, vehicle exhaust and dust.

solutions.question: Which gas is more poisonous, CO₂ or CO?
steps: Carbon monoxide (CO) is more poisonous than carbon dioxide (CO₂).
CO combines with haemoglobin in the blood and reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.
solutions.answer: CO is more poisonous than CO₂ because it reduces the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.

solutions.question: How does acid rain affect forests?
steps: Acid rain damages the leaves and roots of trees.
It reduces photosynthesis and makes the soil less suitable for plant growth.
As a result, trees become weak and forests may be damaged or destroyed.
solutions.answer: Acid rain harms forests by damaging trees and reducing their growth.

solutions.question: In what way sulphur present in fossil fuels becomes dangerous?
steps: When fossil fuels containing sulphur are burned, sulphur dioxide is released into the atmosphere.
Sulphur dioxide reacts with oxygen and water vapour to form acids.
These acids fall with rain as acid rain, which harms plants, animals and buildings.
solutions.answer: Sulphur in fossil fuels becomes dangerous when burning releases sulphur dioxide, which forms acid rain.

solutions.question: Name any three major sources responsible for the greenhouse effect.
steps: Three major sources of greenhouse gases are:
Burning fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide.
Livestock and the decay of organic matter, which release methane.
Refrigerators and air conditioners, which can release chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
solutions.answer: Burning fossil fuels, livestock and organic decay, and the release of CFCs are major sources responsible for the greenhouse effect.

solutions.question: How is wind energy useful for us?
steps: Wind energy is a renewable and non-polluting source of energy.
It is used to generate electricity and to operate windmills for pumping water.
solutions.answer: Wind energy is useful for generating electricity and pumping water.

solutions.question: How is the excessive use of insecticides and pesticides harmful for birds?
steps: Insecticides and pesticides may poison birds directly or when birds eat contaminated insects and seeds.
These chemicals can accumulate in food chains and harm birds’ reproduction.
For example, DDT can cause birds to lay eggs with thin shells, which break easily.
solutions.answer: Excessive insecticide and pesticide use poisons birds and can reduce their reproduction, including by causing thin eggshells.

solutions.question: Percentage of CO₂ in air is only 0.04%. Then how does it become harmful for the ecosystem?
steps: Although carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04% of air, its concentration is increasing because of the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.
Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes to the greenhouse effect and global warming.
Changes in temperature and climate can disturb habitats, affect plants and animals, and upset the balance of ecosystems.
solutions.answer: Increasing CO₂ traps heat, causing global warming and changes that can disturb ecosystems.

solutions.question: Why only some pollutant gases present in the atmosphere cause green house effect while others do not?
steps: Greenhouse gases absorb some of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth and retain heat in the atmosphere.
Gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane and nitrous oxide absorb infrared radiation because of their molecular structure.
The main gases in air, nitrogen and oxygen, do not absorb significant amounts of this radiation; therefore, they do not cause the greenhouse effect in the same way.
solutions.answer: Only gases that absorb Earth’s outgoing infrared radiation act as greenhouse gases.

solutions.question: How can you reduce the emission of CO present in the gases emitted by the burning of fuel in the automobile engines?
steps: Carbon monoxide forms when fuel burns incompletely because of an insufficient supply of oxygen.
Keep automobile engines properly tuned and maintained so that fuel burns more completely.
Use catalytic converters in vehicle exhaust systems to convert carbon monoxide into the less harmful carbon dioxide.
solutions.answer: Properly maintained engines, complete combustion and catalytic converters help reduce carbon monoxide emissions.

solutions.question: Mention three different ways in which solar energy can be useful for us.
steps: Solar energy can be used in solar cookers to cook food.
Solar energy can be used in solar water heaters to heat water.
Solar cells can convert solar energy into electrical energy.
solutions.answer: Solar energy is useful for cooking food, heating water and generating electricity.

solutions.question: Describe the harmful effects of the major pollutants present in the air.
Explain greenhouse effect. How is global warming dangerous for us?
steps: The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth’s surface and lower atmosphere due to greenhouse gases.
These gases allow most incoming sunlight to pass through but absorb some of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth and radiate heat back towards the surface.
An increase in greenhouse gases strengthens this effect and causes global warming.
Global warming can melt glaciers and polar ice, raise sea levels, and cause flooding in coastal areas.
It can also change climate patterns, leading to droughts, floods and harm to living organisms and ecosystems.
solutions.answer: Greenhouse gases trap some of Earth’s outgoing heat; increased warming can raise sea levels and disturb climate and ecosystems.

solutions.question: What is air quality index? What information does it convey?
steps: The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a scale used to report the quality of air.
It conveys the level of air pollution and indicates how clean or polluted the air is.
It also communicates the possible health effects of the pollution, especially for sensitive people.
solutions.answer: The AQI reports how polluted the air is and indicates its possible effects on health.

solutions.question: Who are high risk groups and why is pollution more dangerous for them?
steps: High-risk groups include children, older people, and people with asthma, lung diseases or heart diseases.
Their bodies or respiratory and circulatory systems may be more vulnerable to pollutants.
Air pollution can worsen their existing illnesses and may cause more serious health effects than in healthy adults.
solutions.answer: Children, older people and those with heart or lung illnesses are high-risk groups because pollution can affect them more severely.

solutions.question: Describe three strategies to address environmental issues.
steps: Reduce the use of resources and avoid activities that cause pollution.
Reuse materials and products instead of throwing them away.
Recycle waste materials, such as paper, glass, metals and plastics, to conserve resources and reduce waste.
solutions.answer: Environmental issues can be addressed by reducing resource use, reusing materials and recycling waste.

solutions.question: Major Pakistani cities experience a very high AQI in winter which renders them the most polluted cities in the world. Point out some of the major causes of high AQI in these cities.
steps: Exhaust from the large number of vehicles releases pollutants into the air.
Industries, power plants and brick kilns release smoke and harmful gases, especially when they burn fossil fuels.
Burning crop residues and waste adds smoke and fine particles to the air.
In winter, cold air near the ground and temperature inversion can trap pollutants close to the surface.
Calm winds and limited mixing of air allow pollutants to build up, while construction and road dust add further particles.
solutions.answer: Vehicle and industrial emissions, crop-residue burning, dust, and winter conditions that trap pollutants are major causes of high AQI.

solutions.question: Why does AQI not rise in Pakistan in hot days of summer?
steps: On hot summer days, warm air rises and promotes vertical mixing of the atmosphere.
Wind and convection disperse pollutants over a larger area instead of allowing them to remain concentrated near the ground.
Unlike winter temperature inversion, summer conditions generally do not trap pollutants close to the surface.
solutions.answer: Summer heat promotes air mixing and disperses pollutants, so they do not build up near the ground as they do in winter.

solutions.question: How has climate change affected Pakistan during the last five years?
steps: Pakistan has experienced more frequent and intense heatwaves and unusually high temperatures.
Irregular and intense monsoon rainfall has caused severe flooding, including the devastating floods of 2022.
Rising temperatures have accelerated the melting of glaciers and increased the risk of glacial lake outburst floods.
Some areas have faced drought and water shortages, while changing rainfall and temperature patterns have affected crops and livelihoods.
solutions.answer: Climate change has intensified heatwaves, floods and glacier-related risks in Pakistan, while also contributing to drought, water shortages and damage to crops.

definitions.text: The branch of Chemistry which deals with the study of chemicals and other pollutants in the environment is called environmental chemistry. It also covers the adverse effects of these chemicals on living and non-living things.
Any substance (solid, liquid or gas) in the air which has adverse effect on human health and quality of life is called an air pollutant.
A concentration of one ppm means one part of pollutant per million part of solid, liquid or gas mixture in which the pollutant is formed.
When rain water has pH between 4.2 and 4.4, it is known as acid rain.
The progressive warming up of the Earth's surface due to blanketing effect of man-made carbon dioxide, methane, water vapours and other gases in the atmosphere is called Greenhouse Effect.
Photosynthesis as the reaction between carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen in the presence of chlorophyll and using energy from light.
Renewable resources are those resources that can continue to exist despite being consumed over a period of time even as they are used.
Any substance in the air which has an adverse effect on human health, quality of life and natural functioning of the ecosystem is called a pollutant.

fullMarks: For a definition, write the complete sentence, including the key condition or effect; do not replace it with a vague phrase.
For a question about air pollutants, name the pollutant and connect it to its source and harmful effect. Use separate points so each effect is clear.
For acid rain, show the sequence: sulfur or nitrogen oxides form in the air, react with moisture to make acids, and return to the ground as acidic precipitation.
For greenhouse effect answers, explain that greenhouse gases absorb thermal radiation from Earth and reduce its loss to space; then state the resulting warming or climate effects.
For a chemical equation, write correct formulae and state symbols, balance the equation, and include reaction conditions such as chlorophyll and sunlight when needed.
In descriptive answers, use labelled headings or numbered points for each pollutant or effect; finish with a clear statement of the overall harm or a suitable prevention strategy.
When discussing personal protection, identify the risk or poor-air situation and give a relevant action, such as reducing outdoor activity, using a well-fitted N95 mask, or installing a CO detector.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying CO₂ is poisonous in the same way as CO. Fix: State that CO is extremely poisonous; higher CO₂ levels increase global warming.
Mistake: Naming only sulfur oxides as the cause of acid rain. Fix: Include both sulfur oxides and nitrogen oxides.
Mistake: Saying acid rain harms forests only by wetting them. Fix: Explain that it acidifies soil, washes away nutrients, can dissolve toxic substances, and damages plants.

Mistake: Describing the greenhouse effect as sunlight being blocked before reaching Earth. Fix: Explain that sunlight passes through, while greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing thermal radiation and reduce heat loss to space.
Mistake: Mixing up where ground-level ozone forms and what causes it. Fix: State that it forms when oxides of nitrogen react with volatile organic compounds in the presence of light.

Mistake: Giving prevention methods without linking them to the pollutant. Fix: Match the method to the problem, such as low-sulfur fuels or flue-gas desulfurization for SO₂, and catalytic converters for vehicle emissions.

shortTheory.question: What is the main objective of environmental education?
shortTheory.answer: The objective of environmental education is to enlighten the people particularly the students, about the importance of protection and conservation of our environment.

shortTheory.question: How does acid rain affect forests?
shortTheory.answer: Acid rain can damage vegetation and plants. Many plants cannot live or grow in acidic soil. Tree roots hold the soil together on hills and mountain areas. If the trees are destroyed then the soil is washed away and new plants cannot grow there.

shortTheory.question: In what way sulphur present in fossil fuels becomes dangerous?
shortTheory.answer: Burning of fossil fuels releases harmful gases into the atmosphere. These gases (SO₂, SO₃) are produced due to the presence of sulphur in the fossil fuels.

shortTheory.question: How is the excessive use of insecticides and pesticides harmful for birds?
shortTheory.answer: The excessive use of fertilizers, insecticides and pesticides, etc. for agriculture purposes has proved to be harmful for animals, birds and human beings.

shortTheory.question: Percentage of CO₂ in air is only 0.04%. Then how does it become harmful for the ecosystem?
shortTheory.answer: The remaining carbon dioxide which is not utilized in photosynthesis goes on accumulating in the lower areas of the atmosphere and forms a thick dense layer. This layer behaves like glass sheet of greenhouse that allows the incoming solar radiation but does not allow it to escape outside; as a result of this the average temperature of the Earth rises.

shortTheory.question: How does acid rain damage plants and soil?
shortTheory.answer: Acid rain makes soil more acidic. It dissolves and washes away nutrients present in the soil which are needed by plants. It can also dissolve toxic substances such as aluminium and mercury which are naturally present in the soil.

explain.body: The family of hydrocarbons constitutes a very large number of simple organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only. This means that a hydrocarbon has carbon and hydrogen atoms and no other elements.

explain.title: Why can carbon make so many compounds?
explain.body: Carbon forms four covalent bonds. Its ability to link to itself is called catenation. Carbon can therefore form long, straight and branched chains and rings, which gives many possible structures.

explain.title: Why are hydrocarbons useful?
explain.body: Natural gas, LPG, CNG, petrol, diesel and kerosene oil are examples of everyday fuels identified as simple hydrocarbons. Hydrocarbons also serve as feedstock to prepare useful compounds such as plastics, medicines, synthetic fibres, paints and varnishes.

explain.title: What makes an alkane?
explain.body: Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond. Alkanes are also called saturated hydrocarbons because all the four valencies of carbon in them are fully utilized either by hydrogen atoms or by other carbon atoms. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is an integer.

explain.title: The parts of an IUPAC name
explain.body: Root: It tells us the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain present in the molecule. Suffix: It is added after the root and tells us about the class of organic compounds. Prefix: It is indicated before the root and tells us about the group or groups attached to the longest chain. For an alkane, the suffix is -ane.

explain.title: Roots to remember
explain.body: Meth- means 1 carbon, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4, pent- 5, hex- 6, hept- 7, oct- 8, non- 9 and dec- 10. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and is also called the parent hydrocarbon.

explain.title: How to name a branched alkane
explain.body: Choose the longest continuous chain. Number it from the end closest to a branch, name the branch as a prefix, and attach its position number. For example, the four-carbon chain in CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃ gives the name 2-methylbutane.

explain.title: Alkane structures
explain.body: A methyl group is CH₃ and a methylene group is CH₂. In a straight-chain alkane, the end carbon atoms are usually CH₃ groups, while the carbon atoms in the middle are CH₂ groups.

mistakes: Do not choose a shorter chain just because it looks like the main horizontal line; find the longest continuous carbon chain.
Do not number from the end farther from the branch; use the nearest end to give the lowest possible branch number.
Do not forget the locant (position number) before a branch name, such as 2-methylbutane.
Do not use an alkene suffix such as -ene for an alkane; alkanes take the suffix -ane.
Do not confuse a methyl group, CH₃, with a methylene group, CH₂.

explain.title: Cracking higher hydrocarbons

explain.title: Reducing alkenes and alkynes
explain.body: Alkanes can be prepared by reducing alkenes and alkynes with hydrogen gas in the presence of nickel metal as a catalyst. Methane cannot be prepared by this method. The reaction is also called hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes and is an example of addition reaction. An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.

explain.body: In a substitution reaction, a hydrogen atom in an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom. Chlorine reacts with alkanes in UV light, so this is called photochemical substitution. Methane first forms chloromethane and hydrogen chloride; further substitution can replace more hydrogen atoms.

explain.title: Carbon compounds are numerous
explain.body: Carbon forms strong covalent bonds with itself and other elements. It can make chains, branches and rings, so a very large number of organic compounds exist.

explain.title: Alkanes and their reactions
explain.body: Alkanes have carbon–carbon single bonds. They are relatively unreactive, but undergo combustion, substitution (such as halogenation) and cracking. They do not normally undergo addition.

explain.title: Combustion and safety
explain.body: Complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water and releases heat. Natural gas mixed with air can be explosive if ignited, so leaks need immediate safe attention.

explain.title: Names and properties
explain.body: For an alkane name, select the longest chain, number it from the nearer end to a branch, and name the substituents. As alkane size generally increases, melting and boiling points rise; among isomers, branching usually lowers boiling point.

mistakes: Do not say that addition is a normal reaction of alkanes; addition is characteristic of unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Do not confuse cracking, which breaks hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, with halogenation.
When naming a branched alkane, number from the end nearest the substituent and include its position number.
For complete combustion of propane, do not leave the oxygen coefficient unbalanced: it is 5O₂.
Do not claim organic compounds are all soluble in water; most are generally non-polar and do not dissolve well in polar water.
When comparing n-butane and iso-butane, remember that n-butane has the higher boiling point.

recap.question: What are the two important reactions of alkanes described in this section?
recap.answer: Combustion forms carbon dioxide and water, and releases heat.

recap.question: Why do alkanes show little chemical reactivity towards many laboratory reagents?
recap.answer: The carbon–hydrogen bonds are almost non-polar.

solutions.question: Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.
steps: Organic compounds are compounds of carbon, usually containing carbon–hydrogen bonds; examples are methane (CH₄) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH).
Inorganic compounds are compounds that generally do not contain carbon–hydrogen bonds; examples include water (H₂O) and sodium chloride (NaCl).
Some carbon compounds, such as carbon dioxide, carbonates and carbides, are classified as inorganic compounds.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds usually contain carbon–hydrogen bonds, whereas inorganic compounds generally do not.

solutions.question: Why are organic compounds found in large numbers?
steps: Carbon atoms bond strongly with one another, forming long chains, branched chains and rings. This property is called catenation.
Carbon is tetravalent and forms stable covalent bonds with many other elements, including hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and halogens.
Carbon atoms can form single, double and triple bonds, and many compounds show isomerism.
These properties enable carbon to form a very large number of different compounds.
solutions.answer: Catenation, tetravalency, multiple bonding and isomerism enable carbon to form a large number of organic compounds.

solutions.question: Name the products which are obtained when natural gas is oxidized under controlled conditions.
steps: Under controlled oxidation, natural gas (mainly methane) can produce methanol, formaldehyde and formic acid.
solutions.answer: Methanol, formaldehyde and formic acid.

solutions.question: How naphtha fraction is decomposed to give lower hydrocarbons?
steps: Naphtha is heated strongly, usually in the presence of a catalyst, so that its larger hydrocarbon molecules break into smaller molecules.
This process is called cracking and produces lower hydrocarbons, including alkanes and alkenes.
solutions.answer: Naphtha is cracked by strong heating, usually with a catalyst, to form lower hydrocarbons.

solutions.question: Write down the molecular formula, structural formula and the condensed structural formula for iso-butane.
steps: Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀.
Structural formula:
CH₃
CH₃—CH—CH₃
Condensed structural formula: (CH₃)₃CH.
solutions.answer: Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀; structural formula: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₃; condensed structural formula: (CH₃)₃CH.

solutions.question: How are organic compounds useful for us?
steps: Organic compounds are useful as food and fuels.
They are used to make clothing fibres, medicines, plastics, dyes and perfumes.
They are also used in making many household and industrial products.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds are used in food, fuels, clothing, medicines and many everyday products.

solutions.question: Write down the names of five such organic compounds which exist naturally?
steps: Five naturally occurring organic compounds are glucose, starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.
solutions.answer: Glucose, starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.

solutions.question: Give IUPAC name to the following compound: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃.
steps: The longest continuous carbon chain has four carbon atoms, so the parent name is butane.
Number the chain from the end nearest the branch; the methyl group is attached to carbon 2.
The IUPAC name is 2-methylbutane.
solutions.answer: 2-methylbutane.

solutions.question: How do the melting and boiling points of alkanes change when we move from lower members to higher members?
steps: The melting and boiling points of alkanes increase as we move from lower members to higher members.
Higher alkanes have greater molecular mass and stronger intermolecular forces.
solutions.answer: The melting and boiling points of alkanes generally increase from lower members to higher members.

solutions.question: Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards the other reagents?
steps: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing strong covalent bonds between carbon and hydrogen atoms.
They are non-polar and have no reactive functional group, so they show little reactivity towards other reagents.
solutions.answer: Alkanes are relatively unreactive because they contain strong covalent bonds and have no reactive functional group.

solutions.question: Why does a mixture of natural gas and air explode?
steps: Natural gas mixes with oxygen in air to form a combustible mixture.
When ignited, the mixture burns very rapidly and releases a large amount of heat.
The rapid expansion of hot gases causes an explosion.
solutions.answer: A mixture of natural gas and air explodes because it burns rapidly, releasing heat and expanding gases.

solutions.question: How do you compare the melting and boiling points of inorganic and organic compounds?
steps: Inorganic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points because many are ionic and have strong forces between their ions.
Organic compounds generally have low melting and boiling points because most are molecular covalent compounds with weak intermolecular forces.
solutions.answer: Inorganic compounds generally have higher melting and boiling points than organic compounds.

solutions.question: Reactions of alkanes with chlorine takes place in the presence of sunlight. What is the role of sunlight in the reaction?
steps: Sunlight provides energy to break chlorine molecules into chlorine atoms.
These chlorine atoms initiate the substitution reaction with alkanes.
solutions.answer: Sunlight initiates the reaction by breaking chlorine molecules into chlorine atoms.

solutions.question: How do you compare the boiling point of n – butane with that of iso – butane?
steps: The boiling point of n-butane is higher than that of iso-butane.
The straight-chain molecules of n-butane have a larger surface area of contact than the branched molecules of iso-butane.
Therefore, the intermolecular forces between n-butane molecules are stronger.
solutions.answer: n-Butane has a higher boiling point than iso-butane.

solutions.question: Why are organic compounds not generally soluble in water?
steps: Most organic compounds are non-polar, whereas water is a polar solvent.
Organic compounds do not form strong attractions or hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
Therefore, they are generally not soluble in water.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds are generally insoluble in water because they are non-polar, while water is polar.

solutions.question: Describe the importance of organic compounds in daily life.
steps: Organic compounds are essential for life; carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins are important components of living organisms and food.
They are used as fuels, for example natural gas, petrol and diesel.
They are used to make medicines, plastics, synthetic fibres, detergents, dyes, paints and cosmetics.
Many materials used for clothing, shelter and other daily needs are made from organic compounds.
solutions.answer: Organic compounds are important in food, fuels, medicines and many materials used in daily life.

solutions.question: Why is carbon so important as an element that the whole branch of chemistry is based on it?
steps: Carbon is important because it forms a very large number of compounds.
A carbon atom is tetravalent, so it can form four covalent bonds with other atoms.
Carbon atoms also form strong bonds with one another, making chains, branched chains and rings. This property is called catenation.
Because of these properties, carbon compounds are numerous and are studied in the branch of chemistry called organic chemistry.
solutions.answer: Carbon’s tetravalency and catenation enable it to form a vast number of compounds, which are studied in organic chemistry.

solutions.question: A carbon–carbon single bond (C – C) in alkanes does not behave as a functional group but a carbon carbon double bond (C = C) in alkenes does. Explain.
steps: A carbon–carbon single bond is relatively less reactive and is present in saturated hydrocarbons called alkanes.
The C–C single bond does not usually take part in characteristic reactions, so it is not considered a functional group.
A carbon–carbon double bond is more reactive and is present in unsaturated hydrocarbons called alkenes.
The double bond takes part in characteristic addition reactions and determines the chemical properties of alkenes; therefore, it is a functional group.
solutions.answer: The reactive C=C bond gives alkenes their characteristic reactions, whereas the less reactive C–C bond in alkanes does not act as a functional group.

solutions.question: Explain IUPAC system of nomenclature for alkanes.
How combustion reaction of alkanes is useful for us?
steps: Alkanes burn in oxygen and produce carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat and light energy.
This energy is used for cooking, heating and running engines and industrial processes.
For example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat.
solutions.answer: Combustion of alkanes releases useful heat energy, so alkanes are used as fuels.

solutions.question: When natural gas valve is kept open in the kitchen, the gas spreads through the whole kitchen. This may cause an explosion. What is the reason of this explosion and how can you avoid it?
steps: Natural gas mixes with air and spreads through the kitchen when a valve is left open.
The gas–air mixture is highly inflammable; a spark or flame can ignite it and cause an explosion.
To avoid this, close the gas valve immediately and open doors and windows to ventilate the kitchen.
Do not light a match or operate electrical switches until the gas has dispersed.
solutions.answer: Gas mixed with air can explode if ignited; close the valve, ventilate the kitchen and avoid flames or electrical switches.

solutions.question: “Neem” is a common tree grown throughout our country. Comment on the medicinal benefits of this tree.
steps: Neem is a medicinal tree whose different parts are used in traditional remedies.
Neem leaves and bark are used for their antiseptic properties and in treating skin problems.
Neem is also used in products for dental care, and neem oil is used to help repel insects.
solutions.answer: Neem leaves, bark and oil are used in traditional remedies, antiseptic preparations, dental care and insect repellents.

solutions.question: Name a few popular medicines which are, in fact, organic compounds?
steps: Many medicines are organic compounds.
Examples include aspirin, paracetamol, penicillin, quinine and morphine.
solutions.answer: Examples of medicines that are organic compounds are aspirin, paracetamol, penicillin, quinine and morphine.

definitions.text: This fact has led us to define organic chemistry as the chemistry of carbon compounds.
The self-linking property of carbon is called catenation and due to this it forms long, straight and branched chains and rings.
Compounds in which carbon forms single bond with other atoms are called saturated compounds.
A structural formula thus shows the symbols for the atoms present in the compounds connected by short lines which represent the bonds present in them.
The family of hydrocarbons constitutes a very large number of simple organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.
Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond.
The International Union of Pure & Applied Chemistry has devised a systematic way of naming organic compounds called IUPAC nomenclature.
Cracking is the name of a process in which hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses (which are lesser in demand) are broken up into smaller hydrocarbons which are more in demand.
An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.
The reactions which involve the replacement of hydrogen of alkanes by an atom or a group of atoms like halogen are called substitution reactions.
Since these substitution reactions are carried out in the presence of UV light, these are called photochemical substitution reactions.
Alkanes burn in oxygen or air to form CO₂ and H₂O with the evolution of large amount of heat. The reaction is called combustion.

For IUPAC naming, identify the longest continuous carbon chain first, choose its root, identify the class and suffix, name any branch as a prefix, and number the chain from the end nearest the branch.

mistakes: Mistake: Calling every carbon compound organic. Fix: Remember that carbonates, cyanides, carbides, cyanates, and oxides of carbon are classified as inorganic in this chapter.
Mistake: Describing alkanes as unsaturated. Fix: Alkanes have only single carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonds, so they are saturated hydrocarbons.
Mistake: Numbering a branched alkane from the end farthest from its branch. Fix: Number the longest chain from the end closest to the branch.
Mistake: Forgetting the UV-light condition in methane chlorination. Fix: Show hν or state that the substitution is carried out in UV light.
Mistake: Writing unbalanced combustion or hydrogenation equations. Fix: Count each type of atom on both sides and balance the equation before finishing.
Mistake: Saying cracking simply burns naphtha. Fix: State that high temperature and zeolite break larger hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons.
Mistake: Giving only one formula when asked for all three forms of iso-butane. Fix: Label its molecular formula, structural formula, and condensed structural formula separately.

shortTheory.question: Define alkanes.
shortTheory.answer: Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond.

shortTheory.question: What is cracking?
shortTheory.answer: Cracking is the name of a process in which hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses (which are lesser in demand) are broken up into smaller hydrocarbons which are more in demand.

shortTheory.question: What is a substitution reaction?
shortTheory.answer: The reactions which involve the replacement of hydrogen of alkanes by an atom or a group of atoms like halogen are called substitution reactions.

shortTheory.question: What is an addition reaction?
shortTheory.answer: An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.

shortTheory.question: Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards other reagents?
shortTheory.answer: The unreactivity of alkanes may be explained on the basis of the non-polarity of the bonds present in them. The electronegativity values of carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably and the bonding electrons between C – H and C – C bonds, are almost equally shared. This fact makes alkanes almost non-polar.

shortTheory.question: What is combustion?
shortTheory.answer: Alkanes burn in oxygen or air to form CO₂ and H₂O with the evolution of large amount of heat. The reaction is called combustion.

explain.title: Why scientists use SI units
explain.body: SI units are standard units used internationally. They make it easier for scientists to share, compare and verify measurements. The system is based on 10, so conversions are convenient.

explain.title: Five base units used in chemistry
explain.body: The five are metre (m) for length, second (s) for time, mole (mol) for amount of substance, kilogram (kg) for mass and kelvin (K) for temperature.

explain.title: Derived units and prefixes
explain.body: Derived units are formed from base units. The section lists volume in m³, density in kg m⁻³ and area in m². Prefixes show multiples or fractions of a unit: kilo means 10³, deci 10⁻¹ and milli 10⁻³.

explain.title: Practical laboratory units
explain.body: Chemistry often deals with small quantities, so grams are manageable for mass and cubic centimetres (cm³) are practical for small volumes. Celsius is often convenient for temperature; the section gives K = °C + 273 for conversion to kelvin.

mistakes: Writing Kg or KG instead of kg; symbols have the correct capitalisation and are not pluralised.
Mixing up base units and derived units, such as calling m³ a base unit.
Using kilogram or cubic metre automatically for small laboratory quantities instead of explaining why grams and cm³ are practical.
Giving a prefix's name but the wrong power of ten, especially confusing milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹) and pico (10⁻¹²).
For Celsius-to-kelvin conversion, forgetting to add 273 or giving the answer without the unit K.

explain.title: Error in measurement
explain.body: An error may be defined as the difference between the measured value and the actual value. Errors can happen because an instrument has limitations or because of the skill of the person measuring.

explain.title: Systematic error
explain.body: “Systematic errors may be removed by adding or subtracting a constant adjustment given to each measurement.” These errors affect accuracy. For example, an instrument may deliver a volume slightly different from the volume shown by its graduations.

explain.title: Random error
explain.body: “Random error causes one measurement to differ slightly from the next measurement.” It comes from unpredictable changes, such as environmental factors or slight changes in procedure, and often determines precision.

explain.title: The goal of measurement
explain.body: Experiments aim to produce results that are both accurate and precise. Accuracy concerns the actual value; precision concerns the consistency of repeated measurements.

mistakes: Do not confuse accuracy with precision: accuracy relates to the actual value, while precision relates to agreement among repeated measurements.
Do not say that random error is removed by a constant adjustment; the section gives that correction for systematic error.
Do not describe a random error as a fixed shift; it makes one measurement differ slightly from the next.
When asked for reasons for random error, include unpredictable changes, instrument limitations, environmental factors or slight variation in procedure.

explain.title: Accuracy
explain.body: Accuracy measures how close results are to the true or known value. Compare a reading with the true value to judge accuracy.

explain.title: Precision
explain.body: The closeness of two or more measurements to each other is called precision. Compare repeated readings with one another to judge precision.

explain.title: They are independent
explain.body: Precision is independent of accuracy. Repeated results may agree closely but still be far from the true value; a set of results may also be near the true value but spread apart.

explain.title: Classifying measurements
explain.body: Check two things separately: how close the readings are to the true value, and how close the readings are to each other. Then name accuracy and precision separately.

mistakes: Do not call repeated identical readings accurate unless they are also close to the true or known value.
Do not mix up the meanings: accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness among measurements.
Do not assume that an accurate result must also be precise, or that a precise result must also be accurate.
When classifying a set of readings, state both properties rather than only saying “good measurements.”

explain.title: SI is a shared measurement system
explain.body: SI units provide a common way to measure and communicate quantities. Their decimal prefixes make conversions straightforward. In Chemistry, litre and smaller units are often practical for liquid volumes and small samples.

explain.title: Base and derived units
explain.body: Basic SI units include metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance. Derived units are made by combining base units: area may be measured in m², volume in m³, and density in kg/m³.

explain.title: Accuracy and precision are different
explain.body: Accuracy tells how close a result is to the true value. Precision tells how close repeated measurements are to one another. A result can be precise without being accurate.

explain.title: Measurement errors
explain.body: A systematic error shifts results consistently, often because of instrument bias or a faulty method, and it affects accuracy. A random error varies unpredictably between readings. Calibration, checking zero and using a suitable technique can reduce systematic errors.

explain.title: Standard units support reliable work
explain.body: Using the same units helps people compare results, share measurements and avoid confusion. In daily life and space exploration, unit misunderstandings or conversion errors can cause serious problems.

mistakes: Do not confuse accuracy (closeness to the true value) with precision (agreement among repeated readings).
Use the correct symbol and letter case: kilogram is kg, kelvin is K, and kilo as a prefix is k.
In scientific notation, the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10; 0.000840 = 8.40 × 10⁻⁴.
Do not omit the unit from a numerical answer. Celsius-to-kelvin answers must be given in K.
Do not claim systematic errors are random: systematic errors shift readings consistently, while random errors vary unpredictably.
When explaining the benefit of SI, give a reason such as easier comparison, communication, conversion or fewer mistakes.
