Glucose can be stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
The body can use this stored resource when it needs energy.
notes.checkQuestion: Where is glycogen stored, and what is its role?
notes.checkAnswer: Glycogen is the primary storage form of glucose. It is stored in the liver and muscles.

notes.title: Energy changes in reactions
notes.answer: The energy change depends on the difference between the energy absorbed in breaking bonds and the energy released in forming bonds.
notes.explanation: Energetics studies the energy changes that occur during chemical reactions and physical changes. Breaking bonds absorbs energy; forming bonds releases energy. A reaction is exothermic when more energy is released in forming bonds than is absorbed in breaking them. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to start a reaction.
notes.simple: Think of bonds as needing energy to break and giving out energy when they form. Compare these two amounts to decide whether the overall change releases or absorbs energy.
examples: In an exothermic reaction, the energy released when new bonds form is greater than the energy needed to break the original bonds.
A burning match supplies activation energy to start the reaction between methane and oxygen.
steps: Identify which bonds break and which bonds form.
Add the energy absorbed to break the bonds.
Add the energy released when new bonds form.
For bond-energy calculations, use ΔH = energy of bonds broken − energy of bonds formed.
A negative ΔH means the reaction is exothermic; a positive ΔH means it is endothermic.
notes.checkQuestion: Does breaking a bond release energy or absorb energy?
notes.checkAnswer: Breaking a bond absorbs energy.

notes.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes
notes.answer: It shows that the reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.
notes.explanation: Some reactions proceed only forwards, while others can proceed both forwards and backwards under the same conditions. In a reversible reaction, products can react to form the original reactants.
notes.simple: Some changes can go both ways. Other changes go only forwards.
examples: NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) is an irreversible reaction that goes to completion.
CuSO₄ · 5 H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5 H₂O(g) shows the reversible change between hydrated and anhydrous copper sulphate.
steps: Identify whether the reaction can proceed in both directions under the same conditions.
If it proceeds only forwards, call it irreversible and use →.
If products can form reactants again, call it reversible and use ⇌.
Check whether a product escapes or is removed, because this can make a reversible reaction go to completion.
notes.checkQuestion: What does the symbol ⇌ show?
notes.checkAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions under the same conditions; an irreversible reaction proceeds only in the forward direction.

notes.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
notes.answer: The reaction continues in both directions at equal rates, so the concentrations of reacting species remain constant.
notes.explanation: In dynamic equilibrium, a reversible reaction continues in both directions. The forward and backward reactions happen at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
notes.simple: The reaction has not stopped. Both directions keep happening, but they balance each other, so the amounts of reactants and products do not change.
examples: In a sealed flask, colourless N₂O₄ changes into brown NO₂. As NO₂ forms, the reverse reaction also starts; at equilibrium, the brown colour stops changing.
In a closed container of water at a fixed temperature, evaporation and condensation can occur at equal rates.
steps: A reversible reaction starts in the forward direction.
Products build up and begin to react in the backward direction.
The forward and backward reaction rates become equal.
The reaction continues in both directions, while concentrations stay constant.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the concentrations of reactants and products at dynamic equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward reaction rates are equal, and the concentrations remain constant.

notes.title: Changing conditions at equilibrium
notes.answer: A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions, so equilibrium is reached in less time.
notes.explanation: A reversible reaction at equilibrium can be disturbed by changing the amounts of reactants or products, the temperature, or—when gases are involved—the pressure. The reaction then shifts in a direction that helps establish equilibrium again. A catalyst makes equilibrium happen sooner but does not change the equilibrium position.
notes.simple: If you disturb an equilibrium, the reaction shifts to help restore it. A catalyst only helps it get there faster.
examples: Adding N₂ to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) makes the reaction move forward and form more NH₃.
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), that is the forward side.
steps: Identify what changed: the amount of a substance, temperature, or pressure.
For a changed amount, note whether a reactant or product was added or removed.
For temperature, use whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
For pressure, compare the total moles of gaseous substances on both sides.
Remember that a catalyst speeds up both directions and reduces the time to reach equilibrium.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a catalyst do to a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: The forward and backward reaction rates increase equally; the catalyst makes equilibrium take less time to reach.

notes.title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium
notes.answer: No. Both reactions continue, but at equal rates.
notes.explanation: At equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates. The amounts of reactants and products stay constant, but the reactions have not stopped.
notes.simple: Think of two equally fast streams of people moving in opposite directions. People are still moving, but the number on each side stays the same.
examples: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), both sides have two moles of gas, so increasing pressure does not favour either direction.
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), high pressure favours ammonia because the product side has fewer gas molecules.
steps: A reversible reaction can go in both the forward and backward directions.
In a closed system, the forward reaction starts and products begin to form.
As products build up, the backward reaction rate increases.
At equilibrium, forward and backward reaction rates are equal.
A change in temperature, pressure, or concentration can shift the equilibrium position.
notes.checkQuestion: At dynamic equilibrium, have the forward and backward reactions stopped?
notes.checkAnswer: The concentrations of reactants and products stay constant because the forward and backward reaction rates are equal.

notes.title: Acids, bases and alkalis
notes.answer: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
notes.explanation: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Acids and bases have different properties, and when they react in equal amounts they neutralize each other to form salt and water.
notes.simple: Acids and bases are different kinds of substances. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali.
examples: Sodium hydroxide dissolves in water, so it is an alkali.
Sodium oxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide, a base.
steps: Identify whether the substance is an acid or a base.
If it is a base, check whether it dissolves in water.
A base that dissolves in water is an alkali.
notes.checkQuestion: What is an alkali?
notes.checkAnswer: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.

notes.title: Arrhenius Acids and Bases
notes.answer: Arrhenius acids produce H⁺ or H₃O⁺ in water; Arrhenius bases produce OH⁻ in water.
notes.explanation: The Arrhenius idea classifies acids and bases by what they produce when they dissociate in water. An acid produces H⁺ or H₃O⁺, while a base produces OH⁻. The amount of ionization also helps us describe an acid or base as strong or weak.
notes.simple: In water, acids give H₃O⁺ and bases give OH⁻. Strong substances ionize more completely; weak substances ionize only partly.
examples: HCl ionizes in water to form H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻.
NaOH ionizes in water to form Na⁺ and OH⁻.
steps: An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺).
A base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻).
For example: HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
For example: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
Acid strength depends upon the extent to which it is ionized in water.
notes.checkQuestion: Why is NaOH an Arrhenius base?
notes.checkAnswer: NaOH is an Arrhenius base because it dissociates in water to give OH⁻ ions.

notes.title: Brønsted–Lowry Acids and Bases
notes.answer: An acid donates a proton; a base accepts a proton.
notes.explanation: In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid gives a proton and a base takes a proton. Water can do either, depending on what it reacts with.
notes.simple: An acid hands over H⁺. A base receives H⁺. Water can do either job.
examples: HCl gives a proton to H₂O, so HCl is the acid and H₂O is the base.
NH₃ takes a proton from H₂O, so NH₃ is the base and H₂O is the acid.
steps: Find which substance donates H⁺: it is the acid.
Find which substance accepts H⁺: it is the base.
The acid left after donating H⁺ is its conjugate base.
The base formed after accepting H⁺ is its conjugate acid.
notes.checkQuestion: What is a substance called if it can behave as both an acid and a base?
notes.checkAnswer: Water is amphoteric because it can behave as both an acid and a base.

notes.title: Reactions of Acids and Bases
notes.answer: Acids react with metals, alkalis or metal oxides, and carbonates in characteristic ways. Alkalis also release ammonia from ammonium salts.
notes.explanation: Acids react with alkalis or metal oxides to make salt and water, with reactive metals to make salt and hydrogen, and with carbonates to make salt, water and carbon dioxide. Alkalis also react with ammonium salts to release ammonia.
notes.simple: Different substances react with acids and bases in different ways, often making a salt and a gas.
examples: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
steps: Identify the type of substance reacting with the acid.
Use the matching products: metal gives salt and hydrogen; carbonate gives salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Write and balance the chemical equation.
notes.checkQuestion: What products form when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
notes.checkAnswer: Salt, water and carbon dioxide are formed.

notes.title: Acid Rain and its Effects
notes.answer: Acid rain is rain water with a pH between 4.2 and 4.4.
notes.explanation: Acid rain forms when harmful gases from burning fossil fuels mix with moisture in the air. It can harm soil, plants, aquatic life, and structures.
notes.simple: Some gases mix with water in the air and fall as acidic rain. This can hurt living things and damage buildings.
examples: SO₂ forms SO₃, which then reacts with water to form H₂SO₄.
Acid rain can make lakes too acidic for fish to live in.
steps: Burning fossil fuels releases harmful gases, including SO₂ and NO₂.
The gases mix with moisture in the air and form acid droplets.
The droplets fall to the ground as acid rain.
Acid rain harms soil, plants, aquatic life, and structures.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two effects of acid rain.
notes.checkAnswer: Acid rain can harm soil and plants, make water too acidic for aquatic animals, and damage buildings and other structures.

notes.title: Acids and Bases: Key Ideas
notes.answer: An acid donates H⁺; a base accepts H⁺. Acid–base reactions form products such as salts, water, carbon dioxide or hydrogen, depending on the reactants.
notes.explanation: Acids and bases can be described by the ions they produce in water or by proton transfer. Acids react with some metals, carbonates and bases in characteristic ways. Some substances, such as water and hydrogen carbonate ions, can act as either acids or bases.
notes.simple: An acid can give away a proton, H⁺. A base can accept H⁺. In water, acids produce H₃O⁺ and bases produce OH⁻ or accept H⁺. Reactions help us identify acids and bases.
examples: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂
CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
steps: Identify the acid and base using the definition named in the question.
For a reaction, write the correct products and balance the equation.
For proton transfer, show which species loses H⁺ and which gains H⁺.
For an acid–carbonate reaction, include salt, water and carbon dioxide.
notes.checkQuestion: How does HSO₄⁻ show that it is a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
notes.checkAnswer: HSO₄⁻ donates H⁺ to form SO₄²⁻, so it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.

notes.title: How the Modern Periodic Table Is Arranged
notes.answer: The modern periodic table arranges elements in increasing atomic number, in periods and groups.
notes.explanation: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Elements are placed in horizontal periods and vertical groups. Elements in the same group have similar outermost-shell electronic configurations and therefore similar chemical properties.
notes.simple: Think of the periodic table as a chart: elements go from left to right in increasing atomic number, and elements with similar properties are placed in the same vertical column.
examples: Sodium and chlorine are placed in the same period because they are in the same horizontal row.
Elements in one vertical column belong to the same group.
steps: Arrange the elements in ascending order of atomic number.
Read across each horizontal row, called a period.
Read down each vertical column, called a group.
Notice that properties repeat at regular intervals and that elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the horizontal rows and vertical columns of the periodic table called?
notes.checkAnswer: The horizontal rows are periods, and the vertical columns are groups.

notes.title: Reading periods, groups and blocks
notes.answer: The periodic table has 7 periods and 18 groups. Groups 1 and 2 are s-block; groups 13 to 18 are p-block; groups 3 to 12 are d-block; and the two rows placed at the bottom are f-block elements.
notes.explanation: A period is a horizontal row, and a group is a vertical column. The period tells the number of the shell being filled; the group helps identify how many electrons are in the outermost shell. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
notes.simple: Rows are periods; columns are groups. The row tells which shell is being filled, and the column helps tell the outer-shell electron pattern.
examples: Group 17 has outermost-shell configuration ns² np⁵, so its elements are halogens.
Elements in groups 13 to 18 are p-block elements.
steps: Find whether the element is described by a horizontal row or a vertical column.
Use the period number to identify the shell being filled.
Use the group’s outermost-shell configuration to identify its family and block.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the outermost-shell electronic configuration of group 17?
notes.checkAnswer: Group 17; ns² np⁵; p-block.

notes.title: Why elements in a group behave alike
notes.answer: Group 17 elements usually form 1− ions.
notes.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shells. This is why they tend to form ions in similar ways and show similar chemical properties. Group 1 metals tend to lose one electron; group 2 metals tend to lose two. Group 17 elements tend to gain one electron, while group 16 elements tend to gain two.
notes.simple: Elements in a group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they tend to react in similar ways.
examples: Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺.
Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
steps: Find the group of the element.
Use the group’s outer-shell electron pattern.
Decide whether the element tends to lose or gain electrons.
Write the ion with the correct charge.
notes.checkQuestion: What ion does a group 17 element usually form?
notes.checkAnswer: A group 17 element usually gains one electron and forms a 1− anion.

notes.title: Periodic trends in atomic properties
notes.answer: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group; ionization energy and electronegativity generally change in the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: Atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity show regular trends in the periodic table. For example, atomic radius generally decreases across a period, while ionization energy generally increases.
notes.simple: Across a period, atoms generally get smaller and hold their outer electrons more strongly. Down a group, atoms generally get larger.
examples: A carbon–carbon nucleus distance of 154 pm gives a carbon radius of 77 pm.
In Group 1, the atomic radius increases from Li to Cs.
steps: For atomic radius, remember: generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
For ionization energy, remember: generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.
For the radius of an atom bonded to an identical atom, divide the distance between the two nuclei by 2.
notes.checkQuestion: How does atomic radius generally change from left to right across a period?
notes.checkAnswer: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period.

notes.title: Metallic character and reactivity
notes.answer: Metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group. Metallic character decreases from left to right in a period.
notes.explanation: Metallic character describes how readily an element loses electrons. In a group, metallic character and reactivity generally increase downwards; across a period, metallic character decreases from left to right.
notes.simple: Metals tend to lose electrons. The easier an atom loses electrons, the more metallic it is.
examples: Potassium is more metallic than sodium because potassium is lower in Group 1.
Sodium is more reactive than magnesium in Period 3, as your textbook explains.
steps: Remember that metallic character means the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
Down a group, ionization energy decreases, so atoms lose electrons more easily.
Therefore metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group.
From left to right in a period, the nucleus attracts valence electrons more strongly, so metallic character decreases.
notes.checkQuestion: How does metallic character change down a group?
notes.checkAnswer: Metallic character and reactivity generally increase down a group.

notes.title: How the Periodic Table Organises Elements
notes.answer: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
notes.explanation: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Their electron arrangements explain their positions and help us understand repeating patterns in their properties.
notes.simple: Elements are arranged by atomic number. Their properties repeat in a pattern because their outer-electron arrangements repeat.
examples: Sodium is in Period 3 and Group 1; it has one electron in its outermost shell.
Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period, while ionization energy generally increases.
steps: Find the element's atomic number.
Use its electron arrangement to identify its period and group.
Use its position to predict trends such as atomic radius and metallic character.
notes.checkQuestion: What determines the order of elements in the modern periodic table?
notes.checkAnswer: Atomic number.

notes.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
notes.answer: Group 1 elements are called alkali metals. Down the group, reactivity and density generally increase, while melting point decreases and the metals become softer.
notes.explanation: Group 1 metals become more reactive as you go down the group because their atoms get larger, so the outer electron is easier to lose. They also become softer, their melting points decrease, and their densities generally increase.
notes.simple: Going down Group 1, the atoms get bigger. Their outer electron is easier to remove, so the metals react more strongly.
examples: Lithium reacts steadily with water, while sodium reacts vigorously and potassium reacts violently.
The melting point falls from lithium (180 °C) to caesium (28 °C).
steps: Remember that Group 1 atoms have one electron in their outermost shell.
As you go down the group, atomic size increases.
The outer electron becomes easier to lose.
Therefore, reactivity increases down the group.
Also remember the physical trends: metals get softer, melting points decrease, and density generally increases.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does reactivity increase down Group 1?
notes.checkAnswer: Potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium because it loses its outer electron more easily.

notes.title: Group 17: Halogens
notes.answer: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent. It can displace bromine from a bromide solution.
notes.explanation: Group 17 elements are halogens. They have seven outer-shell electrons and tend to gain one electron. Their reactivity and oxidising power decrease down the group, while their atomic radii and the melting and boiling points increase.
notes.simple: Halogens usually gain one electron. The halogens near the top of the group gain it more easily, so they are more reactive.
examples: Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
Hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable than hydrogen chloride: HCl > HBr in thermal stability.
steps: Identify which halogen is higher in Group 17.
The higher halogen has greater oxidising power.
It can displace a lower halogen from a solution of its halide.
notes.checkQuestion: Which is the stronger oxidising agent, chlorine or bromine, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent, so it gains electrons and displaces bromine from bromide ions.

notes.title: Group Properties of Transition Elements
notes.answer: Transition elements are metals in groups 3 to 12. They often have high strength and high melting and boiling points, show variable oxidation states, and form coloured compounds. Some are used as catalysts.
notes.explanation: Transition elements are metals found in groups 3 to 12. They have properties such as high strength, high melting and boiling points, variable oxidation states, and coloured compounds. Some transition metals or their compounds act as catalysts in important industrial processes and in automobile exhaust systems.
notes.simple: Transition elements are metals in the centre of the periodic table. Some help chemical reactions happen faster as catalysts.
examples: Iron acts as a catalyst in the Haber process to produce ammonia.
Nickel is used as a catalyst to hydrogenate oils and make solid margarine.
steps: Find the transition element named in the question.
Identify the reaction or process in which it is used.
State its role as a catalyst and the product formed, if asked.
notes.checkQuestion: Which transition metal is used as a catalyst to hydrogenate oils?
notes.checkAnswer: Nickel.

notes.title: Properties of Noble Gases
notes.answer: Noble elements are group 18 elements; they are monoatomic gases with very low boiling points and very little chemical reactivity.
notes.explanation: Noble elements are the elements in group 18. They exist as single atoms, have very low boiling points and are mostly unreactive because their outer electron shells are complete. For example, helium has the configuration s², while neon has s²p⁶.
notes.simple: Noble gases are single atoms with full outer shells, so they hardly react.
examples: Helium is a noble element in group 18.
Neon has a complete outer shell with the configuration s²p⁶.
steps: Identify noble elements as group 18 elements.
Check that they exist as single atoms.
Recall that their outer shells are complete, except helium has s².
Link the complete outer shell to very little chemical reactivity.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do noble elements show very little chemical reactivity?
notes.checkAnswer: Noble elements are mostly unreactive because their outer shells are complete.

notes.title: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
notes.answer: Graphite.
notes.explanation: Metals and non-metals have different physical properties. Metals are usually strong, shiny, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are usually brittle and poor conductors. Graphite conducts electricity, and iodine is lustrous, so these are exceptions.
notes.simple: Metals are usually strong and conduct heat and electricity. Non-metals usually break easily and do not conduct them.
examples: Copper is a metal: it is lustrous and conducts electricity.
Sulphur is a non-metal: it is brittle and does not conduct electricity.
steps: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets; this property is called malleability.
Metals can be drawn into wires; this property is called ductility.
Non-metals are generally brittle, so they break when hammered or stretched.
Graphite is the exception among non-metals because it conducts electricity.
notes.checkQuestion: Which non-metal is an exception because it conducts electricity?
notes.checkAnswer: Metals are usually good conductors; non-metals are usually poor conductors. Graphite is an exception.

notes.title: Group Properties and Elements
notes.answer: Group 1 elements become more reactive down the group, while halogens become less reactive down the group.
notes.explanation: This chapter compares the properties and reactions of groups of elements. Down Group 1, metals lose their outer electron more easily and become more reactive. Down the halogens, atoms gain an electron less easily, so their reactivity decreases. Metals usually form positive ions, while halogens form negative ions.
notes.simple: Remember the opposite trends: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group, but halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
examples: Potassium reacts with chlorine to form potassium chloride: 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl.
Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
steps: Identify the group of the elements in the question.
Recall the trend down that group.
Use the trend to compare the elements or predict the reaction.
For a reaction, write the balanced equation and identify any oxidising or reducing agent.
notes.checkQuestion: Which is the stronger oxidising agent, chlorine or bromine, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it oxidises bromide ions to bromine.

notes.title: Composition of the Atmosphere
notes.answer: Clean, dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with the remainder made up of noble gases and carbon dioxide.
notes.explanation: Air is a mixture of gases. By volume, it is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen; the remaining small proportion includes carbon dioxide, noble gases and variable water vapour.
notes.simple: Air is not one gas. It is a mixture, and most of it is nitrogen.
examples: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in air.
Water vapour in air varies with humidity.
steps: Read the gas name in the table.
Match it with its percentage by volume.
Remember that water vapour is variable, depending on humidity.
notes.checkQuestion: Which gas makes up the largest proportion of air, and what is its approximate percentage?
notes.checkAnswer: Nitrogen, about 78%.

notes.title: Air Pollutants
notes.answer: Smog reduces the carbon dioxide absorbed during photosynthesis, so it inhibits plant growth.
notes.explanation: Air pollution is harmful material in the air. It can harm people, other living things and the environment. Pollutants include gases such as carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide, as well as particles such as dust and smoke.
notes.simple: Air pollution means harmful substances in the air. Some are gases; others are tiny particles. They can make people ill and harm plants and the environment.
examples: Carbon monoxide is poisonous and can stop blood from carrying the oxygen the body needs.
Smog can reduce the carbon dioxide plants absorb during photosynthesis, inhibiting their growth.
steps: An air pollutant is a substance in the air that harms human health or quality of life.
The main pollutants include carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur, hydrocarbons, particulates and ozone.
Burning fossil fuels is a major source of air pollution.
Smog forms when smoke in the atmosphere mixes with fog in winter.
Pollutants can cause breathing problems, acid rain, global warming and harm to plants.
notes.checkQuestion: How can smog affect the growth of plants?
notes.checkAnswer: Smog can reduce the carbon dioxide plants absorb during photosynthesis, inhibiting their growth.

notes.title: Acid Rain
notes.answer: H₂SO₄, HNO₃ and HNO₂.
notes.explanation: Acid rain forms when oxides of sulphur and nitrogen mix with moisture in the air. For example, SO₃ reacts with water to make H₂SO₄, while NO₂ reacts with water to make HNO₃ and HNO₂. Acid rain can harm soil, plants, aquatic life, human health, agriculture and human-made structures.
notes.simple: Acid rain is rain containing acids made from gases in the air. It can damage living things and structures.
examples: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄
2NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₃ + HNO₂
steps: Burning fossil fuels releases SO₂ into the air.
SO₂ can be changed into SO₃ in the atmosphere.
SO₃ reacts with water to form H₂SO₄.
NO₂ reacts with water to form HNO₃ and HNO₂.
The acids can reach the ground in rain, hail, snow or fog.
notes.checkQuestion: Which acids form when SO₃ and NO₂ react with water?
notes.checkAnswer: H₂SO₄, HNO₃ and HNO₂.

notes.title: Global Warming (Greenhouse Effect)
notes.answer: A higher concentration of greenhouse gases absorbs more thermal radiation, causing a greater increase in global warming.
notes.explanation: Greenhouse gases let most incoming short-wave sunlight reach Earth’s surface. The warmed surface gives out long-wave radiation, which these gases absorb. This slows the loss of heat to space and raises Earth’s temperature. For example, more CO₂ in the atmosphere increases heat absorption; melting ice and rising sea levels are possible effects of warming.
notes.simple: Sunlight warms Earth. Earth gives off heat, but greenhouse gases trap some of that heat, so Earth warms further.
examples: Example: burning coal, oil and natural gas adds greenhouse gases to the atmosphere.
Example: melting ice in Antarctica and Greenland adds water to the seas and contributes to rising sea levels.
steps: Sunlight passes through greenhouse gases and warms Earth’s surface.
The warmed surface gives out long-wave radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb much of this radiation, so less heat escapes to space.
The temperature of Earth rises; this is global warming.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does a higher concentration of greenhouse gases increase global warming?
notes.checkAnswer: Greenhouse gases absorb some long-wave radiation from Earth and slow the escape of heat to space.

notes.title: Strategies to reduce environmental issues
notes.answer: A catalytic converter reduces harmful emissions from an automobile engine by changing them into less harmful substances.
notes.explanation: Environmental problems can be reduced by lowering pollution at its source and protecting people from polluted air. Planting trees, using catalytic converters, removing sulphur dioxide from flue gas and switching to renewable energy are important strategies. When air quality is poor, people—especially high-risk groups—should reduce outdoor exposure and follow safety advice.
notes.simple: Make less pollution, use cleaner energy, and avoid breathing polluted air.
examples: A catalytic converter changes harmful carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide.
Solar and wind energy can generate electricity without burning fossil fuels.
steps: Plant trees: they absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and trap some particulate matter on their surfaces.
Use catalytic converters: they change nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons into less harmful substances.
Reduce sulphur dioxide: use fuels with less sulphur or remove sulphur dioxide from flue gas using an adsorbent such as calcium oxide.
Use renewable resources such as sunlight, wind, water, geothermal energy and biomass.
When air quality is poor, limit outdoor activity, use a well-fitted N95 mask if going out, keep indoor air clean and seek medical advice for worrying symptoms.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one strategy that can reduce harmful emissions from automobiles.
notes.checkAnswer: Planting trees, using catalytic converters, reducing sulphur dioxide from flue gas and using renewable energy can help reduce environmental issues.

notes.title: Environmental chemistry: air pollution and its effects
notes.answer: Sulphur dioxide is one pollutant gas that can contribute to acid rain.
notes.explanation: Environmental chemistry studies how human activities and natural processes affect the environment. Air pollutants can harm health, plants, animals and climate. Pollution can be reduced by cleaner energy, responsible choices and environmental protection.
notes.simple: Some gases and particles in the air harm living things. Understanding their sources and effects helps us protect people and the environment.
examples: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous pollutant produced by incomplete fuel combustion.
Sulphur and nitrogen oxides can react with water in the atmosphere to form acid rain.
steps: Identify the pollutant and its source.
Explain how it affects people, plants, animals or climate.
Give a practical way to reduce it.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one pollutant gas that can contribute to acid rain.
notes.checkAnswer: Examples include carbon monoxide, sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides.

notes.title: Hydrocarbons: carbon and hydrogen
notes.answer: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.
notes.explanation: Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only. Carbon can form strong covalent bonds with itself, so it can make long chains, branched chains and rings. Many fuels are hydrocarbons, and they are also used to make other useful compounds.
notes.simple: A hydrocarbon is a compound made only from carbon and hydrogen atoms.
examples: Natural gas is a fuel made mainly of hydrocarbons.
Methane is the simplest alkane and has the formula CH₄.
steps: Check which elements are present in the compound.
If it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it is a hydrocarbon.
Remember that carbon can join to other carbon atoms to form chains and rings.
notes.checkQuestion: What are hydrocarbons?
notes.checkAnswer: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.

notes.title: Alkanes and their names
notes.answer: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen single bonds; their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
notes.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single bonds between carbon atoms. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. To name a branched alkane, find the longest carbon chain, number it from the end nearest the branch, then give the branch its prefix and position number.
notes.simple: Alkanes have only single bonds. Their names tell you the length of the main carbon chain and the names and positions of any branches.
examples: CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃ is 2-methylbutane.
CH₃—C(CH₃)₂—CH₂—CH₃ is 2,2-dimethylbutane.
steps: Find the longest continuous carbon chain.
Number the chain from the end closest to a branch.
Name each branch and give its position number.
Use the root for the longest chain and add the suffix -ane.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃?
notes.checkAnswer: 2-methylbutane

notes.title: Preparation of Alkanes
notes.answer: Alkanes are prepared by cracking higher hydrocarbons, reducing alkenes or alkynes with hydrogen, or reducing alkyl halides with hydrogen generated using Zn/HCl.
notes.explanation: Alkanes can be prepared by cracking larger hydrocarbons, adding hydrogen to alkenes or alkynes, or reducing alkyl halides.
notes.simple: There are three methods in this section: break large hydrocarbons into smaller ones, add hydrogen to an unsaturated hydrocarbon, or replace the halogen in an alkyl halide with hydrogen.
examples: Ethene + hydrogen → ethane, using nickel at 200°C.
Chloromethane + [2H] → methane + hydrogen chloride.
steps: For cracking, heat naphtha to around 500°C with zeolite.
For hydrogenation, add hydrogen to an alkene or alkyne with nickel as catalyst at 200°C.
For reduction of an alkyl halide, use hydrogen produced by zinc reacting with hydrochloric acid.
notes.checkQuestion: How can an alkene be changed into an alkane?
notes.checkAnswer: Add hydrogen to the alkene or alkyne in the presence of nickel at 200°C.

notes.title: Important Reactions of Alkanes
notes.answer: The two important reactions are halogenation (substitution) and combustion.
notes.explanation: Alkanes are mostly unreactive, but your textbook describes two important reactions: halogenation and combustion. Halogenation replaces hydrogen atoms with halogen atoms in UV light. Combustion burns an alkane in oxygen to form carbon dioxide, water and heat.
notes.simple: Alkanes do not react easily, but they can react with chlorine in UV light or burn in oxygen.
examples: CH₄ + Cl₂  hν→ CH₃—Cl + H—Cl
CH₄ (g) + 2O₂ (g) → CO₂ (g) + 2H₂O (g) + heat
steps: In halogenation, a halogen replaces a hydrogen atom in an alkane.
UV light is used, so this is called photochemical substitution.
In combustion, an alkane reacts with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O, releasing heat.
Methane reacts with chlorine to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the two important reactions of alkanes described in this section?
notes.checkAnswer: Combustion forms carbon dioxide and water, and releases heat.

notes.title: Hydrocarbons and alkanes
notes.answer: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes have carbon–carbon single bonds and undergo combustion, substitution and cracking reactions.
notes.explanation: Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with single bonds between their carbon atoms. Their reactions and physical properties depend on their structure and size.
notes.simple: Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only. When they burn completely, they produce carbon dioxide, water and heat.
examples: Methane (CH₄) is the main component of natural gas.
Complete combustion of propane produces carbon dioxide and water.
steps: Identify the type of hydrocarbon and its structure.
For combustion, write the hydrocarbon reacting with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
Balance the equation by balancing carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen.
For comparisons, consider molecular size and whether the molecules are straight-chain or branched.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
notes.checkAnswer: A mixture of natural gas and air can explode when ignited because the gas burns rapidly in oxygen and releases heat.

notes.title: SI Units in Chemistry
notes.answer: SI units are standard units that make scientific measurements easier to communicate, compare and use. The five base units used in chemistry are metre (m), second (s), mole (mol), kilogram (kg) and kelvin (K).
notes.explanation: SI units are standard units used around the world. In chemistry, they help scientists share and compare measurements clearly. Smaller units such as grams and cubic centimetres are practical for the small amounts often measured in a laboratory.
notes.simple: Scientists use the same measuring units so they can understand one another's results. In chemistry, grams and cm³ are handy for small amounts.
examples: A mass of a small laboratory sample is usually easier to write in grams than in kilograms.
A small liquid volume is usually easier to measure in cm³ than in m³.
steps: Identify the quantity being measured.
Choose its SI unit: for example, mass uses kilogram (kg) and time uses second (s).
Use a suitable prefix or smaller unit when it makes a laboratory measurement more manageable.
Write the unit symbol correctly; symbols do not change in the plural form.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the SI unit of amount of substance and its symbol.
notes.checkAnswer: The five SI base units used in chemistry are metre (m), second (s), mole (mol), kilogram (kg) and kelvin (K).

notes.title: Systematic and random errors
notes.answer: Systematic error affects accuracy; random error causes measurements to differ slightly and often determines precision.
notes.explanation: A systematic error shifts measurements in a consistent way and affects accuracy. A random error makes repeated measurements differ slightly and often affects precision. Systematic errors can be corrected by applying a constant adjustment.
notes.simple: Systematic error is a consistent measurement shift. Random error is a small, unpredictable change between measurements.
examples: If a measuring cylinder delivers slightly more liquid than its scale indicates each time, it has a systematic error.
If a student reads a measuring cylinder from a different angle each time, the readings may vary because of random error.
steps: Check whether the measurements are shifted consistently or vary unpredictably.
A consistent shift suggests a systematic error; changing results suggest a random error.
For a systematic error, apply the constant adjustment given to each measurement.
notes.checkQuestion: A student reads a measuring cylinder from a different angle each time. What type of error may this cause, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: It is a random error because the reading changes when the student views the cylinder from different angles.

notes.title: Accuracy and Precision
notes.answer: They are precise but not accurate.
notes.explanation: Accuracy tells how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision tells how close repeated measurements are to one another. A result can be precise without being accurate, or accurate without being precise.
notes.simple: Accuracy means close to the true value. Precision means repeated results are close to each other.
examples: True value: 5.0 g; repeated readings: 5.2 g, 5.2 g, 5.2 g. These readings are precise but not accurate.
True value: 20 g; readings: 19.8 g, 20.5 g, 19.6 g. These readings are more accurate overall but not precise.
steps: Find the true or known value.
Check whether each reading is close to that true value. This tells you about accuracy.
Compare the readings with one another. If they are close together, they are precise.
State accuracy and precision separately.
notes.checkQuestion: A true mass is 10 g. A student gets 11.2 g every time. Are the readings precise, accurate, both, or neither?
notes.checkAnswer: The readings are precise but not accurate.

notes.title: Measuring consistently with SI units
notes.answer: Use SI units and check measurements for both accuracy and precision.
notes.explanation: SI units give people a shared, decimal-based way to record measurements. Good measurements should be both accurate (close to the true value) and precise (consistent when repeated). Systematic errors shift measurements in a regular way; random errors cause unpredictable variation.
notes.simple: Use the same standard units so measurements can be compared. Check both whether a result is close to the true value and whether repeated results agree.
examples: A length of 2 metres can be written as 200 centimetres using a decimal conversion.
If repeated readings are close together but far from the true value, they are precise but inaccurate.
steps: Choose the appropriate standard unit for the quantity.
Record the measurement with its unit.
Repeat measurements when needed and compare the results.
Check for systematic causes, such as an incorrectly calibrated instrument.
Use suitable SI prefixes or derived units when they make the measurement clearer.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of error causes readings to be consistently too high or consistently too low?
notes.checkAnswer: Systematic error

notes.title: Staying safe around chemical hazards
notes.answer: Use the precautions that match the chemical hazard. For example, use a fume hood for corrosive vapours and add acid slowly to water when diluting concentrated acid.
notes.explanation: Chemical hazards can injure people or damage property. Recognize the hazard, follow the safety instructions, use suitable protective equipment, and get help from the teacher or trained staff when needed.
notes.simple: A hazard is something that can cause harm. Know what kind of harm a chemical may cause and take the right precautions.
examples: A corrosive acid can attack skin and eyes.
A gas such as carbon monoxide can cause suffocation.
steps: Identify the chemical hazard before starting work.
Follow the teacher's instructions and use the smallest required quantity.
Wear protective equipment suitable for the hazard.
Use a fume hood for hazardous vapours when instructed.
Dispose of waste according to the safety instructions.
notes.checkQuestion: When diluting concentrated acid, which substance is added slowly to the other?
notes.checkAnswer: Add acid slowly to water, never water to acid.

notes.title: Understanding Hazard Signs
notes.answer: Hazard signs warn people about dangers and indicate the precautions they must follow.
notes.explanation: Hazard signs tell people about dangers or safety rules in a particular area or on a chemical bottle. They help people notice the hazard and take the right precautions.
notes.simple: A hazard sign is a warning picture or message. It tells you what danger to look out for and how to behave safely.
examples: A flame with “Highly flammable” warns that the material can catch fire easily.
A corrosive symbol warns that contact with the material can destroy living tissue.
steps: Look at the symbol and read the words on the sign.
Identify the danger or instruction it shows.
Take the required precaution and follow any safety instructions.
notes.checkQuestion: What danger does a sign marked “Risk of asphyxiation” warn about?
notes.checkAnswer: The sign warns that the material may cause suffocation or asphyxiation.

notes.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
notes.answer: Examples include a lab coat and protective glasses.
notes.explanation: Personal protective equipment (PPE) helps students face emergencies in the laboratory and reduces exposure to hazardous chemicals. Your textbook lists lab coats, protective glasses, face shields, aprons, boots and hearing protection as PPE.
notes.simple: PPE is protective clothing or equipment used in the lab to help keep students safe.
examples: Protective glasses are an example of PPE.
A lab coat is another example of PPE.
steps: Recognise situations in which protective equipment may be needed.
Make suitable PPE available to students.
Use items such as lab coats and protective glasses to help reduce exposure to hazards.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two items of PPE listed in your textbook.
notes.checkAnswer: PPE helps students face emergencies and reduces exposure to hazardous chemicals.

notes.title: Fire Extinguishers and Emergency Drills
notes.answer: Students should know the location of the fire extinguisher and safety shower and learn how to use them. Emergency drills help them practise responding to an emergency without panic.
notes.explanation: A fire extinguisher and safety shower help people respond to emergencies in a laboratory. Students should know where they are and should be trained before using emergency equipment.
notes.simple: Know where the emergency equipment is. Practise what to do before an emergency happens.
steps: Know where the portable fire extinguisher is kept.
Learn how to handle and apply it during a training session.
Know where the safety shower is and how it works.
Follow the laboratory's emergency instructions calmly.
notes.checkQuestion: Why should students take part in emergency drills?
notes.checkAnswer: Emergency drills should be compulsory so students practise responding calmly and safely.

notes.title: Handling a Laboratory Emergency
notes.answer: Stay calm, alert people to evacuate, follow the correct fire or chemical safety procedure, and call emergency staff.
notes.explanation: In a laboratory emergency, stay calm, warn people to evacuate, and follow the correct safety steps. For a fire, close doors to confine it and use a fire extinguisher if it is safe to do so. Call and assist emergency staff.
notes.simple: Stay calm. Warn people. Get everyone to safety. Follow the right procedure and call for help.
examples: For a fire: alert people, evacuate, close doors to confine the fire, use a fire extinguisher if safe, and call emergency staff.
For a chemical emergency: follow the safety procedures for that chemical and call emergency staff.
steps: Stay calm and do not panic.
Alert people in the area to evacuate.
In case of fire, close doors to confine fire. Use fire extinguisher to put down the fire.
In case of chemical emergency adopt safety procedures as mentioned in article 13.1.
Call and assist emergency staff.
notes.checkQuestion: Name two actions to take during a laboratory emergency.
notes.checkAnswer: Stay calm, alert people to evacuate, close doors to confine the fire, use a fire extinguisher if safe, and call emergency staff.

notes.title: Laboratory safety and hazards
notes.answer: Always add acid to water.
notes.explanation: Laboratory safety is a shared responsibility. Learn the warning signs, follow instructions, use protective equipment, and know what to do in an emergency. Keep chemicals labelled and handle hazardous substances only as instructed.
notes.simple: Be careful with chemicals, read their labels, and know how to respond to danger.
examples: Add acid to water, never water to acid.
Carry out reactions that produce harmful gases in a fume cupboard.
steps: Read labels and warning signs before handling chemicals.
Follow safety instructions and wear suitable protective equipment.
Keep flames, sparks, and sudden shocks away from hazardous chemicals.
Use a fume cupboard for reactions that may release harmful gases.
In an emergency, alert others, follow the emergency plan, and get help.
notes.checkQuestion: When diluting an acid, which should be added to which?
notes.checkAnswer: Add acid to water; never add water to acid.

quiz.stem: How is a single covalent bond formed?
options: The atoms share an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms
One atom transfers a proton to another
The atoms attract because they have opposite ionic charges
One atom donates both electrons in a shared pair
rationales: Correct: a single covalent bond is formed by mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms.
Incorrect: proton transfer is not how the section defines a covalent bond.
Incorrect: attraction between oppositely charged ions is the basis of an ionic bond.
Incorrect: donation of both shared electrons by one atom describes a coordinate covalent bond.

quiz.stem: Which structural formula represents a double covalent bond?
rationales: Incorrect: H—H has one line and represents a single covalent bond.
Correct: O=O has two lines and represents a double covalent bond.
Incorrect: N≡N has three lines and represents a triple covalent bond.
Incorrect: Na⁺Cl⁻ represents oppositely charged ions, not a double covalent bond.

quiz.stem: What happens to the shared electron pair in a polar covalent bond?
options: The shared pair lies midway between the atoms
The shared pair bends towards the more electronegative atom
Electrons are completely transferred to the less electronegative atom
The shared pair is donated by a third atom
rationales: Incorrect: a pair midway between identical atoms gives a non-polar covalent bond.
Correct: in a bond between non-identical atoms, the shared pair bends towards the more electronegative atom.
Incorrect: the section describes a shared pair bending towards the more electronegative atom, not complete transfer to the less electronegative atom.
Incorrect: a coordinate covalent bond involves donation by one of the bonded species, not a third atom.

quiz.stem: In a coordinate covalent bond, what is the name for the species that donates the electron pair?
options: The atom with the greatest number of shells
The ion that loses a proton
rationales: Correct: the species which donates the electron pair is called the donor.
Incorrect: the species that accepts the electron pair is called the acceptor.
Incorrect: number of shells does not define the donor.
Incorrect: proton loss does not define the donor in a coordinate covalent bond.

quiz.stem: In which direction does the arrow point when representing a coordinate covalent bond?
options: An arrow pointing towards the donor
An arrow pointing towards the acceptor
A plus sign between the bonded atoms
rationales: Incorrect: the arrow points away from the donor and towards the acceptor.
Correct: the arrow head points towards the acceptor.
Incorrect: two parallel lines represent a double covalent bond.
Incorrect: a plus sign is not the section's symbol for a coordinate covalent bond.

quiz.stem: Which ions form when an electron transfers from sodium to chlorine?
rationales: Correct: sodium loses an electron to become Na⁺, and chlorine gains it to become Cl⁻.
Incorrect: these are the uncharged atoms before electron transfer.
Incorrect: the charges are reversed; sodium loses an electron and chlorine gains one.
Incorrect: each atom transfers or gains one electron in this example, not two.

quiz.stem: Which feature of metallic bonding helps metals conduct electricity?
options: Mobile electrons move through the metal
The metal atoms form separate molecules
The metal ions remain fixed in one place with no electrons
The metal becomes a solution in water
rationales: This is correct because mobile electrons can move through the metal and carry charge.
This is wrong because metallic solids are not made of separate molecules in this section's model.
This is wrong because mobile electrons are present and are not all fixed in place.
This is wrong because dissolving in water is not the reason metals conduct electricity.

quiz.stem: Why is the metallic bond in sodium described as not very strong?
options: Each sodium atom releases one electron
Each sodium atom releases two electrons
Sodium atoms gain electrons from magnesium
rationales: This is correct because each sodium atom sets free only one electron.
This is wrong because the section says each sodium atom releases only one electron.
This is wrong because the section does not describe sodium bonding by gaining electrons from magnesium.
This is wrong because sodium does have mobile electrons in the metallic-bond model.

quiz.stem: Why is magnesium's metallic bond stronger than sodium's?
options: Magnesium releases two electrons per atom
Magnesium has fewer positive charges than sodium
rationales: This is correct because each magnesium atom releases two electrons and becomes a two-positive ion.
This is wrong because magnesium releases two electrons according to the section.
This is wrong because the section explains magnesium using metallic bonding, not covalent molecules.
This is wrong because magnesium has two positive charges per ion, compared with sodium's one.

quiz.stem: What happens when pressure changes the shape of a metal?
options: The upper rows of atoms can slip past the lower rows
Metal atoms break into separate molecules
The mobile electrons become positively charged
The metal loses all its positive ions
rationales: This is correct because the section explains that upper rows of atoms slip past lower rows under pressure.
This is wrong because the section does not describe metals as separate molecules.
This is wrong because the electrons do not become positively charged.
This is wrong because the metal's positive ions remain present.

quiz.stem: Which feature of a metal helps it conduct heat?
options: Mobile electrons are present in the metal
The metal contains only covalent bonds
The metal has no particles that can move
Metal atoms are arranged as individual gas particles
rationales: This is correct because freely moving electrons help metals conduct heat.
This is wrong because the section explains this property using mobile electrons in metallic bonding.
This is wrong because electrons are able to move through the metal.
This is wrong because the section describes metal atoms arranged in rows, not as gas particles.

quiz.stem: According to the section, why are metals usually hard and heavy?
options: They are strongly held and arranged in rows
rationales: This is correct because the atoms are strongly held and arranged in rows one above the other.
This is wrong because positive ions are part of the metallic-bond model.
This is wrong because the section describes closely arranged rows of atoms.
This is wrong because the section says electrons move freely in metals.

quiz.stem: What does it mean if a metal is highly electropositive?
rationales: Correct: highly electropositive metals lose electrons easily.
Incorrect: gaining electrons is not the property described for metals in this section.
Incorrect: sharing electrons does not define electropositive character.
Incorrect: metals can form positive ions by losing electrons.

quiz.stem: What positive ions form when metals lose electrons?
rationales: Correct: positive ions formed by losing electrons are called cations.
Incorrect: anions are negative ions, not positive ions.
Incorrect: an atom that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
Incorrect: the section names these positive ions cations.

quiz.stem: Which of these is identified in the section as an alkali metal that is highly electropositive?
rationales: Correct: sodium is named as a highly electropositive alkali metal.
Incorrect: magnesium is an alkaline earth metal and is less electropositive than alkali metals.
Incorrect: calcium is an alkaline earth metal and is less electropositive than alkali metals.
Incorrect: aluminium is highly electropositive, but it is not an alkali metal.

quiz.stem: Why are alkaline earth metals such as magnesium and calcium less electropositive than alkali metals?
options: They lose their outer electrons less easily
rationales: Correct: the section says they lose their outer electrons less easily.
Incorrect: the section compares how easily they lose electrons, not how easily they gain them.
Incorrect: the section says their reactions towards water are less vigorous, not that they cannot react.
Incorrect: magnesium and calcium are metals.

quiz.stem: According to the section, why do sodium and potassium react very easily?
options: They are highly electropositive and lose electrons easily
They gain electrons to form negative ions
They are less reactive than alkaline earth metals
They do not react with halogens
rationales: Correct: they are highly electropositive and lose electrons easily.
Incorrect: the section describes these metals as losing electrons, not gaining them.
Incorrect: the section describes alkali metals as highly reactive compared with alkaline earth metals.
Incorrect: the section says they react with halogens.

quiz.stem: Which statement about aluminium agrees with the section?
options: It reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen
It is an alkaline earth metal
It gains electrons easily to form anions
rationales: Correct: the section says aluminium reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen.
Incorrect: aluminium is not identified as an alkaline earth metal.
Incorrect: the section specifically describes its reaction with mineral acids.
Incorrect: aluminium is described as a highly electropositive metal, not as forming anions by gaining electrons.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the electron behaviour of non-metals?
options: They do not take part in chemical reactions.
rationales: Correct: non-metals have an affinity towards electrons and tend to gain them.
Incorrect: losing electrons is the behaviour associated with metals in this section.
Incorrect: the section states that non-metals react with metals and with other non-metals.
Incorrect: gaining electrons forms negatively charged ions, not positive ions.

quiz.stem: What are negatively charged ions formed by non-metals called?
rationales: Incorrect: cations are positively charged ions.
Correct: non-metals gain electrons and become negatively charged ions called anions.
Incorrect: molecules are groups of atoms, not the name for these negatively charged ions.
Incorrect: isotopes are forms of an element with different numbers of neutrons.

quiz.stem: Which element is the most electronegative in the periodic table, according to this section?
rationales: Incorrect: oxygen follows fluorine in the order given in the section.
Incorrect: nitrogen follows oxygen in the order given in the section.
Correct: the section identifies fluorine as the most electronegative element.
Incorrect: chlorine follows nitrogen in the order given in the section.

quiz.stem: Which list gives the order of electronegativity stated in the section, from highest to lower?
rationales: Correct: this is the sequence given in the section after identifying fluorine as the most electronegative.
Incorrect: oxygen is placed before fluorine, reversing the first two elements.
Incorrect: this sequence does not follow the order stated in the section.
Incorrect: this list reverses the stated order.

quiz.stem: According to this section, which pair readily reacts to form an ionic bond?
options: A metal and a noble gas
rationales: Correct: the section says non-metals readily react with metals forming ionic bonds.
Incorrect: the section does not state that two metals form ionic bonds.
Incorrect: the section says non-metals combine with other non-metals to form molecular substances.
Incorrect: this pair is not identified in the section as forming an ionic bond.

quiz.stem: What can happen when non-metals combine with other non-metals?
options: They form a wide variety of molecular substances.
They cannot combine with one another.
rationales: Correct: non-metals combine with other non-metals to form a wide variety of molecular substances.
Incorrect: the section does not say that non-metals always form ionic bonds with one another.
Incorrect: non-metals tend to gain electrons and become negatively charged ions.
Incorrect: the section specifically says that non-metals combine with other non-metals.

quiz.stem: Which description best fits an ionic compound?
options: It has a crystalline arrangement of oppositely charged ions.
It consists only of neutral molecules.
It has no forces of attraction between its particles.
It is made only of non-metals.
rationales: Correct: Ionic compounds have oppositely charged ions arranged in a crystalline structure.
This describes many covalent compounds, not ionic compounds.
Ionic compounds have strong electrostatic forces of attraction between their ions.
Ionic compounds are generally formed from metals and non-metals, not only non-metals.

quiz.stem: Why can molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: The ions are free to move.
The compound becomes a non-polar solvent.
rationales: The ions remain ions when molten; they do not become neutral molecules.
Correct: In the molten state, ions can move and carry electric charge.
Melting sodium chloride does not turn it into a solvent.
The key reason for conductivity is that ions can move, not that attraction becomes stronger.

quiz.stem: Which feature helps explain why ionic compounds usually have high melting points?
options: They have strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.
They consist of low molecular mass molecules.
rationales: Correct: Strong attraction between oppositely charged ions takes considerable energy to overcome.
Freely moving electrons are not the reason for the high melting points of ionic compounds.
Low molecular mass molecules are associated with many covalent substances, not ionic lattices.
Solubility in non-polar solvents is not the reason ionic compounds have high melting points.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the usual solubility of covalent compounds?
options: They are usually soluble in non-polar solvents.
They are usually insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar solvents.
They always conduct electricity in solid form.
They always have higher melting points than ionic compounds.
rationales: This reverses the usual pattern stated for covalent compounds.
Correct: Covalent compounds are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents.
Covalent compounds are usually bad conductors of electricity.
Covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the particles in most covalent compounds?
options: They have free ions in the solid state.
They mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules.
They have crystalline structures made of oppositely charged ions.
rationales: Free ions are characteristic of ionic compounds, not most covalent compounds.
Covalent compounds mostly consist of neutral molecules.
Correct: Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules.
This describes the arrangement in ionic compounds.

quiz.stem: In which situation are the ions of an ionic compound usually free to conduct electricity?
options: An ionic compound dissolved in water.
A covalent compound in solid form.
A covalent compound in a non-polar solvent.
rationales: In a solid ionic compound, the ions are held in fixed positions in the crystal.
Correct: In solution, the ions can move and carry electric charge.
Covalent compounds are usually bad conductors of electricity.
A covalent compound in a non-polar solvent does not provide the free ions needed for ionic conduction.

quiz.stem: What is the usual physical state of lower molecular mass covalent compounds?
options: They are generally gases or low-boiling liquids.
They have strong attractions between oppositely charged ions.
They are always good conductors of electricity.
rationales: Correct: Lower molecular mass covalent compounds are gases or low-boiling liquids.
The section says high molecular mass covalent compounds may exist as solids, not that all covalent compounds are solids.
Strong attraction between oppositely charged ions describes ionic compounds.
Covalent compounds are usually bad conductors of electricity.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly explains the electrical conductivity of ionic compounds?
options: They are usually good conductors because their ions can move when molten or in solution.
They conduct only because their molecules are neutral.
They conduct because they dissolve in every solvent.
They conduct because they have low melting points.
rationales: Correct: Molten or dissolved ionic compounds have free ions that can carry charge.
Neutral molecules do not explain the electrical conductivity of ionic compounds.
Ionic compounds are generally soluble in polar solvents, not every solvent.
Ionic compounds usually have high melting points, and low melting points do not explain their conductivity.

quiz.stem: Why does water have a relatively high boiling point compared with many small molecules?
options: The H₂O molecules have strong hydrogen bonds between them.
The H₂O molecules have ionic bonds between them.
Water molecules have no attractive forces between them.
The covalent O—H bonds break when water boils.
rationales: Correct: strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules require considerable energy to overcome.
Incorrect: water consists of covalent molecules, not ions held together by ionic bonds.
Incorrect: water molecules do attract each other, particularly through hydrogen bonding.
Incorrect: boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions; it does not normally break the O—H covalent bonds.

quiz.stem: What attraction occurs between the partially positive end of one HCl molecule and the partially negative end of another?
rationales: Correct: oppositely charged ends of polar molecules attract by dipole-dipole forces.
Incorrect: HCl molecules are not ions joined by ionic bonds.
Incorrect: HCl is not a metal and does not have metallic bonding.
Incorrect: covalent bonds join atoms within an HCl molecule, not separate HCl molecules.

quiz.stem: In which molecule is hydrogen bonding expected between the molecules?
rationales: Correct: hydrogen is covalently bonded to highly electronegative fluorine, so hydrogen bonding can occur between HF molecules.
Incorrect: chlorine is not one of the elements F, O or N specified for hydrogen bonding in this section.
Incorrect: bromine is not one of the elements F, O or N specified for hydrogen bonding in this section.
Incorrect: iodine is not one of the elements F, O or N specified for hydrogen bonding in this section.

quiz.stem: If the intermolecular forces between molecules of a liquid become stronger, what generally happens to its boiling point?
options: The same boiling point in every case
rationales: Correct: stronger attractions require more energy to overcome, so the boiling point is higher.
Incorrect: stronger attractions do not make it easier for molecules to separate.
Incorrect: a liquid has a boiling point under a given pressure.
Incorrect: boiling point depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces and is not always the same.

quiz.stem: Among the three states of matter, where does this section say intermolecular forces are weakest?
rationales: Correct: the section states that these forces are weakest among molecules of gases.
Incorrect: the section places liquid molecules between gases and solids in relative force strength.
Incorrect: the section states that intermolecular forces are strongest among molecules of solids.
Incorrect: this option refers to bonding within molecules, not forces between molecules in the three states.

quiz.stem: Why do water molecules form strong hydrogen-bond attractions with one another?
options: A larger difference in electronegativity makes the O—H bond highly polar.
Oxygen and hydrogen have equal electronegativity.
The water molecules are held together by ionic bonds.
The O—H covalent bonds are broken whenever water molecules attract.
rationales: Correct: the large electronegativity difference makes the O—H bonds highly polar, allowing strong attractions between molecules.
Incorrect: the section says the difference in electronegativity makes the O—H bond highly polar.
Incorrect: water consists of covalent molecules, not molecules joined to one another by ionic bonds.
Incorrect: hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules; it does not require breaking the O—H covalent bonds.

quiz.stem: Why do solid ionic compounds not conduct electricity?
options: The ions are fixed in position.
The ions have no electrical charge.
The crystal lattice contains mobile electrons.
The ions are too small to conduct.
rationales: Correct: the ions are tightly held in the solid and cannot move to carry charge.
Incorrect: ions are charged particles; this is not why the solid fails to conduct.
Incorrect: mobile electrons are not the reason solid ionic compounds fail to conduct.
Incorrect: ion size is not the cause; the ions cannot move in the solid.

quiz.stem: Why can molten ionic compounds conduct electricity?
options: The compound becomes a covalent molecule.
rationales: Incorrect: melting does not make the ions neutral.
Correct: in the molten state, ions are free to move and carry charge.
Incorrect: melting does not change the compound's ionic bonding into covalent bonding.
Incorrect: an increase in ion size is not the reason for conductivity.

quiz.stem: What is the orderly arrangement of oppositely charged ions in an ionic solid called?
rationales: Correct: the orderly arrangement of ions is called a crystal lattice.
Incorrect: the section identifies the arrangement as a crystal lattice, not a molecular chain.
Incorrect: ions in a solid lattice are held in place rather than forming a layer of mobile ions.
Incorrect: the lattice consists of ions, not a gas of neutral atoms.

quiz.stem: Why can graphite be used as a lubricant?
options: The layers can slip past each other.
Its carbon atoms form isolated molecules.
It has a very high proportion of water.
rationales: Correct: graphite's layers are not strongly bonded, so they can slip past each other.
Incorrect: graphite is described as a layered structure made of hexagonal rings, not isolated molecules.
Incorrect: water is not the reason graphite acts as a lubricant.
Incorrect: graphite is a covalent form of carbon, not a layered ionic solid.

quiz.stem: According to the section, why does water have a high boiling point?
options: Its molecules have strong intermolecular forces.
Its molecules are much larger than those of H₂S.
rationales: Correct: the section states that strong intermolecular forces are present between water molecules.
Incorrect: water is described as a covalent molecule, not an ionic compound.
Incorrect: the stated explanation is the strong intermolecular forces, not molecular size.
Incorrect: water molecules do have intermolecular forces, and these are described as strong.

quiz.stem: What happens to ions during hydration?
options: The water molecules surround and interact with the ions.
The ions turn into covalent molecules.
The water removes the charges from the ions.
The ions become fixed in a crystal lattice.
rationales: Correct: hydration is the process in which water molecules surround and interact with ions or molecules.
Incorrect: hydration does not turn ions into covalent molecules.
Incorrect: the section does not say that water removes the ions' charges.
Incorrect: hydration surrounds free ions in solution; it does not fix them in a lattice.

quiz.stem: Which crystalline form of carbon has mobile electrons between its layers?
rationales: Incorrect: diamond has a rigid structure of carbon atoms linked by strong covalent bonds.
Incorrect: coal is described as the amorphous form of carbon.
Correct: graphite has mobile electrons between its layers and conducts electricity.
Incorrect: sulphur is not a form of carbon.

quiz.stem: How many atoms are present in one gram of H₂O?
rationales: One gram of water is 1/18 mole of molecules, and each molecule has three atoms, giving about 1.002 × 10²³ atoms.
This is approximately the number of water molecules in one gram, not the number of atoms.
This is about one-third of the correct atom count because it does not account for all three atoms in each molecule.
This is about twice the correct atom count and does not follow from the molar mass and three atoms per molecule.

quiz.stem: Which is the correct formula of calcium phosphide?
rationales: CaP does not balance the charges of Ca²⁺ and P³⁻ ions.
CaP₂ does not balance the charges of Ca²⁺ and P³⁻ ions.
Ca₂P₃ has a net charge rather than the neutral ratio required for the compound.
Three Ca²⁺ ions and two P³⁻ ions balance to form neutral Ca₃P₂.

quiz.stem: How many atomic mass units (amu) are there in one gram?
rationales: One gram contains vastly more than one atomic mass unit.
This is far fewer than the number of atomic mass units in one gram.
Since one atomic mass unit is about 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁴ g, one gram contains about 6.022 × 10²³ amu.
This is one-tenth of the correct number of atomic mass units in one gram.

quiz.stem: Structural formula of 2-hexene is CH₃ – CH = CH – (CH₂)₂ – CH₃. What will be its empirical formula?
rationales: C₂H₂ does not give the simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen in C₆H₁₂.
CH has a 1:1 carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, unlike the 1:2 ratio in C₆H₁₂.
C₆H₁₂ is the molecular formula, not the simplest empirical formula.
Dividing the subscripts in C₆H₁₂ by six gives the empirical formula CH₂.

quiz.stem: How many moles are there in 25 g of H₂SO₄?
rationales: 0.765 moles is too many for 25 g of a substance with a molar mass of about 98 g/mol.
0.51 moles is about twice the amount calculated from 25 g and the molar mass of H₂SO₄.
The amount is 25 g ÷ 98 g/mol, which is approximately 0.255 moles.
0.4 moles would require substantially more than 25 g of H₂SO₄.

quiz.stem: A necklace has 6g of diamonds in it. What are the number of carbon atoms in it?
rationales: 6.02 × 10²³ atoms is the number of carbon atoms in one mole, or 12 g, of carbon.
12.04 × 10²³ atoms is twice the amount present in 6 g of carbon.
1.003 × 10²³ is too small because 6 g of carbon is half a mole, not one-sixth of a mole.
Six grams of carbon is 0.5 mole, containing about 3.01 × 10²³ atoms.

quiz.stem: What is the mass of Al in 204g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.
rationales: 26 g is not the aluminum mass fraction of Al₂O₃ applied to 204 g.
27 g is not the aluminum mass fraction of Al₂O₃ applied to 204 g.
54 g is the aluminum content of one mole of Al₂O₃, which has a mass of about 102 g, not 204 g.
Aluminum makes up 54/102 of Al₂O₃ by mass, so 204 g contains 108 g of aluminum.

quiz.stem: Which one of the following compounds will have the highest percentage of the mass of nitrogen?
rationales: Urea has 28 g of nitrogen in about 60 g of compound, a smaller percentage than hydrazine.
N₂H₄ has 28 g of nitrogen in about 32 g of compound, giving the highest nitrogen mass percentage among these choices.
NH₃ has 14 g of nitrogen in about 17 g of compound, a lower percentage than N₂H₄.
NH₂OH has 14 g of nitrogen in about 33 g of compound, a lower percentage than N₂H₄.

quiz.stem: When one mole of each of the following compounds is reacted with oxygen, which will produce the maximum amount of CO₂?
rationales: One mole of carbon atoms can produce one mole of CO₂, which is less than ethane produces.
Diamond is elemental carbon, so one mole of its carbon atoms produces one mole of CO₂.
Each ethane molecule contains two carbon atoms, so one mole of ethane can produce two moles of CO₂.
Each methane molecule contains one carbon atom, so one mole of methane produces one mole of CO₂.

quiz.stem: What mass of 95% CaCO₃ will be required to neutralize 50 cm³ of 0.5M HCl solution?
rationales: 9.5 g is much more CaCO₃ than needed to react with the stated amount of HCl.
1.25 g is the mass of pure CaCO₃ needed, but the sample is only 95% CaCO₃.
The reaction requires 0.0125 mol CaCO₃, or 1.25 g pure CaCO₃; allowing for 95% purity gives about 1.32 g of sample.
1.45 g exceeds the amount required after correcting the pure CaCO₃ mass for 95% purity.

quiz.stem: Which formula represents an element shown by its symbol alone?
rationales: Na represents sodium as an element shown by its symbol alone.
O₂ represents an element whose atoms are bonded in a molecule.
H₂O is a compound containing hydrogen and oxygen.
O₃ is a molecule of the element oxygen, not its symbol alone.

quiz.stem: How many oxygen atoms are in one molecule of O₂?
rationales: O₂ has a subscript 2, so it contains two oxygen atoms.
The subscript 2 means there are two oxygen atoms in one molecule.
Three oxygen atoms would be written O₃.
Four oxygen atoms would be written O₄.

quiz.stem: What does the molecular formula H₂O show about one molecule of water?
options: One hydrogen atom and one oxygen atom
Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom
One hydrogen atom and two oxygen atoms
Two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms
rationales: H₂ has a subscript 2, so water has two hydrogen atoms, not one.
H₂ means two hydrogen atoms and O with no subscript means one oxygen atom.
O has no subscript, so there is one oxygen atom, not two.
